**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 3, verses 1–2:**

**Surat Al 'Imran**

It is Madani, and its verses number two hundred.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif Lam Mim.﴾ ﴿Allah, there is no god but He.﴾ The widely transmitted reading vocalizes the *mim* with a fatha (*fath al-mim*). Its proper form would be to pause on it (*waqf*), placing the vowel of the hamza upon it (*ilqa' harakat al-hamza*), to indicate that it is treated as though it were pronounced in full, because the hamza was dropped for lightness (*li-l-takhfif*) and not in continuous recitation (*li-l-darj*). The *mim* is treated as in pause, as in the saying of the Arabs *wahidun ithnan* (*wahidun* and *ithnan*), with the vowel of the hamza placed on the *dal*. This is not for the sake of avoiding the meeting of two sukun (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*), since that is not objectionable in the case of pause. For this reason the *mim* was not vocalized before a *lam*. It has also been read with a kasra, by analogy with vocalizing it to avoid the meeting of two sukun. Abu Bakr read it with a sukun, beginning the next word after it, which is the original form.

﴿The Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾

It has been related that he, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "The Greatest Name of Allah is in three surahs: in al-Baqarah, *Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting*; in Al 'Imran, *Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting*; and in Ta-Ha, *and the faces will be humbled before the Living, the Self-Subsisting*."

Their derivation (ishtiqāq) is from *al-warā* (progeny) and *al-najl* (offspring). Measuring them by the patterns *tafʿilah* and *if'īl* is a forced exercise, because both are foreign words. This is supported by the fact that *al-Injīl* was recited with a fatḥah on the hamzah, and that is not among the patterns of Arabic. Nāfiʿ and Ḥamzah recited it between the two pronunciations, except that Qālūn recited it with a fatḥah like the rest of the readers.

﴿Before﴾, that is, before the sending down of the Qur'an. ﴿A guidance for the people﴾ in general, if we say that we are obligated to follow the law of those before us. Otherwise, what is meant is their own people.

﴿And He sent down the Criterion﴾. By this he means the class of divine books, since they all distinguish between truth and falsehood. He mentioned it after mentioning the three books so that it would include whatever else is in that category, as if he said: "And He sent down all that by which truth is distinguished from falsehood," or [it refers to] the Psalms or the Qur'an. He repeated mention of it with a description of it as praise, exaltation, and to display its excellence, in that it shares with them the quality of being a revealed inspiration, and it is distinguished by being a miracle that separates the one who is right from the one who is wrong. Or [it means] the miracles.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God﴾, that is, in His revealed books and other things. ﴿For them is a severe punishment﴾ because of their disbelief. ﴿And God is Mighty﴾, dominant, not prevented from punishing. ﴿Owner of retribution﴾, none can match Him in exacting retribution. *Niqmah* is the punishment of the criminal, and its verb is *naqama*, with fatḥah or kasrah in the vowel of the middle letter. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 5–6:

﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah.﴾ "Anything" (ay shay'): whatever exists in the world, whether universal or particular, whether faith or disbelief. He expressed this by "the heaven and the earth," since the senses do not extend beyond them. He mentioned the earth first, ascending from the lower to the higher (taraqqiyan min al-adna ila al-a'la), and because what is meant by the mention is what is committed upon it. This is like the evidence that He is living. And His saying: ﴿He is the One who forms you in the wombs however He wills.﴾ That is, from among the various forms. This is like the evidence for His being self-subsisting (al-qayyumiyya, the attribute of sustaining all things), and the inference that He is knowing from the perfection of His action in creating and shaping the embryo. It was also recited as "taṣawwarakum," meaning He formed you for Himself and for His worship. ﴿There is no god but Him﴾, since no one other than Him knows the totality of what He knows, nor is able to do what He does. ﴿The Mighty, the Wise﴾ indicates the perfection of His power and the limitlessness of His wisdom.

It was said: this is an argument against those who claimed that Jesus was a lord. When the delegation of Najran disputed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning him, the surah was revealed from its beginning up to some eighty-odd verses, affirming what he argued against them with and answering their doubts.

He it is Who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive (muhkamat), which have been made firm in their expression by being safeguarded from generality (ijmal) and multiplicity of possible meanings (ihtimal). ﴿They are the foundation of the Book﴾: its origin, to which the others are referred. By analogy it should have been "its foundations" (ummahat), but it is given in the singular in consideration of each one, or because all of them are like a single verse. ﴿And others are allegorical (mutashabihat)﴾: possible in meaning, whose intended sense is not clear, either because of generality or because of conflict with the apparent meaning, ﴿none knows their interpretation except God and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾, in that they have been made firm and established in it. Whoever stops at "except God" explains the allegorical verses as what God has kept exclusive knowledge of, such as the duration of the world, the time of the Hour, and the special properties of numbers, such as the number of the guardians of Hell; or as what a decisive proof has shown is not the apparent meaning, without that proof indicating what is actually meant.

﴿Those who are firmly rooted say: "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord"﴾: this is a resumptive sentence clarifying the state of those firmly rooted, or a circumstantial clause concerning them, or a predicate if you make it the subject. ﴿All of it is from our Lord﴾: that is, both the allegorical and the decisive verses are from Him. ﴿And none will be mindful except people of understanding﴾: a praise of those firmly rooted for their keen intellect and sound reflection, and an indication of the readiness they have for being guided to its interpretation, which is the freeing of the intellect from the veils of the senses. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that the preceding verses describe the spirit with knowledge and its nurture, while the verses before that describe the body and its shaping. Alternatively, it is a reply to the Christians' clinging to such words as His saying, ﴿and His word which He cast to Mary, and a spirit from Him﴾.

It is also a reply to their saying that Jesus has no father except God, so it is established that He is his Father, since He is the Fashioner of embryos as He wills, forming them from the sperm of a father or from other than it, and since He fashioned him in the womb, and the one who fashions does not become the father of what he fashions.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 8–9:

﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾ is from the speech of those firmly grounded in knowledge (al-rasikhun). It is also said that it is a resumed statement (isti'naf), and the meaning is: do not let our hearts swerve from the path of truth toward following the ambiguous (mutashabih) through an interpretation (ta'wil) that You do not approve. The Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him said: "The heart of the son of Adam lies between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful. If He wills, He keeps it upright upon the truth, and if He wills, He makes it deviate from it." It is also said: do not test us with trials through which our hearts would deviate, after You have guided us to the truth and to faith in both kinds, the clear (muhkam) and the ambiguous (mutashabih). The word ba'd (after) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), and idh (when) is in the genitive position because it is attached to it. It is also said that idh here means inna (indeed). ﴿And grant us from Yourself mercy﴾ that brings us near to You and by which we attain success with You, or grant us success in remaining steadfast upon the truth, or forgiveness of sins. ﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾ of every request. In this there is evidence that guidance and misguidance are from Allah, and that He is bounteous in what He bestows upon His servants; nothing is obligatory upon Him.

﴿Our Lord, indeed You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day﴾ for the reckoning of a Day, or for its recompense. ﴿About which there is no doubt﴾ regarding the occurrence of the Day and what it contains of resurrection and recompense. By this they draw attention to the fact that the greater part of their aim in the two requests is what relates to the Hereafter, for it is the ultimate goal and the true wealth. ﴿Indeed Allah does not fail in His promise﴾ for divinity (al-ilahiyya) is incompatible with failing to fulfill it. For the sake of indicating this and magnifying what is promised, He varied the address. The Wa'idiyya (those who hold that the threat of punishment must be carried out) used this as evidence. It is answered that the threat against sinners is conditional upon the absence of pardon, by separate evidences, just as it is conditional upon the absence of repentance, by consensus.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 10–11:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ is general, applying to disbelievers in general. It is also said that what is meant is the delegation of Najran, or the Jews, or the polytheists of the Arabs. ﴿Their wealth will not avail them, nor their children, against Allah at all﴾, i.e., from His mercy, or His obedience, in the sense of substitution, or from His punishment. ﴿And they are the fuel of the Fire﴾, its firewood. It is also read with a ḍamma (fuel), meaning the people of its fuel.

﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾ is connected to what precedes it, i.e., their wealth and children will not avail against those (the disbelievers), or they will be fuel through them just as those were fuel. Or it is a resumed (independent) statement, nominative in its place, its estimate being: "the custom of these is like their custom in disbelief and punishment." Here "daʾb" (custom, habit) is a verbal noun of daʾaba in work, when one exerts oneself in it, and then it was transferred to the meaning of "affair, state." ﴿And those before them﴾ is conjoined to "the people of Pharaoh." It is also said to be a resumed statement. ﴿They denied Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) with an implied qad, or a resumed statement explaining their condition, or the predicate if you begin with "those before them." ﴿And Allah is severe in punishment﴾ is an amplification of the seizing and an increase in frightening the disbelievers.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 3, verse 12:**

﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome and gathered to Hell,"﴾ That is: say to the polytheists of Makkah, "You will be overcome," meaning on the Day of Badr. It has also been said that this was addressed to the Jews, for when the Prophet (ﷺ) gathered them after Badr in the marketplace of Banu Qaynuqa', he warned them that what had befallen Quraysh might befall them. They said, "Do not let it deceive you that you defeated some inexperienced men who had no knowledge of war. If you fought us, you would know that we are the (real) people." Then this verse was revealed. Allah fulfilled His promise to them: the killing of Banu Qurayzah, the expulsion of Banu al-Nadir, the conquest of Khaybar, and the imposition of the jizya (poll tax) on others besides them. This is among the proofs of prophethood.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿سَيُغْلَبُونَ﴾ and ﴿يُحْشَرُونَ﴾ with the "ya'" in both, on the basis that the command is that he should relay to them what he had been told of their threat in its own wording.

﴿And how evil is the resting place!﴾ This completes what is said to them. Or it is a new sentence, and the sense is: "How evil is the resting place: Hell, or what they have prepared for themselves."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 13:

﴿There has indeed been for you a sign﴾. The address is either to the Quraysh or to the Jews, and it has been said that it is to the believers. ﴿In two hosts that met﴾ on the Day of Badr. ﴿One host fighting in the way of Allah, and another disbelieving, seeing them as twice their number﴾. The polytheists saw the believers as twice the number of the polytheists, and they were nearly a thousand. Or they saw them as twice the number of the Muslims, who were three hundred and some ten. This was after He had made them seem few in their eyes, so that they became bold against them and advanced toward them. Then when they met, the enemy appeared many in their eyes, until they were overcome, by a reinforcement from Allah the Exalted for the believers. Or the believers saw the polytheists as twice the number of the believers, though they were three times their number, so that they would be steadfast and certain of the victory which Allah had promised them in His saying: ﴿If there are among you a hundred patient ones, they will overcome two hundred﴾. This is supported by the recitation of Nafi' and Ya'qub with the letter ta' (ترونهم, "they see you" in the second person), and it was also read with both (forms) in the passive voice (يُرَوْنَهم / تُرَوْنَهم), meaning: Allah shows them, or shows you, that by His power. And the word ﴿فِئَةٍ﴾ (fi'ah) in the genitive is in apposition (badal) to ﴿فِئَتَيْنِ﴾ (fi'atayn), and in the accusative it is by specification (ikhtisas) or as a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the subject of ﴿التَقَتا﴾ (iltaqata). ﴿Seeing with the eye﴾: a manifest and direct sight. ﴿And Allah strengthens with His help whom He wills﴾: He helped them as He strengthened the people of Badr. ﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, in the making few and the making many, or in the victory of the few, who had no equipment, over the many, who were armed, and in the fact that the event is also a sign, which admits of both (readings), and admits that the matter occurred as the Messenger ﷺ had reported. ﴿Surely there is a lesson for those who have insight﴾: that is, a admonition for those possessing perceptions. It has been said: for those who saw them.

﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires﴾, i.e., the things desired. He called them "desires" (shahawat) as an intensification and an indication that people have immersed themselves in loving them, to the point that they have come to love the desire itself, as in His saying: ﴿I have loved the love of good﴾. The one who beautifies is God, Exalted, because He is the Creator of actions and their motivations. Perhaps He beautified it as a trial, or because it becomes a means to the happiness of the Hereafter when it is done in a manner that God, Exalted, is pleased with, or because it is among the means of livelihood and the continuation of the species. It was said that the one who beautifies is Satan, for the verse is in the context of censure. Al-Jubba'i (al-Jubba'i) distinguished between the permissible and the forbidden.

﴿Of women, sons, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, and tilth﴾: this is an explanation of the desires. The qintar (qintar) is a large amount of wealth. It was said that it is one hundred thousand dinars. It was said that it is the filling of an ox-hide with gold. It has been disputed whether it is of the form fi'lal or fin'al, and al-muqantara (the heaped-up) is derived from it for emphasis, as in their saying badrah mubdarah (a purse that is spent to the full). Al-musawwamah (the branded) means the marked, from the sawmah (sawmah), which is a mark, or the pastured, from asama al-dabbah wa sawwamaha (he let the animal graze freely and marked it), or the well-proportioned (al-mutahhamah). Al-an'am (cattle) are camels, cows, and sheep. ﴿That is the enjoyment of the worldly life﴾: a reference to what has been mentioned.

﴿And with God is the best return﴾, i.e., the place of return. This is an exhortation to exchange what is with Him of true and everlasting pleasures for the deficient, perishing desires.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 15–16:

﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something better than that?"﴾ He intends by this to establish that the reward of Allah the Exalted is better than the pleasures of this world. ﴿For those who fear Allah, with their Lord are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining what is better. It is also permissible for the lam to be connected to "better" (khayr), and for "gardens" (jannat) to be in the nominative, as if to say "it is gardens." This is supported by the reading of the one who put it in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for "better" (bi-khayr). ﴿And purified spouses﴾ from what is repugnant among women. ﴿And approval from Allah﴾. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read it throughout the Qur'an with a ḍamma on the rā' (riḍwān), except the second instance in al-Ma'idah, which is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿His approval, the paths of peace﴾, which he read with a kasra on the rā' (riḍwān). Both are dialectal forms (lughatān). ﴿And Allah is Seeing of the servants﴾, that is, of their deeds, so He rewards the doer of good and punishes the doer of evil; or, of the states of those who fear Allah, and therefore He has prepared for them gardens. In this verse He has drawn attention to His blessings: the lowest of them is the enjoyment of the life of this world, the highest is the approval of Allah the Exalted, according to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And approval from Allah is greater﴾, and the middle of them is the Garden and its bliss.

(p-9) ﴿Those who say, "Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire"﴾ is a description (ṣifah) of "those who fear Allah" or of "the servants," or it is a laudatory apposition (madḥ), either in the accusative or the nominative. In the ordering of the supplication upon mere faith there is evidence that it is sufficient for deserving forgiveness, or for being prepared for it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 15–16:

﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something better than that?"﴾ He intends by this to establish that the reward of Allah the Exalted is better than the pleasures of this world. ﴿For those who fear Allah, with their Lord are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining what is better. It is also permissible for the lam to be connected to "better" (khayr), and for "gardens" (jannat) to be in the nominative, as if to say "it is gardens." This is supported by the reading of the one who put it in the genitive as a substitute (badal) for "better" (bi-khayr). ﴿And purified spouses﴾ from what is repugnant among women. ﴿And approval from Allah﴾. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read it throughout the Qur'an with a ḍamma on the rā' (riḍwān), except the second instance in al-Ma'idah, which is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿His approval, the paths of peace﴾, which he read with a kasra on the rā' (riḍwān). Both are dialectal forms (lughatān). ﴿And Allah is Seeing of the servants﴾, that is, of their deeds, so He rewards the doer of good and punishes the doer of evil; or, of the states of those who fear Allah, and therefore He has prepared for them gardens. In this verse He has drawn attention to His blessings: the lowest of them is the enjoyment of the life of this world, the highest is the approval of Allah the Exalted, according to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And approval from Allah is greater﴾, and the middle of them is the Garden and its bliss.

(p-9) ﴿Those who say, "Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire"﴾ is a description (ṣifah) of "those who fear Allah" or of "the servants," or it is a laudatory apposition (madḥ), either in the accusative or the nominative. In the ordering of the supplication upon mere faith there is evidence that it is sufficient for deserving forgiveness, or for being prepared for it.

﴿The patient, the truthful, the obedient, those who spend, and those who seek forgiveness at dawn﴾ is a restriction (ḥaṣr) of the stations (maqāmāt) of the wayfarer (al-sālik, the one traveling the spiritual path) in the best order. His dealing with God, exalted is He, is either a means of drawing near (tawassul) or a request (ṭalab). The means of drawing near is either through the soul (nafs), which is restraining it from vices and confining it to virtues, and patience (ṣabr) encompasses both of these; or through the body, which is either verbal, namely truthfulness (ṣidq), or practical, namely devout obedience (qunūt), which is constant adherence to obedience; or through wealth, which is spending in the ways of good (infāq). As for the request, it is through seeking forgiveness (istighfār), because forgiveness is the greatest of requests, indeed the one that comprises all of them. The placing of the conjunction "and" (wāw) between them serves to indicate the independence of each one of them and their perfection within them, or the difference of those described by them. The specification of the pre-dawn hours (asḥār) is because supplication at that time is closer to being answered, because worship at that time is more arduous, the soul is purer, and the spirit (rawʿ) is more gathered for those who strive (mujtahidīn). It was said that they used to reach the last part of the night (saḥar), then they would seek forgiveness and supplicate.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 18:

﴿God bears witness that there is no god but He﴾ He made His oneness evident by setting up the proofs that indicate it and sending down the verses that declare it.

﴿And the angels﴾ by affirming it. ﴿And those of knowledge﴾ by believing in it and arguing for it. He likened this to the testimony of a witness in clarity and disclosure. ﴿Standing firm in justice﴾ maintaining justice in His apportioning and His judgment, and it is placed in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from God. It is permissible for it to be singular in this way, though one would not say "Zayd and ʿAmr came riding" (jāʾa Zaydun wa-ʿAmrun rākiban), because there is no ambiguity, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift﴾. Or [the ḥāl is] "who is," and its governing element is the meaning of the sentence, i.e., He alone is standing [in justice]. Or it is "more worthy of it" (aḥaqquhu), since it is an emphatic ḥāl. Or it is in the mode of praise (ʿalā al-madḥ). Or it is an attribute of the negated [i.e., of "no god"], though there is weakness in this due to the separation, and it is included in what is witnessed to when you make it an attribute, or a ḥāl from the pronoun. It has been read as "al-qāʾimu bil-qisṭi" [in the nominative], either as a substitute (badal) for "He," or as the predicate of an omitted subject. ﴿There is no god but He﴾ He repeated it for emphasis and for greater attention to knowing the proofs of tawḥīd and passing judgment by it after establishing the argument, and so that He may build upon it His saying: ﴿the Mighty, the Wise﴾, so that one knows that He is the one described by both. He placed "the Mighty" first because the knowledge of His power precedes the knowledge of His wisdom. Their being in the nominative is either as a substitute from the pronoun or as an attribute of the subject of "bore witness."

It has been narrated concerning its virtue that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Its reciter will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and God, exalted is He, will say: 'Indeed, this servant of Mine has a covenant with Me, and I am most worthy of those who fulfil covenants. Admit My servant into Paradise.'"

It is evidence for the excellence of the knowledge of the foundations of religion (uṣūl al-dīn) and the nobility of its people.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 19:

﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah) that emphasizes the first: that is, there is no religion accepted by Allah other than Islam, which is monotheism (al-tawhid) and adherence to the sacred law (al-shar') that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. Al-Kisai read it with a fath (inna being read as anna), in which case it is a substitute (badal): a badal al-kull (substitution of the whole) if Islam is interpreted as faith (iman) or as that which faith entails, and a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion) if it is interpreted as the sacred law (shari'a). It was also read as innahu with a kasra and anna with a fath, with the verb (shahida, "bore witness") governing the second, and the intervening material being a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraq); or the verb shahida is treated as if it were qala (said) at one time and 'alima (knew) at another, since it includes the meaning of both.

﴿And those given the Scripture did not differ﴾ among themselves, namely the Jews and the Christians, or the adherents of the earlier scriptures regarding the religion of Islam. Some said it is true, some said it is restricted to the Arabs, and others denied it absolutely. Or [they differed] regarding monotheism: the Christians became trinitarian, and the Jews said, "Ezra is the son of Allah." It was also said they are the people of Moses, who differed after him. And it was said they are the Christians, who differed concerning the matter of Jesus, peace be upon him. (p-10) ﴿Except after knowledge had come to them﴾, that is, after they knew the reality of the matter and became firmly established in knowledge of it through the signs and proofs.

﴿Out of envy among themselves﴾: jealousy among them and a desire for leadership, not due to any doubt or obscurity in the matter. ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah – indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾: a threat to those among them who disbelieved.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 20:

﴿Then if they argue with you﴾ about the religion, or dispute with you concerning it after you have presented the proofs. ﴿Then say: I have submitted my face to God﴾ I have devoted my self and my whole being to Him, associating no other with Him in them; and this is the upright religion, by which the proofs have been established and to which the signs and the messengers have called. The face is used here to mean the self because it is the most noble of the visible limbs and the place where the faculties and senses appear. ﴿And those who follow me﴾ is conjoined to the "ta'" in "aslamtu" (I have submitted), and the separation justifies it; or it is an object in the sense of "together with" (maf'ul ma'ahu). ﴿And say to those who were given the Book and to the unlettered﴾ those who have no book, like the idolaters of the Arabs. ﴿Have you submitted?﴾ as I have submitted, now that the proof has become clear to you, or are you still upon your disbelief? Its counterpart is His saying:

﴿So will you desist?﴾ and in it is a rebuke to them for dullness or obstinacy. ﴿Then if they submit, they have indeed been guided﴾ they have certainly benefited themselves by bringing themselves out of error. ﴿But if they turn away, then upon you is only the conveyance﴾ meaning they cannot harm you, since your duty is only to convey, and you have conveyed.

﴿And God is Seeing of His servants﴾ a promise and a warning.

Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right, and kill those who enjoin justice among people, give them tidings of a painful punishment. ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ يَكْفُرُونَ بِآياتِ اللَّهِ ويَقْتُلُونَ النَّبِيِّينَ بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ ويَقْتُلُونَ الَّذِينَ يَأْمُرُونَ بِالقِسْطِ مِنَ النّاسِ فَبَشِّرْهم بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾ They are the People of the Book who were in his time (peace be upon him). The first of them killed the prophets, and their followers, and they were content with it, and they intended to kill the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, but Allah protected them. A similar case has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah. Hamzah recited «وَيُقاتِلُونَ الَّذِينَ» (with the verb يُقاتِلُونَ, "fight"). Sibawayh prohibited inserting the fa' (فاء) into the predicate (khabar) of إنَّ, كَلَيْتَ and لَعَلَّ, and for this reason it was said that the predicate is... 

﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ حَبِطَتْ أعْمالُهم في الدُّنْيا والآخِرَةِ﴾ Like your saying: زَيْدٌ فافْهَمْ رَجُلٌ صالِحٌ (Zayd, fa-fham, rajul salih), and the difference is that it does not change the meaning of the al-ibtida' (the grammatical state of a sentence beginning with a subject) unlike these two. ﴿وَما لَهم مِن ناصِرِينَ﴾ who would repel the punishment from them.

Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right, and kill those who enjoin justice among people, give them tidings of a painful punishment. ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ يَكْفُرُونَ بِآياتِ اللَّهِ ويَقْتُلُونَ النَّبِيِّينَ بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ ويَقْتُلُونَ الَّذِينَ يَأْمُرُونَ بِالقِسْطِ مِنَ النّاسِ فَبَشِّرْهم بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾ They are the People of the Book who were in his time (peace be upon him). Sibawayh prohibited inserting the fa' (فاء) into the predicate (khabar) of إنَّ, كَلَيْتَ and لَعَلَّ, and for this reason it was said that the predicate is... 

﴿أُولَئِكَ الَّذِينَ حَبِطَتْ أعْمالُهم في الدُّنْيا والآخِرَةِ﴾ Like your saying: زَيْدٌ فافْهَمْ رَجُلٌ صالِحٌ (Zayd, fa-fham, rajul salih), and the difference is that it does not change the meaning of the al-ibtida' (the grammatical state of a sentence beginning with a subject) unlike these two. ﴿وَما لَهم مِن ناصِرِينَ﴾ who would repel the punishment from them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 23:

﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ That is, the Torah, or the category of heavenly scriptures in general. The particle "min" (ﻣِﻦ) here is either partitive (li-l-tab'id), meaning "a portion of," or explanatory (li-l-bayan), meaning "that is." The indefiniteness of "nasib" (portion) allows for either magnifying or belittling it.

﴿They are called to the Book of Allah so that it may judge between them.﴾ The one calling is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the Book of Allah is the Qur'an, or it is the Torah, based on what has been narrated: "(That he (ﷺ) entered their house of study (midrasahum), and Nu'aym ibn 'Amr and al-Harith ibn Zayd said to him, 'Upon which religion are you?' He said, 'Upon the religion of Ibrahim.' They said, 'Ibrahim was a Jew.' He said, 'Come to the Torah, for it is between us and you.' They refused, so this was revealed.)" It is also said that it was revealed concerning stoning (al-rajm). It has been read as "liyuhkama" in the passive voice, in which case the disagreement is among them. In this is evidence that the transmitted (sam'iyya) proofs are authoritative in matters of the foundations of religion (usul).

﴿Then a party of them turn away﴾ This is an expression of astonishment at their turning away, given their knowledge that returning to it is obligatory.

﴿while they are averse.﴾ They are a people whose habit is aversion. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "fariq" (a party), and it was permissible because it is specified by the descriptive qualifier.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 24–25:

﴿That﴾ refers to the turning away and aversion. ﴿Because they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."﴾ This is because they made light of the matter of punishment for themselves, due to this deviant belief and empty hope. ﴿And what they used to invent deluded them in their religion﴾ regarding the claim that the Fire would not touch them except for a few days, or that their forefathers, the prophets, would intercede for them, or that God Most High promised Jacob, peace be upon him, that He would not punish his descendants except for the "tahillat al-qasam" (the dissolving of an oath, i.e., a punishment lasting only as long as it takes to fulfil an oath).

﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt?﴾ This is an expression of the magnitude of what will befall them in the Hereafter, and a refutation of their saying, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."

It is narrated: "The first banner raised on the Day of Resurrection among the banners of the disbelievers will be the banner of the Jews. God Most High will expose them before the witnesses, then He will order them to the Fire." ﴿And every soul will be paid in full for what it has earned﴾, meaning the recompense for what it has earned. In this there is evidence that "ʿibadah" (worship) is not nullified ("tuhbatu") and that the believer does not abide forever in the Fire, because the full repayment of his faith and deed does not occur in the Fire nor before entering it; hence it is after deliverance from it. ﴿And they will not be wronged﴾. The pronoun refers to "every soul" according to its sense, since it carries the meaning of "every person."

﴿That﴾ refers to the turning away and aversion. ﴿Because they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."﴾ This is because they made light of the matter of punishment for themselves, due to this deviant belief and empty hope. ﴿And what they used to invent deluded them in their religion﴾ regarding the claim that the Fire would not touch them except for a few days, or that their forefathers, the prophets, would intercede for them, or that God Most High promised Jacob, peace be upon him, that He would not punish his descendants except for the "tahillat al-qasam" (the dissolving of an oath, i.e., a punishment lasting only as long as it takes to fulfil an oath).

﴿Say: O Allah﴾. The mim is a substitute for "ya" (the vocative particle), and for this reason the two are not combined. It is one of the distinctive features of this name, as is the prefixing of "ya" to it together with the definite article *lam* (*lam al-ta'rif*), the cutting off of its hamza, and the *ta'* of oath (*ta' al-qasam*).

It is said that its origin is "ya Allahumma, amunna bi-khayr" (O Allah, grant us security with goodness), and it was lightened by deleting the vocative particle, the dependents of the verb, and its hamza.

﴿Master of the Kingdom﴾ He disposes of what can be disposed of with the disposal of owners over what they own. It is a second vocative according to Sibawayh, for the mim, in his view, prevents it from being a descriptive (*wasfiyya*).

﴿You give the kingdom to whom You will and You take the kingdom away from whom You will﴾. You give from it what You will to whom You will, and You take it back. So the first "kingdom" is general, and the other two are parts of it.

It is said that the intended meaning of "kingdom" is prophethood, and its removal is its transfer from one people to another.

﴿And You exalt whom You will and You abase whom You will﴾, in this world or in the Hereafter, or in both, by victory and defeat, by success (*tawfiq*) and forsaking (*khidhlan*).

﴿In Your hand is the good. Indeed You are over all things competent﴾. Mention is made of the good alone because it is what is decreed essentially, whereas evil is decreed incidentally, since no particular evil exists without including a universal good. Or it is for the sake of observing courtesy in address. Or because the discourse occurred concerning it, as it is reported that: "When he (ﷺ) dug the trench and marked out forty cubits for every ten men, they began digging, and a huge rock appeared which the picks did not affect. They sent Salman to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to inform him. He came, peace be upon him, took the pick from him, and struck it a blow that split it. A flash of light came from it that illuminated what lay between its two sides, as if there were a lamp inside a dark house. He exclaimed 'Allahu akbar' and the Muslims exclaimed it with him, and he said: 'The palaces of al-Hirah have been illuminated for me by it, as if they were the fangs of dogs.' Then he struck the second blow and said: 'The red palaces of the land of Rome have been illuminated for me by it.' Then he struck the third blow and said: 'The palaces of San'a have been illuminated for me by it. Jibril, peace be upon him, has informed me that my community will prevail over them, so rejoice.' The hypocrites said: 'Do you not wonder? He promises you and gives you false hopes, and tells you that from Yathrib he sees the palaces of al-Hirah and the cities of Kisra, and that they will be opened to you, while you are merely digging a trench out of fear!' Then this verse was revealed."

He thereby drew attention to the fact that evil is also in His hand, by His saying: ﴿Indeed You are over all things competent﴾.

﴿You cause the night to enter into the day and You cause the day to enter into the night, and You bring forth the living from the dead and You bring forth the dead from the living, and You provide for whom You will without reckoning.﴾ He followed this with a demonstration of His power over the alternation of night and day, and of death and life, and of the vastness of His bounty, (p-12) as an indication that whoever has power over these has power over the alternation of humiliation and honor, and over granting dominion and removing it.

Al-walij (الوُلُوجُ) means entering into a narrow place. The "causing the night to enter into the day" (إيلاجُ اللَّيْلِ والنَّهارِ) means causing one of them to enter into the other, either by succession or by increase and decrease. "Bringing forth the living from the dead" and the reverse means:

the bringing into existence of living beings from their matter and their causing to die, or the bringing into existence of an animal from a sperm-drop and of a sperm-drop from an animal. It was said that it means bringing forth the believer from the disbeliever and the disbeliever from the believer.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read *al-mayt* (المَيْتِ) with lightening (بِالتَّخْفِيفِ), that is, without the doubled consonant, instead of *al-mayyit* (المَيِّتِ).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 28:

﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies﴾ They were forbidden from allying with them out of kinship, pre-Islamic friendship, and the like, so that their love and hatred would be for the sake of God alone. Or [they were forbidden] from seeking the disbelievers' help in raids and in all other religious affairs. ﴿Rather than the believers﴾ indicates that the believers are the rightful ones to be allied with, and that in allying with them there is a substitute (mandūḥah) for allying with the disbelievers. ﴿And whoever does that﴾ meaning, takes them as allies. ﴿Then he has nothing to do with God﴾ meaning, he has no share of God's guardianship (wilayah) that could properly be called guardianship, for the alliances of two opposing parties do not come together. He said:

"You love my enemy, then claim that I am your friend. Foolishness is not far from you."

﴿Except when you fear a danger from them﴾ except when you fear from their side something that must be guarded against, or as a precaution (ittiqa'). The verb is followed by min because it has the sense of "to beware" and "to fear." Ya'qub (a reader) recited "taqiyyah." [The believers] were prohibited from allying with them, outwardly and inwardly, at all times except the time of fear, for then showing allegiance is permissible, as Jesus (upon him be peace) said: "Be moderate and walk on the side." ﴿And God warns you of Himself, and to God is the final return﴾ so do not expose yourselves to His wrath by opposing His rulings and allying with His enemies. This is a great threat, implying the extreme gravity of the prohibition, and the mention of "Himself" (nafs) is so that one knows that what is to be guarded against is a punishment issued by Him, the Exalted; thus one should not heed, in comparison to it, what one guards against from the disbelievers.

Say: "Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or disclose it, Allah knows it." That is, He knows your inner thoughts, including allegiance to the disbelievers and other matters, whether you conceal them or disclose them. ﴿And He knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾, so He knows your secret and your open conduct. ﴿And Allah is over all things Competent﴾, so He is able to punish you if you do not desist from what you have been forbidden. The verse explains His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾. It is as if He said: "He warns you of Himself, because He is characterized by an essential knowledge that encompasses all known things, and an essential power that extends to all things within its scope. So do not dare to disobey Him, for there is no act of disobedience except that He is aware of it and able to punish for it."

﴿On the Day every soul finds what it has done of good present, and what it has done of evil, it will wish that between it and that were a far-off term﴾. "Yawm" (the Day) is in the accusative (manṣūb, the object-of-time case) governed by "tawaddu" (it wishes), meaning "tatamannā" (it desires). That is: on the Day every soul finds the records of its deeds, or the recompense of its deeds, good and evil, present before it, it desires that between itself and that Day there were a far-off term. Or it is governed by an implied verb, such as "udhkur" (remember). "Tawaddu" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "ʿamilat" (did), or it is the predicate (khabar) of "mā ʿamilat min sūʾ" (what it has done of evil). "Tajidu" is restricted to "mā ʿamilat min khayr" (what it has done of good). "Mā" cannot be a conditional particle (sharṭiyya), because "tawaddu" is in the nominative. It has been read as "waddat" (she wished), and on this reading "mā" can be conditional. However, taking it as a predicate is more precise in meaning, because it narrates an existing state, and it agrees better with the well-known reading. ﴿And God warns you of Himself﴾. He repeated it for emphasis and reminder. ﴿And God is Compassionate to His servants﴾. This indicates that He forbade and warned them only out of compassion for them and in consideration of their welfare. Or it means that He is the One of forgiveness (dhū maghfira) and the One of painful punishment (dhū ʿiqāb alīm), so that His mercy is hoped for and His punishment is feared. (p-13)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 31–32:

﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins.﴾ Love (mahabbah) is the soul's inclination toward a thing because of a perfection it has perceived in it, to such a degree that it drives the soul toward whatever brings it closer to that thing. When the servant knows that true perfection belongs to Allah alone, and that every perfection he sees in himself or in others is from Allah, through Allah, and toward Allah, his love is for none but Allah and is in Allah. This requires the desire to obey Him and the eagerness for what brings him near to Him. Therefore love has been explained as the desire for obedience, and it has been made to necessitate following the Messenger in worship and eagerly striving to comply with him. ﴿Allah will love you and forgive you your sins﴾ is the answer to the imperative, meaning: He will be pleased with you and will remove the veils from your hearts by overlooking what has passed from you, so He brings you near to the court of His might and settles you in the neighborhood of His holiness. This is expressed with "love" by way of metaphor (isti'arah) or as a counterpart (muqabalah).

﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ toward whoever makes himself beloved to Him through obedience to Him and following His Prophet ﷺ.

It is narrated that it was revealed when the Jews said, "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 31–32:

﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins.﴾ Love (mahabbah) is the soul's inclination toward a thing because of a perfection it has perceived in it, to such a degree that it drives the soul toward whatever brings it closer to that thing. When the servant knows that true perfection belongs to Allah alone, and that every perfection he sees in himself or in others is from Allah, through Allah, and toward Allah, his love is for none but Allah and is in Allah. This requires the desire to obey Him and the eagerness for what brings him near to Him. Therefore love has been explained as the desire for obedience, and it has been made to necessitate following the Messenger in worship and eagerly striving to comply with him. ﴿Allah will love you and forgive you your sins﴾ is the answer to the imperative, meaning: He will be pleased with you and will remove the veils from your hearts by overlooking what has passed from you, so He brings you near to the court of His might and settles you in the neighborhood of His holiness. This is expressed with "love" by way of metaphor (isti'arah) or as a counterpart (muqabalah).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 33–34:

﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of ʿImran over the worlds﴾ with prophethood and with spiritual and bodily distinctions, and for this reason they were able to do what others were not able to do. When He made obedience to the Messenger obligatory, and explained that it is what brings about the love of Allah, He followed this immediately with an account of their virtues, as an encouragement to it. By this verse the excellence of these (prophets) over the angels is also inferred. The family of Abraham are Ishmael, Isaac, and their descendants. The Messenger ﷺ is included among them. The family of ʿImran are Moses and Aaron, the two sons of ʿImran ibn Yaṣhar ibn Qahath ibn Lawi ibn Yaʿqub; or Jesus and his mother Mary, daughter of ʿImran ibn Mathan ibn al-ʿAzar ibn Abi Yudh ibn Yuzan ibn Zurbabil ibn Salyan ibn Yuhanna ibn Ushiya ibn Amun ibn Munshakan ibn Hazqa ibn Akhaz ibn Yutham ibn ʿUzaya ibn Yuram ibn Saqit ibn Aysha ibn Rajaʿim ibn Sulayman ibn Dawud ibn Aysha ibn ʿUbad ibn Salmun ibn Yaʿaz ibn Nahshun ibn ʿAmyad ibn Ram ibn Hasrum ibn Faris ibn Yahuda ibn Yaʿqub ʿalayhi al-salam. Between the two ʿImrans there were one thousand eight hundred years.

﴿Offspring, one of the other﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or a substitute (badal) for the two families, or for them and Noah; that is, they are one offspring, branching out, one from the other. It has also been said that "one of the other" means in religion. Dhurriyyah (offspring) refers to a child, and applies to one or many. It is either on the pattern fuʿlīyah from dharr, or on the pattern fuʿūlah from dhar'; its hamzah was replaced by a yā', then the wāw was changed into a yā' and they were assimilated. ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ of people's sayings and deeds, so He chooses whoever is upright in word and deed; or, He is All-Hearing of the words of the wife of ʿImran, All-Knowing of her intention.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 35:

﴿When the wife of ʿImran said: "My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb"﴾. Idh (when) is in the accusative by virtue of the verb in the sentence, through the grammatical device of tanazu' (contention between two governing verbs). It is also said that its accusative is due to an implied verb: udhkur (remember).

This was Hannah bint Faqudh, the grandmother of ʿIsa (Jesus). ʿImran ibn Yasahar had a daughter named Maryam, who was older than Musa and Harun. Some thought that the intended meaning was his wife, but this is refuted by the fact that Zakariyya was responsible for her upbringing, for he was a contemporary of Ibn Mathan and had married his daughter Ishaʿ. Yahya and ʿIsa, peace be upon them both, were cousins on the father's side.

It is narrated that she was barren and elderly. Once, while she was in the shade of a tree, she saw a bird feeding its chick, and she yearned for a child and wished for one. So she said: "O Allah, I have a vow to You: if You grant me a child, I will dedicate him in charity to the Temple (Bayt al-Maqdis), so that he will be among its servants." Then she conceived Maryam, and ʿImran died. This kind of vow was prescribed in their time for boys, so perhaps she framed the matter as a supposition, or she was asking for a male child.

﴿Muharraran﴾ means freed, released for its service, with nothing from me occupying him; or devoted exclusively to worship. Its accusative is as a circumstantial state (hal).

﴿So accept from me﴾ what I have vowed. ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ of my words and my intention.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 36:

﴿So when she had given birth to her, she said: "My Lord, I have given birth to a female."﴾ The pronoun refers to what is in her womb, and its feminine form is because it was female. The accusative ("female") may be a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of it, since the feminine character of the child is known from it, for the circumstantial qualifier and its referent are one in essence. Or it is taken as referring to a feminine noun, such as "soul" (nafs) or "pregnancy" (ḥabla).

She said this out of regret and grief, addressing her Lord, because she had hoped to give birth to a male, and for that reason she had vowed to dedicate it. ﴿And God knows best what she had given birth to.﴾ That is, the thing she had given birth to. This is a resumption from God Most High, to magnify her offspring and to show that she (the mother) did not know its true status. Ibn ʿĀmir, Abu Bakr (from ʿĀṣim), and Yaʿqūb read "wa-ḍaʿtu" (I have given birth), taking it as part of her own speech, a consolation to herself, meaning: perhaps God, glorified and exalted, has a secret in it, or the female was better. It has also been read "wa-ḍaʿti" (you have given birth), as a direct address from God Most High to her. ﴿And the male is not like the female.﴾ This explains His words "God knows best": that is, the male she sought is not like the female that was given to her. The lām in both is for a specific reference (ʿahd). It may also be from her speech, meaning: the male and the female are not equal in what she vowed, so the lām is for the category (jins).

﴿And I have named her Mary.﴾ It is conjoined to what precedes it of her speech, and what lies between them is a parenthetical remark. She mentioned this to her Lord seeking nearness to Him and asking that He protect her and set her right, so that her conduct would correspond to her name, for Mary in their language means "one who worships." This is evidence that the name, the named, and the act of naming are distinct things. ﴿And I seek refuge for her in You﴾, meaning: I place her under Your protection by Your safeguarding. ﴿And her offspring from the accursed Satan﴾, meaning the one who is driven away. The root of rajm is to pelt with stones.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no child born but that Satan touches it at the moment of its birth, so it cries out from his touch, except Mary and her son." Its meaning is that Satan seeks to lead astray every newborn, and is affected by it, except Mary and her son, for God Most High protected them by the blessing of this seeking of refuge.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 37:

﴿So her Lord accepted her﴾ with favour in the vow in place of a male. ﴿With a good acceptance﴾ meaning, in a good manner by which He accepts the vowed offerings: by setting her in place of a male, or by receiving her immediately after her birth, before she grew up and became fit for the service (sadana) of the sanctuary.

It is narrated that when Hannah gave birth to her, she wrapped her in a cloth, carried her to the mosque, and placed her among the rabbis (ahbar), saying: "Take this vowed offering (nadhira)." They competed for her, because she was the daughter of their leader and the master of their sacrifices, for the family of Mathan were the chiefs and kings of the Children of Israel. Zakariyya said: "I have the greatest right to her, for her maternal aunt is with me." But they refused except by lot. They were twenty-seven in number, so they went to a river and cast their pens into it. The pen of Zakariyya floated, while their pens sank, so Zakariyya took charge of her.

It is also possible that qabul is a verbal noun (masdar) with an omitted modifier, meaning "with one possessing a good acceptance," and that tqabbal carries the meaning of istaqbal (to receive), like taqadda and ta'ajjala, meaning that He took her at the beginning of her life, the moment she was born, with a good acceptance. ﴿And He made her grow up with a good growth﴾: a metaphor for raising her in a manner that makes her righteous in all her conditions. ﴿And Zakariyya took charge of her﴾: Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Asim read kaffala with the letter fa' doubled and read Zakariyya as a short form (qasara); except that Asim, in the transmission of Ibn Ayyash, read it so that the agent is God Most High and Zakariyya is the object, meaning He made him her guardian and surety for her welfare. The rest read it with the fa' single (takhfif). They read "Zakariyya'" (with the alif and hamza) in the nominative case (marfu'an). ﴿Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab﴾: that is, the chamber built for her, or the mosque, or the most noble part of its places and its forefront. It was named mihrab because it is the place where Satan is fought (muharabat al-shaytan), as though she was placed in the most noble position of Bayt al-Maqdis. ﴿He found with her provision﴾: this is the answer (jawab) to kullama and its governing verb.

It is narrated that no one entered upon her except him, and when he left he locked seven doors upon her. He would find with her winter fruit in summer and summer fruit in winter. ﴿He said: "O Mary, from where is this for you?"﴾: from where has this provision come to you, arriving out of its season while the doors are locked upon you? This is evidence for the permissibility of karamat (wondrous gifts) for the saints (awliya'). He made this a miracle for Zakariyya, which removed the confusion of the matter from him. ﴿She said: "It is from God"﴾: so do not find it strange. It is said that she spoke while still a child, as Jesus (peace be upon him) did, and she never suckled from a breast, and her provision was sent down to her from Paradise. ﴿Indeed God gives provision to whom He wills without reckoning﴾: without measure, because of its abundance, or without it being deserved, as a bounty from Him. It may be that this is part of their speech, or that it is part of the speech of God Most High.

It is narrated that Fatima, may God be pleased with her, sent to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) two loaves and a piece of meat. He returned them to her and said: "Come here, my daughter." She uncovered the tray, and behold, it was full of bread and meat. He said to her: "From where is this for you?" She said: "It is from God; indeed God gives provision to whom He wills without reckoning." He said: "Praise be to God who has made you like the mistress of the women of the Children of Israel." Then he gathered Ali, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and gathered his household around it, until they were satisfied, and the food remained as it was, and she distributed generously to her neighbours.

﴿There Zechariah called upon his Lord﴾: in that place, or at that time, since *hunā* (here), *thamma* (there) and *ḥaythu* are used metaphorically for time, when he saw Mary's honour and her rank with God, exalted is He. ﴿He said: "My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring"﴾, as You granted it to Ḥinnah, the aged barren woman. It is also said that when he saw fruits out of their season, he became aware of the possibility of a barren woman bearing children to an old man, so he asked and said: ﴿grant me from Yourself offspring﴾, because it was not in the usual manner nor through the customary causes. ﴿Indeed You are the Hearer of supplication﴾, its Answerer.

﴿Then the angels called him﴾, i.e., one of their kind, as in saying "Zayd rides horses" (meaning he is among the horsemen), for the caller was Gabriel alone. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read *fanādāhu* (فَناداهُ) with *imālah* (vowel-inclination, a phonetic shift toward the i-sound) and the masculine form. ﴿while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary﴾, i.e., standing in the prayer. The word (يُصَلِّي) *yuṣallī* may be a qualifier (ṣifah) of *qā'im* (standing), or a predicate (khabar), or another circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), or a circumstantial phrase relating to the pronoun in *qā'im* (قائِمٌ).

﴿that God gives you good news of Yaḥyā﴾, i.e., *bi-anna Allāh* (بِأنَّ اللَّهَ). Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read *inna* (إنَّ) with a kasra, considering it as a saying, or because calling (*nidā'*) is a type of saying. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read (يُبَشِّرُكَ) *yubashshiruka* and (يَحْيى) *Yaḥyā*. Yaḥyā is a non-Arabic name; and if it is taken as Arabic, its being diptote (not taking tanwīn) is due to its definiteness and its matching the pattern of a verb.

﴿confirming a word from God﴾, i.e., Jesus, peace be upon him. He was so named because he came into being by God's command without a father, and so resembled the originated things (*al-bid'iyyāt*), which are the realm of command (*'ālam al-amr*). Or [the word refers] to the Book of God, which is called a word, as it is said "the word of al-Ḥuwaydirah" for his *qaṣīdah* (ode).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 40:

﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a son,﴾ expressing astonishment from the standpoint of custom, or magnification, or wonder, or a question about the manner of its occurrence (p-16).

﴿when old age has already reached me?﴾ That is, the advanced age of old age has overtaken me and affected me. He was ninety-nine years old, and his wife was ninety-eight years old.

﴿and my wife is barren,﴾ unable to bear children, from *al-'uqr* (ʿuqr), which means cutting off, because she is one who has been cut off (*dhāt ʿuqr*) from children. ﴿He said: "Thus Allah does what He wills,"﴾ that is, He does what He wills of wonders like that act, namely producing a child from an aged old man and a barren old woman; or, "as you are, and your wife with your old age and barrenness, Allah does what He wills of creating a child." Or "thus" (*kadhālika*) is a subject and predicate: that is, Allah is in such an attribute, and "He does what He wills" is an explanation of it. Or "thus" is the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, the matter is thus, and "Allah does what He wills" is an explanation of it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 41:

﴿He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign."﴾ A sign (ʿalāmah) by which I may know the conception (al-ḥabal), so that I may receive it with cheerfulness and thankfulness, and so that it relieves the hardship of waiting.

﴿He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days."﴾ That is, you will not be able to speak to people for three (days). The restraint of his tongue from conversing with them specifically was so that he might devote the period entirely to the remembrance of God Most High and to giving thanks to Him, fulfilling the right of the blessing. It is as if He said: your sign is that your tongue will be restrained from everything except thanksgiving. And the best answer is that which is derived from the question.

﴿except by gestures﴾ a signal by means of a hand or a head. Its root meaning is movement, and from it comes ar-rāmūz (the signs/undercurrents) for the sea. The exception is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ); it is also said to be connected (muttaṣil), and by "speech" is meant that which indicates what is in the mind.

It has been read as "ramazan" with two fatḥahs, like khadam, the plural of rāmiz (one who gestures), and as "rumuzan" like rusul, the plural of ramūz, taken as a state (ḥāl) of him and of the people, in the sense of "gesturing to one another," as in the poet's words:

"Whenever you meet me as two individuals, the fleshy parts of your buttocks tremble and are dispersed."

﴿And remember your Lord much⁠﴾ during the days of confinement. This is emphatic of what precedes it and clarifies the purpose of it. Restricting the command to abundance indicates that it does not imply repetition.

﴿and glorify [Him] in the evening﴾ from midday until sunset. It is also said: from the afternoon or sunset until the passing of the first part of the night.

﴿and at dawn﴾ from the break of dawn until forenoon. It has been read with a fatḥah on the hamzah, as the plural of bakar, like saḥar and asḥār.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 42–43:

﴿And when the angels said: "O Mary, indeed Allah has chosen you, purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds."﴾ They spoke to her directly (mushafahan), as an honour to her. Whoever denies this honour claims that it was a miracle (mu'jizah) for Zakariyya, or a preparation (irhas) for the prophethood of Isa, peace be upon him. But there is consensus (ijma') that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, did not appoint a woman as a prophet, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send before you except men﴾. It was also said that they were inspired (ulhimu) to her. The first choosing (al-istifa' al-awwal) is that He accepted her from her mother, and no female before her had been accepted; that He dedicated her to worship; that He made her independent of earning by providing her with provision from Paradise; and that He purified her from what is considered repulsive in women. The second choosing is His guiding her, sending the angels to her, singling her out with extraordinary honours such as a child without a father, clearing her of what the Jews accused her of by making the infant speak, and making her and her son a sign for the worlds.

﴿O Mary, be obedient to your Lord, prostrate yourself, and bow with those who bow.﴾ She was commanded to pray in congregation by mentioning its pillars (arkan), emphasising her commitment to them. He mentioned prostration before bowing either because it was so in their law (shari'ah), or to alert that the particle "wa" (and) does not necessitate sequence, or so that "irka'i" would be paired with "al-raki'in" to signal that those who have no bowing in their prayer are not worshippers. It was also said that qunut here means continuous obedience, as in His saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing﴾; that prostration means prayer, as in His saying: ﴿and after the prostrations﴾; and that bowing means humble submission and lowliness.

He mentioned prostration before bowing either because it was so in their law (shari'ah), or to alert that the particle "wa" (and) does not necessitate sequence, or so that "irka'i" would be paired with "al-raki'in" to signal that those who have no bowing in their prayer are not worshippers. It was also said that qunut here means continuous obedience, as in His saying: ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing﴾; that prostration means prayer, as in His saying: ﴿and after the prostrations﴾; and that bowing means humble submission and lowliness.

ذَلِكَ مِن أنْباءِ الغَيْبِ نُوحِيهِ إلَيْكَ
"That is among the news of the unseen which We reveal to you." That is, the stories we have mentioned are among the unseen matters which you could not have known except through revelation.

وَما كُنْتَ لَدَيْهِمْ إذْ يُلْقُونَ أقْلامَهُمْ
"And you were not with them when they cast their pens (aqlam)." That is, their arrows (aqdah, sing. qidh; the arrows used for casting lots, al-iqtiraa'). It is said that they drew lots with the pens with which they used to write the Torah, seeking blessing (tabarruk). The purpose is to establish that it is revelation, by way of mockery toward those who deny it. For the way of knowing events is by witnessing them or by hearing about them, and the absence of hearing is known to them without any doubt. So what remains is that the accusation would be that he could have witnessed it, and no rational person would suspect this.

أيُّهم يَكْفُلُ مَرْيَمَ
"Which of them would take charge of Maryam." This is connected to a omitted element indicated by "they cast their pens," meaning: they cast them so that they would know, or so that they would say: "Which of them would take charge of Maryam?"

وَما كُنْتَ لَدَيْهِمْ إذْ يَخْتَصِمُونَ
"And you were not with them when they disputed," competing over her guardianship.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 45–46:

﴿When the angels said﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿when the angels said﴾ mentioned earlier, with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (i'tirad); or it is a substitute for ﴿when they disputed﴾, on the basis that the occurrence of the dispute and the glad tidings took place over an extended period of time, like your saying "I met him in such-and-such year." ﴿O Mary, indeed Allah gives you glad tidings of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary﴾. "Al-Masih" (the Messiah) is his title, and it is one of the honorific titles, like al-Siddiq (the Truthful). Its origin in Hebrew is mashiha, meaning "the blessed." "Isa" is an arabized form of Yeshua. Both derive from masḥ (wiping/anointing): either because he was anointed with blessing or with what purified him from sins; or because he wiped the earth and did not settle in one place; or because Jibril wiped him. Deriving it from al-'ays (a whiteness overlaid with redness) is a forced opinion with no benefit. Since "son of Mary" is a descriptive attribute that distinguishes in the manner of proper names, it has been strung together with them. This does not conflict with the multiplicity of the predicate and the singularity of the subject, for it is a common noun in construct form, and it may be meant that by which he is known and distinguished from others is these three (names), since a name is the sign of the named and what distinguishes him from others. It is also permissible for "Isa" to be the predicate of an omitted subject, with "son of Mary" as its attribute. It was said "son of Mary" while the address is to her, as an alert that he would be born without a father, since children are attributed to their fathers and are not attributed to the mother except when the father is absent. ﴿Honoured in this world and the hereafter﴾ is a conditional/anticipated circumstantial state (hal muqaddarah) from "word"; and although it is indefinite, it is qualified, and its masculine form is for the sense. Honour (wajaha) in this world is prophethood, and in the hereafter it is intercession. ﴿And of those brought near﴾ to Allah. It was also said it indicates the elevation of his rank in Paradise, or his being raised to heaven and companionship with the angels.

﴿And he will speak to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾, i.e., he will speak to them while being a child and while being mature, with the speech of the prophets, without any difference.

Al-mahd is a verbal noun used to name what is prepared for the infant in his bed. It was said that he was raised as a young man, and that the intended meaning of "and in maturity" is after his descent. He mentioned his varying and mutually contrasting states as guidance that he is far removed from divinity. ﴿And of the righteous﴾ is a third circumstantial state from "word," or from its pronoun that is in "he will speak."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 3, verses 48–49:

﴿And He will teach him the Book and wisdom, and the Torah and the Gospel.﴾ This is an independent new statement (*kalam mubtada'*, a sentence that begins a new clause and is not grammatically dependent on what precedes it). It was mentioned to comfort her heart and to remove what worried her, the fear of blame, since she knew that she would give birth without a husband. It may also be a conjunction (*'atf*) with "He will give you good tidings" or with "a noble one (*wajihan*)." "The Book" means the writing (*al-kataba*), or it refers to the genus of the revealed books. The two books (the Torah and the Gospel) are singled out for their excellence. Nafi' and 'Asim recited *wa-yu'allimuhu* (وَيُعَلِّمُهُ) with the *ya'* (يَ).

﴿And a messenger to the Children of Israel, [saying]: "Indeed I have come to you with a sign from your Lord."﴾ It is in the accusative (*mansub*) governed by an implied verb, with the meaning of "saying." Its estimated form is: "And he says: I have been sent as a messenger, [saying] that I have come to you." Or it is coordinated (*'atf*) with the preceding circumstantial phrases (*al-ahwal*), with the sense of speech implied, so it is as if he said: "And speaking, [saying] that I have come to you." The specification of the Children of Israel is due to the particular scope of his mission to them, or to refute the one who claimed that he was sent to others besides them.

﴿"That I create for you from clay the likeness of a bird."﴾ It is in the accusative as a substitute (*badal*) for "that I have come to you," or in the genitive as a substitute for "a sign," or in the nominative as [the predicate of an implied subject], "it is that I create for you." The meaning is: I determine for you and shape something like the form of a bird. Nafi' recited *inni* (إنّى) with the kasra (i.e., with the *kasra* on the *nun*). The pronoun in *fa-anfukhu fihi* (فَأنْفُخُ فِيهِ) refers to the *ka* (the "you" in *lakum*), meaning "into that similar thing."

﴿So it becomes a bird by the permission of Allah.﴾ That is, it becomes a living thing that flies by the command of Allah. By this he points out that its being given life comes from Allah, the Exalted, and not from him. Nafi' recited here and in al-Ma'idah *ta'iran* (طَائِرًا) with the *alif* and the *hamza*.

﴿And I heal the blind from birth and the leper.﴾ *Al-akmah* is the one born blind, or the one whose eye is wiped smooth (having no eye).

It is narrated that a great number of sick people would gather around him, thousands of them; whoever was able came to him, and whoever could not come, he (*'Isa*) went to them, peace be upon him. He healed only by supplication.

﴿And I bring the dead to life by the permission of Allah.﴾ He repeated "by the permission of Allah" to repel the suspicion of divinity, for giving life is not of the kind of human acts.

﴿And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses.﴾ [I inform you] of the unseen matters of your states, of which you have no doubt.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers.﴾ That is, if you are granted success to faith, for others do not benefit from miracles. Or [it means]: if you are truth-accepting ones, not stubborn opponents.

﴿And confirming what was before me of the Torah﴾. It is conjoined to *rasūlan* (ﷺ... rather, "a messenger") according to both possibilities, or it is in the accusative (*manṣūb*) by the implied verb indicated by *qad jiʾtukum* ("I have come to you"), meaning: "and I have come to you confirming." ﴿And that I may make lawful for you﴾ is either supplied by an implied verb, or it is referred back to his saying, "that I have come to you with a sign," or it is conjoined to the meaning of *muṣaddiqan* (confirming), as in the saying, "I came to you apologizing and to console your heart." ﴿Some of that which was forbidden to you﴾, that is, in the law of Moses, peace be upon him, such as fats, the fat around the kidneys, fish, camel meat, and work on the Sabbath. This points to completing the theoretical faculty (al-quwwa al-nazariyya) through the true belief whose ultimate aim is tawhid. And he said: ﴿So worship Him﴾, which points to completing the practical faculty (al-quwwa al-'ilmiyya), for it is by constant obedience, which is performing the commands and refraining from the prohibitions. Then he confirmed this by making clear that combining the two matters is the path witnessed to be upright. A parallel to this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Say: I have believed in Allah, then be steadfast."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 52:

﴿When Jesus perceived their disbelief﴾: their disbelief became certain to him in the way that what is perceived by the senses is certain. ﴿He said: "Who are my helpers in the cause of God?"﴾ meaning, seeking refuge with God Most High, or going towards Him, or joining Himself to Him. It is also permissible for the preposition (al-jar) to be connected to "helpers" (ansari) with the sense of "addition" implied, i.e., who are those who attach themselves to God Most High in supporting me? It has been said that "ila" (to) here means "ma'a" (with), or "fi" (in), or the "lam" (for).

﴿The disciples said﴾: the hawari (disciple) of a man is his close companion, from al-hawar, which is pure whiteness, and from it comes al-hawariyyat (the urban women), because of the purity of their complexions. The companions of Jesus, peace be upon him, were named with this because of the purity of their intention and the cleanness of their inner state. It has been said that they were kings who wore white garments, whom Jesus, peace be upon him, sought help from against the Jews. It has also been said that they were launderers who whitened clothes, i.e., made them white. ﴿We are God's helpers﴾, i.e., helpers of God's religion. ﴿We believe in God, and bear witness that we are Muslims﴾, so that You may bear witness for us on the Day of Resurrection, when the messengers bear witness for their peoples and against them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 53–54:

﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down and followed the Messenger, so record us among the witnesses.﴾ That is, among those who witness to Your oneness; or among the prophets, who bear witness for their followers; or among the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), for they are witnesses over mankind.

﴿And they schemed﴾, that is, those among the Jews who sensed disbelief from him (ʿĪsā) by appointing someone to kill him secretly. ﴿And Allah schemed﴾ when He raised ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) and cast his likeness upon the one who intended to assassinate him, so that he was killed. Strictly speaking, *makr* (scheming) is a stratagem by which one leads another into harm, and it is not attributed to Allah Most High except in the sense of reciprocity and pairing (*muqābalah* and *izdiwāj*, i.e., the figure of speech in which a term is matched with its counterpart). ﴿And Allah is the best of schemers﴾, the most powerful of them in scheming and the most capable of bringing harm from where it is not expected.

﴿When God said﴾ is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) governed either by "God plotted" (makara Allah) or by "the best of plotters" (khayr al-makirin), or by an implied verb such as "that happened" (waqaʿa dhalika). ﴿O Jesus, I am going to cause you to die﴾ means: I will take in full your term (mustawfin ajalaka) and defer you until your appointed term (ajalika al-musamma), protecting you from their killing. Or it means: I will take you from the earth, from the expression tawaffaytu mali (I took my property in full). Or it means: I will cause you to die in your sleep, since it is reported that he was raised while asleep. Or it means: I will cause you to die to the desires that hinder ascent to the realm of malakut (the invisible dominion of the heavens). It has also been said that God caused him to die for seven hours and then raised him to heaven, and the Christians adopted this view. ﴿And raising you to Me﴾ means to the place of My honour and the abode of My angels. ﴿And purifying you from those who disbelieve﴾ means from the evil of their company or their intentions. ﴿And making those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection﴾ means He aids them with proof or with the sword in most matters. His followers are those who believed in his prophethood among the Muslims and the Christians. Until now, no victory of the Jews over them has been heard of, and no dominion or state has been granted to them. ﴿Then to Me is your return﴾: the pronoun refers to Jesus, upon him be peace, and to those who followed him and those who disbelieved in him, and the addressees are given precedence over the absent ones. ﴿So I will judge between you concerning that wherein you used to differ﴾ means concerning matters of religion.(p-20)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 56–57:

﴿As for those who disbelieve, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.﴾ "As for those who believe and do righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full." This is an elaboration (tafsir) of the ruling (hukm) and a detailing of it. Hafs read "fa-yuwaffihim" with the ya' (in the third person). ﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ This is a confirmation (taqrir) of that.
