This is the commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 58:

﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to what preceded of the account of ʿIsa (Jesus) and others, and it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is: ﴿We recite it to you﴾. And his saying: ﴿of the signs﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun (hāʾ) [in "natluhu"]. It is permissible that the predicate be "natluhu" and that it be a circumstantial clause, on the basis that the governing element (ʿāmil) is the meaning of the demonstrative; and that both be predicates; and that it be in the accusative governed by an implied verb which "natluhu" explains. ﴿And the wise Reminder﴾ — the one containing the ruling (ḥukm), or the one that is firmly established (muḥkam), protected from the intrusion of any flaw into it. He means by it the Qur'an. It has also been said: the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 59–60:

﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before God is like the likeness of Adam﴾ Indeed, his strange state is like the state of Adam, peace be upon him. ﴿He created him from dust﴾ This is an explanatory clause (jumla mufassira) for the comparison, clarifying the respect in which the resemblance lies, namely that he was created without a father, just as Adam was created from dust without a father or a mother. He compared his condition to something even stranger than it, in order to silence the opponent and cut off the sources of doubt. The meaning is: He created his form (qalib) from dust. ﴿Then He said to him: Be!﴾ That is, He brought him into being as a human (bashar), as in His saying, Exalted is He: "Then We produced him as another creation" (23:14). Or it means He decreed his formation from dust and then formed him. It is also permissible that "then" (thumma) indicates a delay in the report, not in the event reported. ﴿So he was﴾ a narration of a past state.

﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾ The predicate is omitted, meaning: it is the truth. It has also been said that "the truth" is the subject and "from your Lord" is its predicate, meaning: the truth mentioned is from God, Exalted is He. ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾ This is an address to the Prophet ﷺ in the manner of stirring him up to increase his firmness, or it is addressed to every listener.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 3, verse 61:**

﴿Whoever argues with you about it﴾ from among the Christians. ﴿About it﴾ concerning Jesus. ﴿After the knowledge has come to you﴾ i.e., after the clear proofs that necessitate knowledge. ﴿Then say: "Come"﴾ hurry up, with resolve and determination. ﴿Let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves﴾ i.e., each of us and you should call upon himself, his dearest family members, and those closest to his heart, to join in mubahala (mutual invocation of curse) and urge them to it. He mentioned the sons and women before the selves because a man risks himself for them and fights in their defense. ﴿Then let us invoke earnestly﴾ i.e., let us call down a curse (mubahala) by cursing the liar among us. The word bahla, with a dammah or a fathah, means curse. Its root meaning is "leaving," from the saying "bahaltu al-naqa" when one leaves the she-camel without a tether. ﴿And let the curse of Allah be upon the liars﴾ this is a coordinated clause that serves as an explanation.

It is narrated that when they were called to mubahala, they said, "Let us wait and consider." When they withdrew privately, they said to al-Aqib, who was their man of opinion, "What do you think?" He said: "By Allah, you have known his prophethood, and he has brought you the decisive word concerning the matter of your companion. By Allah, no people have ever invoked curses upon a prophet without being destroyed. So if you refuse except to hold to your religion, then make peace with the man and depart." So they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who had gone out embracing al-Husayn, holding the hand of al-Hasan, with Fatima walking behind him and Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) behind her. He was saying: "When I supplicate, say Amen." Their bishop (usquf) said: "O assembly of Christians, I see faces which, if they asked Allah Most High to remove a mountain from its place, He would remove it. So do not invoke curses, lest you perish." Thus they submitted to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and offered him the jizya (poll tax) of two thousand red garments and thirty iron coats of mail. Then the Messenger (ﷺ), upon whom be blessings and peace, said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, had they invoked curses, they would have been transformed into apes and swine, the valley would have blazed with fire over them, and Allah would have uprooted Najran and its people, even the birds upon the trees." This is evidence of his prophethood and of the excellence of those whom he brought with him from his household (ahl al-bayt).

Indeed, this (i.e., what has been related of the story of Jesus and Mary) is the true narrative. In terms of its whole clause, it is the predicate (khabar) of inna (إنَّ). Or it is a separating pronoun (fasl, ﻓَﺼْﻞ), which indicates that what He mentioned about Jesus and Mary is true, not what they (the Christians) claimed. What follows it is the predicate. The lam (اللّام) entered upon it because it is closer to the subject (mubtada) than the predicate is, whereas its original place is to enter upon the subject.

﴿And there is no god except Allah.﴾ Here He explicitly used min (مِن) as an added particle for generality, to emphasise the refutation of the Christians in their trinitarian doctrine. ﴿And indeed Allah, He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.﴾ No one other than Him equals Him in complete power and consummate wisdom, so that anyone could share with Him in divinity.

﴿Then if they turn away, indeed Allah is All-Knowing of the corrupters.﴾ This is a warning to them. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate that turning away from the proofs and aversion from monotheism is a corruption of the religion and of belief, which leads to the corruption of the soul, and indeed to the corruption of the world.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 64:

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you﹣﻿ ...﴾ This encompasses the People of the Two Scriptures (ahl al-kitab). It was also said that it refers to the delegation of Najran, or to the Jews of Medina. ﴿...that we worship none but Allah﴾ — that we make Him one in worship (tawhid al-'ibadah) and devote worship to Him sincerely. ﴿and not associate anything with Him﴾ — and not make anything other than Him a partner with Him in deserving worship, nor consider anyone worthy of being worshipped.

﴿And not take one another as lords besides Allah﴾ — and we do not say "Uzayr is the son of Allah," nor "the Messiah is the son of Allah," nor obey the rabbis (ahbar) in what they have innovated of prohibition and permission, because each of them, like us, is a human being.

It is narrated that when the verse ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ was revealed, 'Adi ibn Hatim said: "We did not worship them, O Messenger of Allah." He (ﷺ) said: "Do they not make lawful for you and make unlawful, and you follow their word?" He said: "Yes." He said: "That is it."

﴿But if they turn away﴾ from monotheism, ﴿then say, "Bear witness that we are Muslims"﴾ — that is, the proof has been established against you, so acknowledge that we are Muslims apart from you; or acknowledge that you are disbelievers in what the Scriptures have declared and upon which the messengers were in agreement.

(Note: Observe what he took into account in this narrative of gentle guidance and the graceful progression of argument, between: first, the circumstances of Jesus, peace be upon him, and the various states through which he passed that are incompatible with divinity; then the mention of what unties their knot and removes their doubt; then, when he saw their obstinacy and stubbornness, he invited them to mutual invocation (mubahala) through a kind of miracle; then, when they turned away from it and submitted only partially, he returned to guiding them and took an easier and more binding path, inviting them to what Jesus, the Gospel, and all the prophets and scriptures agreed upon; then, when he found that this too did not succeed with them and knew that signs and warnings would not avail them, he set that aside and said, "Then say: Bear witness that we are Muslims.")

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 65:

﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him?﴾ The Jews (yahud) and the Christians (nasara) disputed concerning Abraham, peace be upon him, and each group claimed that he was of them. They brought their dispute before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed.

The meaning is that Judaism and Christianity came into being after the revelation of the Torah and the Gospel to Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both. Abraham was a thousand years before Moses and two thousand years before Jesus, so how could he be upon either of them? ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ That is, will you not understand, so that you would not claim the impossible?

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 66:

﴿Ah, you are those who argued about what you have knowledge of, so why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of?﴾ Ha (ha) is a particle of alerting (harf tanbih); they were alerted by it to their state, of which they had been heedless. Antum (you) is the subject (mubtada'), ha'ulaa' (these) is its predicate (khabar), and hajajtum (you argued) is another clause explaining the first. That is: you are these fools, and the explanation of your foolishness is that you argued about what you have knowledge of, from what you found in the Torah and the Gospel, out of obstinacy; or you claim that it is in them. So why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of, and which is not mentioned in your books, concerning the religion of Ibrahim (Abraham)? It has also been said that ha'ulaa' means alladhina (those who), and hajajtum is its relative clause (silah). It has also been said that ha antum originally was a'antum, a question for the sake of expressing wonder at their foolishness, and the hamza was changed into ha. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read ha antum wherever it occurs with a long vowel (madd) and without hamza; Warsh has a shorter madd; Qunbul reads with hamza and without an alif after the ha; the rest read with madd and hamza; and al-Bazzi reads with short madd according to his own principle.

﴿And Allah knows﴾ what you argued about in it.

﴿And you do not know﴾ and you are ignorant of it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 67–68:

﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾ This is an explicit statement in accordance with what was established by the proof (al-burhan) he had presented. ﴿But he was a ḥanīf﴾ inclining away from the deviant creeds (al-ʿaqāʾid al-zāʾigha). ﴿A muslim﴾ submitting to God. It is not meant that he was upon the religion of Islam, for otherwise the obligation would be shared (lalazima al-ilzām anyone would be included). ﴿Nor was he of the polytheists﴾ an allusion that they (the polytheists) are polytheists, because of their associating with Him ʿUzayr and the Messiah, and a refutation of the polytheists' claim that they are upon the religion of Abraham, peace be upon him.

﴿Indeed, the people most entitled to Abraham﴾ indeed, those most particularly connected to him and closest to him, from al-walī (the close ally), which means nearness, ﴿are those who followed him﴾ from among his community. This Prophet (ﷺ) and those who believe are included, because of their agreement with him in most of what was legislated for them originally. It has been read as wa-l-nabiyya in the accusative, as a conjunction with the pronoun in ittabaʿūhu, and in the genitive, as a conjunction with Ibrahim. ﴿And God is the Guardian of the believers﴾ He supports them and rewards them with the best (al-ḥusnā) for their faith.

﴿And they do not lead astray except themselves⦆ The misguidance does not go beyond them, and its burden returns only upon them, since their punishment is thereby multiplied. Or, it means: they lead astray none but their own likes.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 70–71:

﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God﴾ in what the Torah and the Gospel have declared and what indicated the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿while you witness﴾ that they are the signs of God; or [it means]: ﴿while you witness﴾ with the Qur'an [that it is the signs of God]; or [it means]: ﴿while you witness﴾ his description in the two Books, or ﴿while you know﴾ through the miracles that he is the truth.

(p-23) ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you clothe the truth with falsehood﴾ by distorting it and presenting falsehood in the guise of truth, or by failing to distinguish between them. It was read as "tulabbisūna" with doubling of the ba' (to confuse/obscure), and as "talbasūna" with a fatha on the ba' (to mix), meaning: you mix the truth with falsehood, like his saying, peace be upon him: "like one who wears two garments of falsehood" (kalabisi thawbay zūr).

And you conceal the truth, the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his description. ﴿while you know﴾ that you are concealing it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 72:

﴿And a group of the People of the Scripture said: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, that perhaps they will return."﴾ That is: show belief in the Qur'an at the beginning of the day. ﴿And disbelieve at its end, that perhaps they will return.﴾ That is: disbelieve in it at its end, so that perhaps they will doubt their religion, thinking that you have returned (to your old faith) because of a flaw that has appeared to you. The group is meant to be Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Malik ibn al-Sayf, who said to their companions when the qibla was changed: "Believe in what has been revealed to them concerning the prayer toward the Ka'ba, and pray toward it at the beginning of the day; then pray toward the Rock at its end, so that perhaps they will say, 'They are more knowledgeable than us, and they have returned, so they return.'" It was also said: twelve of the rabbis of Khaybar conspired together that they would enter Islam at the beginning of the day and say at its end, "We examined our book and consulted our scholars, and we did not find Muhammad (ﷺ) to have the description that came in the Torah," so that perhaps his companions would doubt him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 3, verses 73–74:

﴿And do not believe except for those who follow your religion.﴾ That is, do not reveal the affirmation of the heart except to the people of your religion. Or it means: do not make your faith apparent at the beginning of the day to anyone who is of your religion, for their returning (to disbelief) is more hoped for and more important. ﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God.﴾ He guides whom He wills to faith and keeps him firm upon it. ﴿That anyone should be given the like of what you were given.﴾ This is connected to an elided element (*mahdhuf*), meaning: you devised this and said, "Let no one be given..." The meaning is that envy moved you to this, or it is connected to "do not believe," meaning: do not make your faith apparent, lest anyone be given the like of what you were given, except to your partisans. Do not spread it to the Muslims, lest their steadfastness increase, nor to the polytheists, lest they be invited to Islam. As for His saying:

﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God⦆ is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD*) indicating that their scheming is of no avail. Or it is the predicate of *inna* (indeed), with "the guidance of God" being a substitute (*badal*) for "guidance." The reading of Ibn Kathir, ﴿an yu'ta﴾ (that anyone be given), in the form of an interrogative for rebuke (*istifham li-al-taqri'*), supports the first interpretation, meaning: "Do you devise that anyone be given?" The reading "in" (if) has also been recited as a negative particle, in which case it is part of the speech of the group, meaning: ﴿And do not believe except for those who follow your religion﴾, and say to them: nothing is given ﴿to anyone like what you were given, or they will argue with you before your Lord﴾. This is conjoined to "that anyone should be given" according to the first two interpretations, and according to the third its meaning is: "until they argue with you before your Lord, and thus refute your proof before your Lord." The waw (in *yuhajjukum*) is the pronoun of "anyone," because it carries the sense of the plural, since what is meant by it is other than their followers. ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills, and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

﴿He specifically chooses for His mercy whom He wills, and God is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ This is a rejection and nullification of what they claimed, by means of clear proof.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 75:

﴿And among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you﴾. Like ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, with whom a man of Quraysh deposited one thousand two hundred ounces of gold, and he returned it to him. And among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you﴾, like Finhas ibn ʿAzuraʾ, with whom another man of Quraysh deposited a dinar, and he denied it. (p-24)

It has also been said: the trustworthy ones regarding the large amount are the Christians, since trustworthiness is predominant among them, and the treacherous ones regarding the small amount are the Jews, since treachery is predominant among them. Ḥamza, Abu Bakr and Abu ʿAmr read *yuʾaddihi ilaykum* and *lā yuʾaddihi ilaykum* with the *hāʾ* sukūn (silent). Qalun read with *ikhtilās* (the brief, partial vocalization) of the kasra of the *hāʾ*, and it is likewise narrated from Ḥafs. The rest read with *ishbāʿ* (full vocalization) of the kasra.

﴿Except so long as you stand over him﴾: except for the duration of your continuing to stand over him, insistently demanding it from him through litigation, legal contention, and the establishing of proof. ﴿That﴾ refers to the abstention from repayment indicated by his saying *lā yuʾaddihi*. ﴿Because they say﴾: due to their saying. ﴿There is no blame upon us regarding the gentiles﴾: that is, there is no blame upon us concerning those who are not of the People of the Book and who were not upon our religion, is a reproach and a condemnation. ﴿And they speak falsehood against Allah﴾ by their claiming this, ﴿while they know﴾ that they are lying. That is because they deemed it lawful to wrong those who opposed them, and they said: "No sanctity has been ordained for them in the Torah."

It has also been said: the Jews dealt with men of Quraysh, and when they embraced Islam, the Jews demanded their dues from them, saying: "Your right has lapsed since you abandoned your religion," and they claimed that this was so in their Book.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said when this verse was revealed: "The enemies of Allah have lied. There is nothing from the days of ignorance that is not under my feet, except trustworthiness, for it is to be returned to the righteous and the wicked."

"Yes" is an affirmation of what they denied, i.e., yes, there is a way (of blame) over them concerning them. ﴿Whoever fulfils his covenant and is mindful of God—indeed God loves the mindful.﴾ This is a resumptive clause that confirms the sentence which "yes" has taken the place of. The pronoun in the genitive refers either to "whoever" or to God, and the generality of "the mindful" stands in for the returning pronoun of the consequent back to "whoever." I perceive that taqwa (God-consciousness, mindfulness of God) is the essence of the matter, and it encompasses fulfilling covenants and other things, such as performing obligations and abstaining from prohibitions.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 77:

﴿Indeed, those who exchange﴾ (yashtaruna) means: those who substitute (yastabdiluna). ﴿the covenant of Allah﴾ means: that which they covenanted with Allah regarding, namely faith in the Messenger and fulfilling the trusts (al-amanat). ﴿and their oaths﴾ means: and what they swore by, such as their saying, "By Allah, we will surely believe in him and surely support him." ﴿for a small price﴾ means: the enjoyment of this worldly life. ﴿Those will have no share in the Hereafter, and Allah will not speak to them﴾ means: He will not speak to them with anything that would please them, or at all. It is also said that the angels will question them on the Day of Resurrection, or that they will not benefit from the words of Allah and His signs. The apparent meaning is that it is a metaphor (kinaya) for His anger toward them, based on His saying: ﴿And He will not look at them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, for whoever is angry with another and holds him in contempt turns away from him, from speaking with him and from turning toward him, just as whoever values another converses with him and looks at him often. ﴿And He will not purify them﴾ means: and He will not praise them. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ for what they did. It has been said that it was revealed concerning rabbis who distorted the Torah and altered the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), the rulings on trusts and other matters, and took a bribe for that. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning a man who displayed merchandise in the market and swore that he had purchased it for a price he had not paid. It has further been said that it was revealed concerning a dispute that took place between al-Ash'ath ibn Qays and a Jew over a well or a piece of land, and the oath was directed at the Jew.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 78:

﴿And indeed, among them is a group﴾ meaning the distorters, such as Ka'b, Malik and Huyayy ibn Akhtab. ﴿who distort their tongues with the Book﴾ they twist them with its recitation, inclining them away from the revealed text toward the altered one, or they bend them with something resembling the Book. It is also read as "yalūna" (يَلْوُنَ), by changing the damma on the waw into a hamza and then easing it by dropping it and placing its vowel on the consonant before it. ﴿So that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book﴾ The pronoun refers to the altered text implied by their words "who distort". It is also read as "liyaḥsabūhu" (لِيَحْسَبُوهُ) with the yā' (the verb being third person plural), and the pronoun then also refers to the Muslims.

﴿And they say, "It is from Allah," but it is not from Allah﴾ This is an emphasis of their statement "and it is not from the Book," a denunciation of them, and an explanation that they claim this explicitly, not by allusion, meaning: it has not been sent down from Him. This does not imply that the act of the servant cannot be the act of Allah the Exalted.

﴿And they speak falsehood against Allah while they know﴾ This is an emphasis and a recording against them of lying against Allah and of deliberateness in it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 79:

﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Book, the judgment and the prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be servants of mine rather than of Allah."﴾ This is a refutation and rejection of His servant Jesus, peace be upon him.

It is also said: "That Abu Rafi' al-Qurazi and the Najrani leader said: 'O Muhammad, do you want us to worship you and take you as a lord?' He said: 'I seek refuge in Allah from worshipping other than Allah or commanding the worship of other than Allah. It is not for this that I was sent, nor was I commanded with this.' So it was revealed."

It is also said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, shall we greet you as some of us greet one another, and shall we not prostrate to you?' He said: 'It is not fitting that prostration be made to anyone other than Allah. Rather, honour your Prophet and recognise the rights of those who deserve them.'"

﴿But rather, be rabbis﴾: "but rather, He says, 'Be rabbis (rabbaniyyin).'" The rabbani (rabbaniyy, one devoted to the Lord) is attributed to the Lord (rabb) with the addition of the alif and nun, like al-lihyani and al-ruqbani, and it means the one who is perfect in knowledge and action. ﴿Because you have been teaching the Book and because you have been studying it﴾: because of your being teachers of the Book and because of your being students of it, for the benefit of teaching and learning is knowing the truth and the good, for belief and action. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read *ta'lamuna* (with a fathah on the lam, from 'alima) in the sense of "knowing." It was also read *tadrusuna* from *al-tadris* (teaching), and *tadrusuna* from *adrusa* in the sense of *darasa* (to study), like *akrama* and *karuma*. It is also permissible that the well-known reading carries this meaning as well, on the presumption of *wa-bima kuntum tadrusunahu 'ala al-nas* (and because you have been studying it to the people).

﴿And He would not command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾ was read with the accusative (نَصَبَهُ, *naṣabahu*) by Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqūb, as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with ثُمَّ يَقُولَ (*thumma yaqūla*, "then say"). In this reading the لا (*lā*) is an extra particle (*zāʾidah*, redundant) that emphasizes the negation in the phrase ما كانَ (*mā kāna*, "it is not for"). The meaning is: it is not for a human whom God has granted prophethood to then command people to worship himself and to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Alternatively, the لا is not extra, and the meaning is that it is not for him to command worship of himself, nor to command taking his equals as lords. Rather, he forbids that, and this is less than worship. The rest read it with the nominative (رَفَعَهُ, *rafaʿahu*), as a resumptive new sentence (al-istiʾnāf). It may also be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Abū ʿAmr read it according to his own practice, in the transmission of al-Dūrī, with ikhtilās (rapid, half-voiced pronunciation) of the ḍamm (الضَّمّ).

﴿Would he command you to disbelief﴾ is a rebuke (inkār), and the pronoun in it refers to the human. It was also said that it refers to God.

﴿After you have submitted﴾ is evidence that the address is to the Muslims, and they are the ones who asked permission to prostrate to him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 81:

﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets: "Whatever I have given you of the Book and wisdom, and then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and you must help him."﴾ It has been said that it is on its apparent meaning. And if this is the ruling for the Prophets, then the nations are more deserving of it. It has also been said that its meaning is that He, exalted is He, took the covenant from the Prophets and their nations, and by mentioning them He dispensed with mentioning the nations. It has also been said that the attribution of the covenant to the Prophets is an attribution to the agent, and the meaning is: "And when Allah took the covenant which the Prophets affirmed upon their nations." It has also been said that what is meant is the sons of the Prophets, with the omission of the modifier (muḍāf), and they are the Children of Israel; or He called them "Prophets" in mockery, because they used to say, "We are more deserving of prophethood than Muhammad, because we are the People of the Book, and the Prophets were from among us." The lam in "lamā" is a preparatory lam (lam al-muwaṭṭi'ah) for the oath, because taking the covenant carries the sense of making someone swear an oath; and "mā" may be conditional, and "la-tu'minunna" serves in place of the answer to both the oath and the condition, and it may also be declarative. Ḥamzah read "limā" with a kasra, on the basis that "mā" is verbal-masdarial (maṣdariyyah), meaning: because of my giving you some of the Book, then the coming of a Messenger confirming it; Allah took the covenant that you must believe in him and must help him. Or "mā" is relative (mawṣūlah), and the meaning is: He took it for the sake of that which I have given you, and there comes to you a Messenger confirming it. "Lammā" was also read, in the sense of "when" (ḥīna) I gave you; or "lamin ajli mā ātaytukum," on the basis that its origin is "lamin mā," which by assimilation (idghām) had one of the three mīms deleted due to heaviness. Nāfi' read "ātaynākum" with a nūn and an alif together. ﴿He said: "Do you affirm and accept this My covenant upon that?"﴾ That is, My pact (ʿahd); it was named "iṣr" because it is bound (yu'ṣar), that is, tied fast. It was also read with a ḍammah, and this is either a dialectal variant of it, like ʿibar and ʿabr, or the plural of iṣār, which is that by which something is tied. ﴿They said: "We affirm."  He said: "Then bear witness."﴾ That is, let some of you bear witness against others to the affirmation. It has also been said that the address in it is to the angels. ﴿And I am with you among the witnesses.﴾ And I too am a witness to your affirmation and your mutual witnessing, and this is a great emphasis and a serious warning.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 82–83:

﴿Whoever turns away after that﴾ — after the covenant and the affirmation through acknowledgment and testimony. ﴿Then those are the defiant ones (al-fasiqun)﴾ — the rebellious ones among the disbelievers.

﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾ It is conjoined to the preceding sentence, with the interrogative hamza (alif of denial, al-hamza li-l-inkar) placed between them. Or it is elided, its estimated form being: "Do you then turn away, and seek other than the religion of Allah?" The object is placed first because it is the focus of the denial. The verb is in the third-person form (yabghun) according to Abu 'Amr and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs, and Ya'qub, and in the second-person form (tabghun) according to the rest, on the assumption of an implied "and say to them" (qul lahu). ﴿And to Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly﴾ — that is, willing through reflection and following the proof, and unwilling through the sword and witnessing what compels one to Islam, such as the lifting of the mountain over them, the drowning, and the approach of death. Or: willing, like the angels and the believers, and compelled, like the disbelievers, for they cannot refrain from what has been decreed for them. ﴿And to Him they will be returned﴾ — it was also read with the ya' (yurja'un), on the basis that the pronoun refers to "whoever."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 84:

﴿Say: "We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord."﴾ This is a command to the Messenger ﷺ to inform, concerning himself and his followers, of their faith. The Qur'an, just as it is sent down upon him, is sent down upon them through the mediation of his conveying it to them. Also, what is attributed to one member of a group may be attributed to all of them. Or it is a command for him to speak of himself in the manner of kings, out of honor for him. The verb "nuzul" (descent) is construed with "ila" (to) as it ends with the Messengers, and it is construed with "ʿala" (upon) because it comes from above. He mentioned the one upon whom it was sent down, peace be upon him, before what was sent down to the rest of the Messengers, because he is the one who makes them known and the standard by which they are measured. ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾ in affirmation or denial. ﴿And to Him we are submitting﴾, that is, obedient, or sincerely devoted in His worship.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 85:

﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion﴾ — that is, other than monotheism (tawhid) and submission to the judgment of God. ﴿it will never be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers﴾ — those who fall into loss. The meaning is that one who turns away from Islam and seeks other than it is devoid of benefit and falls into loss, by nullifying the sound natural disposition (fitrah) upon which God created people. It has been used as evidence that faith (iman) is Islam, since if it were other than it, it would not be accepted. The reply is that it negates the acceptance of every religion that is different from it, not the acceptance of everything that is different from it; and perhaps "religion" (din) here also refers to deeds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 86:

﴿How will Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief, and who had testified that the Messenger was true and the clear proofs had come to them?﴾ This is an expression of astonishment (istib'ad) at the idea that Allah would guide them, for one who turns away from the truth after it has become clear to him is immersed in misguidance and far from rectitude. It has also been said that it is a negation and a denial of guidance for them, and this entails that the repentance of the apostate is not accepted. "And had testified" (wa-shahidu) is coordinated (ʿutifa) with what is in "after their belief" of the meaning of a verb, and its parallel is in fa-asaddaqa wa-akun (﴿so I would give charity and be among the righteous﴾). Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) with an implied qad, [referring to] "those who disbelieved." On both interpretations, it is evidence that verbal affirmation is outside the reality of faith (haqiqat al-iman).

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾, who wronged themselves by neglecting reflection (al-nazar) and placed disbelief in the place of faith. So how much more so [is it true of] one to whom the truth has come, who has recognized it, and then turned away from it.

﴿Those, their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together.﴾ By its explicit meaning (manṭūq) it indicates the permissibility of cursing them, and by its implicit meaning (mafhūm) it indicates the negation of the permissibility of cursing others. Perhaps the distinction is that they are sealed upon disbelief, barred from guidance, and utterly despaired of mercy, unlike others. The intended meaning of "mankind" is the believers, or it is general, for the disbeliever also curses the one who denies the truth and the apostate from it, but he does not know the truth in its specific form.

﴿Abiding therein﴾ in the curse, or the punishment, or the Fire, though mentioning these is not permissible, due to the indication of the speech upon them. ﴿The punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾

﴿Those, their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together.﴾ By its explicit meaning (manṭūq) it indicates the permissibility of cursing them, and by its implicit meaning (mafhūm) it indicates the negation of the permissibility of cursing others. Perhaps the distinction is that they are sealed upon disbelief, barred from guidance, and utterly despaired of mercy, unlike others. The intended meaning of "mankind" is the believers, or it is general, for the disbeliever also curses the one who denies the truth and the apostate from it, but he does not know the truth in its specific form.

﴿Abiding therein﴾ in the curse, or the punishment, or the Fire, though mentioning these is not permissible, due to the indication of the speech upon them. ﴿The punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 89:

﴿Except those who repent after that﴾, i.e., after the apostasy. ﴿And make amends﴾ for what they corrupted. It is also permissible that no object be supposed for it, with the meaning: and enter into righteousness. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Oft-Forgiving﴾, accepting their repentance. ﴿Most Merciful﴾, bestowing grace upon them.

It has been said: it was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Suwayd, when he regretted his apostasy and sent to his people, [saying]: "Ask whether there is any repentance for me." His brother al-Julas sent to him with the verse, so he returned to Madinah and repented.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 90:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief﴾ – like the Jews, who disbelieved in Jesus and the Gospel after believing in Moses and the Torah, then increased in disbelief by [rejecting] Muhammad and the Qur'an. Or [it refers to] those who disbelieved in Muhammad after they had believed in him before his mission (ba'th), then increased in disbelief by persisting [in it], showing enmity, slandering him, barring [others] from faith and breaking the covenant. Or [it refers to] a people who apostatized and joined Makkah, then increased in disbelief by their saying, "We await for Muhammad the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun)," or "We will return to him and feign [faith] to him by displaying it." ﴿Their repentance will never be accepted﴾ – because they do not repent; or, they do not repent except when they are on the brink of destruction, so the non-repentance is expressed metonymically by the non-acceptance of repentance, as an intensification concerning their state and a depiction of their condition in the form of the condition of those who have despaired of mercy. Or, because their repentance would be nothing but hypocrisy, given their apostasy and increase in disbelief; and for this reason the particle fa' (then/so) does not enter into it.

﴿And those are the astray⁠—﴾ those who are firmly established in misguidance.

Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, never will there be accepted from any one of them the fill of the earth in gold﴾. Since death upon disbelief is the cause for the impossibility of accepting ransom, He placed the *fa'* (the particle "then/so") here to indicate this. "The fill of a thing" (*mil'* al-shay') is what fills it. "Gold" (*dhahaban*) is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification, the accusative noun that clarifies the preceding quantity). It was also read in the nominative, as a *badal* (substitution, in apposition) for *mil'*, or as the predicate (*khabar*) of an elided subject (*mahdhuf*).

﴿And even if he should ransom himself with it﴾ is construed according to the sense (*mahmul 'ala al-ma'na*), as if it were said: "There will never be accepted from any one of them a ransom, even if he ransomed himself with the fill of the earth in gold." Or it is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) with an implied element, its estimated sense being: "There will never be accepted from any one of them the fill of the earth in gold, even if he drew near with it in this world, and even if he ransomed himself with it from the punishment in the Hereafter." Or the intended meaning is "even if he ransomed himself with its like" (*bi-mithlihi*), as in His saying: ﴿And if those who did wrong had all that is in the earth and the like of it with it﴾. The *mithl* (like) is often elided and intended, because two like things are in the ruling of one thing.

﴿Those, for them is a painful punishment﴾: this is an intensification in warning and a cutting off of hope, because one from whom ransom is not accepted may perhaps be pardoned out of generosity.

﴿And they have no helpers﴾ in repelling the punishment. The *min* here is superfluous (*za'idah*), used for generalization (*li-l-istighraq*).

(p-28)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 92:

﴿You will never attain righteousness﴾ i.e., you will never reach the reality of righteousness (al-birr), which is the perfection of goodness; or, you will never attain the righteousness of God (birr Allah), which is mercy, approval and Paradise. ﴿Until you spend from what you love﴾ i.e., from wealth, or from whatever encompasses it and other things, such as expending standing (jah) in helping people, the body in obedience to God, and the life-blood (muhjah) in His way.

It is narrated: "When it was revealed, Abu Talhah came and said: 'O Messenger of God, the dearest of my wealth to me is Bayruha'. So place it wherever God shows you.' He said: 'Bakh, bakh! That is profitable wealth (mal rabih aw ra'ih), and I think you should give it to your nearest relatives.'" And Zayd ibn Harithah came with a horse he loved and said: "This is for the sake of God." So the Messenger of God ﷺ mounted Usamah ibn Zayd on it. Zayd said: "I only meant to give it in charity." He (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed God has accepted it from you."

Or that indicates that spending the dearest wealth on the closest relatives is more excellent, and that the verse covers obligatory and recommended spending. It was also read as "some of what you love" (ba'd ma tuhibbun), which indicates that min (from) is partitive (lil-tab'id) and may also be explanatory (lil-tabyin). ﴿And whatever you spend of anything﴾ i.e., of any beloved thing or other, and min here is explanatory (li-bayan ma). ﴿Indeed God is Knowing of it﴾, so He will reward you according to it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 93:

﴿All the food﴾, that is, the foods, and what is meant is eating them. ﴿Was lawful for the Children of Israel﴾, meaning permitted to them. The word *hill* (lawful) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) used as an adjective, which is why it is the same for the singular and plural and for the masculine and feminine. God the Exalted says: ﴿They are not lawful for them﴾ (60:10). ﴿Except what Israel had forbidden﴾, that is, Ya'qub (Jacob), ﴿for himself﴾, such as the flesh of camels and their milk. It is said that he had sciatica, so he vowed that if he were healed he would not eat the food he loved most, and that was camel's milk, which he loved most. It is also said that he did this as a treatment, on the advice of physicians. Those who permit the Prophet to exercise independent reasoning (*ijtihad*) cite this as evidence, and those who oppose it say that he did so by permission from God in this matter, so it is like forbidding it from the outset. ﴿Before the Torah was sent down﴾, that is, before its revelation, containing the prohibition of what was forbidden to them as a punishment and an aggravation for their wrongdoing and transgression. This is a refutation of the Jews' claim of innocence regarding what was censured of them in God the Exalted's words: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things﴾ (4:160), and His words: ﴿And for those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾ (6:146), the two verses. They said: "We are not the first to whom these things were forbidden; they were forbidden to Noah, Abraham, and those after him, until the matter reached us, and so they were forbidden to us as they were forbidden to those before us." Rejecting abrogation (*naskh*, the cancellation of an earlier ruling by a later one) and challenging the Messenger's claim (peace be upon him) involves agreement with Abraham (peace be upon him) in permitting the flesh of camels and their milk. ﴿Say: "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful."﴾ This is a command to argue with them using their own Book and to rebuke them with what it contains, namely that certain things were forbidden to them because of their wrongdoing, which had not been forbidden before.

It is narrated: "When he (peace be upon him) said this to them, they were stunned and did not dare to bring out the Torah." In this there is evidence of his prophethood.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 94–95:

﴿So whoever fabricates a lie against God after that﴾ he invented it against God by claiming that He had forbidden that before the revelation of the Torah to the Children of Israel and those before them. ﴿after that﴾ after the proof had been established against them. ﴿it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾ those who do not deal justly with themselves and who obstinately reject the truth after it has become clear to them.

﴿Say: God has spoken the truth﴾ this is an allusion to their lying, meaning: it is established that God is truthful in what He has revealed, and you are the liars. ﴿So follow the religion (millah) of Abraham, a hanif (one who turns away from falsehood to pure monotheism)﴾ meaning the religion of Islam, which is in origin the religion of Abraham, or like his religion, so that you may free yourselves from Judaism, which compelled you to distort and to be obstinate in order to make worldly aims agree, and which obliged you to forbid good things that God had made lawful for Abraham and those who followed him. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾ this contains an indication that following him is obligatory in pure monotheism, in uprightness in religion, and in avoiding both excess and negligence, and it is an allusion to the polytheism of the Jews.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 96:

﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind﴾ i.e., it was established for worship and made a place of worship for them. The one who established it is Allah, the Exalted. This is indicated by the fact that it is also read in the passive form with the verb in the active voice (i.e., "Allah established"). ﴿is the one at Bakkah﴾, i.e., the House that is at Bakkah. Bakkah is a dialectal variant of Makkah, like al-Nabit and al-Namit (both referring to the same people, with the letter b and m interchanged), and like raatib and raatim, laazib and laazim (both meaning "fixed" or "constant"). It is also said that Bakkah is the specific place of the mosque. Makkah is the city, derived from bakk (to crowd), if it crowds (its people), or from bakkah (to crush), since it crushes the necks of tyrants.

It has been narrated that (ﷺ) was asked about the first House established for mankind, and he said: "The Sacred Mosque, then Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem)." He was asked how many years lay between them, and he said: "Forty years." It is also said that the first to build it was Ibrahim (Abraham), then it was demolished, and a people of Jurhum rebuilt it, then the Amalekites, then the Quraysh. It is also said that it was the first House built by Adam, which was obliterated in the Flood, and then Ibrahim rebuilt it. It is also said that before Adam there was a House at its location called al-Dirah, which the angels circumambulated; when Adam was sent down, he was commanded to make pilgrimage to it and circumambulate around it, and it was raised to the fourth heaven during the Flood, where the angels of the heavens circumambulate it. However, this does not fit the apparent meaning of the verse. It is also said that what is meant is that it is the first House in terms of honor, not in terms of time. ﴿Blessed﴾, abundant in good and benefit for whoever makes pilgrimage to it, performs the lesser pilgrimage (umrah) to it, observes seclusion (i'tikaf) at it, and circumambulates around it. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun within the adverbial phrase (zarf). ﴿And a guidance for the worlds﴾, because it is their qibla and place of worship, and because in it are wondrous signs, as he said:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 97:

﴿In it are clear signs﴾ such as the birds' deflection from passing over the House throughout the ages, and that ravening beasts mingle with game within the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) without attacking it, and that every tyrant who intends harm to it is overcome by God, like the People of the Elephant. The clause explains the guidance, or is another circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿The station of Abraham﴾ is a deleted subject (mubtada') whose predicate is: "from them is the station of Abraham," or it is a substitute (badal) for "signs," a substitution of part for whole (badal al-ba'd min al-kull). It has been said that it is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan), on the basis that the intended "signs" is the trace of a foot in the hard rock, and its sinking into it up to the ankles. Its singling out with this softening from among the rocks, and its preservation, unlike the other traces of the prophets, and its being kept for thousands of years despite the multitude of its enemies, are themselves signs. This is supported by the reading of "āyatun bayyinatun" in the singular. The cause of this trace is that when the building of the Ka'bah was raised, he stood upon this stone so that he could reach to lift the stones, and his feet sank into it.

﴿And whoever enters it is secure﴾ is either an independent clause (jumlah ibtida'iyyah), or a conditional clause coordinated in meaning with "station," since it means "the one who enters it is made secure," i.e., "and from them is the security of whoever enters it." Or [the meaning is]: "in it are clear signs: the station of Abraham and the security of whoever enters it." He mentioned only these two of the many signs and omitted mention of others, as in his saying, peace be upon him: "Three things of your world have been made dear to me: perfume, women, and the coolness of my eye in prayer."

Because in them is sufficiency over other things in both abodes: the lasting of the trace through the ages, and security from punishment on the Day of Resurrection.

He, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever dies in one of the two sanctuaries will be raised on the Day of Resurrection secure." According to Abu Hanifah, whoever is liable to execution for apostasy, retaliation, or other causes, and seeks refuge in the Haram, is not to be touched, but is compelled to come out.

﴿And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by mankind﴾: intending it for visitation in the specific manner. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and ʿAsim in the narration of Hafs read ḥijj with a kasrah, and it is the dialect of Najd. ﴿For whoever is able to make his way there﴾ is a substitute for "mankind," a substitution of part for whole, specified by it. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, explained "ability" as "provision and mount," and this supports the view of al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, that it is by wealth; for this reason he made it obligatory to appoint a deputy for one who is disabled, if he finds the wage of one who will perform it on his behalf. Malik, may God have mercy on him, said that it is by the body, so it is obligatory upon whoever is able to walk and earn along the way. Abu Hanifah, may God have mercy on him, said that it is (p-30) by the combination of both matters. The pronoun in "ilayhi" refers either to the House or to the pilgrimage, and whatever reaches a thing is its way.

﴿And whoever disbelieves — God is Independent of the worlds﴾: he placed "disbelieved" in the position of "whoever does not perform pilgrimage," to emphasise its obligation and to make its abandonment grave. For this reason he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever dies without having performed pilgrimage, let him die, if he wishes, as a Jew or a Christian."

The command of pilgrimage has been stressed in this verse in several ways of indication: by expressing it in the form of a statement, by presenting it in the nominal form, by stating it in a manner indicating that it is a right and obligation due to God upon the necessity of mankind; by generalising the ruling first and then specifying it second, for this is like clarification after ambiguity, and repetition and reiteration of the intended meaning; by calling the abandonment of pilgrimage disbelief, insofar as it is the act of disbelievers; and by mentioning independence (of God from the worlds), for in this context it indicates aversion and abandonment. His saying "from the worlds" also indicates this, because of the intensity of generality it contains, and the indication of being independent of it by proof, and the implication of great wrath, for it is an arduous obligation combining the breaking of the self, the exhaustion of the body, the expenditure of wealth, detachment from desires, and turning toward God.

It is narrated that when the first part of the verse was revealed, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, gathered the followers of the religions, addressed them, and said: "God, Exalted is He, has prescribed for you the pilgrimage, so perform it." One religion believed in it, and five religions disbelieved in it, so there was revealed: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 98–99:

﴿Say: O People of the Book, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God?﴾ That is, His signs, both revealed (sam'iyyah) and rational ('aqliyyah), which indicate the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) in what he claims regarding the obligation of the hajj (pilgrimage) and other matters. The specification of the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) as the addressees is evidence that their disbelief is more heinous, because their knowledge of the signs is stronger. Although they claim that they believe in the Tawrat (Torah) and the Injil (Gospel), they are disbelievers in both. ﴿And God is witness over what you do.﴾ While He is a witness, aware of your deeds, He will recompense you for them. Distortion and concealment will not benefit you.

﴿Say: O People of the Book, why do you bar from the way of God those who believe?﴾ He repeated the address and the interrogative for the sake of emphasis in rebuke and in negating any excuse for them, and to indicate that each of the two matters is abhorrent in itself and independently brings about punishment. The way of God in His religion is the truth that is commanded to be followed, and it is Islam. It was said: they used to seduce the believers and stir up strife among them until they came to the Aws and the Khazraj and reminded them of what had existed between them in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance) of enmity and warfare, so that they would return to the like of it. They also devised schemes to bar them from it. ﴿Seeking to make it crooked﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw (of the plural subject): that is, seeking for it crookedness, by confusing people and making them imagine that there is deviation from the truth in it, through denying naskh (abrogation) and altering the description of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the like. Or it means stirring discord among the believers so that their word divides and the affair of their religion is disrupted. ﴿While you are witnesses﴾ that it is the way of God and that barring from it is misguidance and misleading; or it means that you are trustworthy (udul) among the people of your religion, who rely on your statements and call upon you as witnesses in legal cases. ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do.﴾ This is a warning to them. Since the reprehensible matter in the first verse was their disbelief, which they openly proclaimed, he concluded it with "God is witness over what you do." Since in this verse it is their barring of the believers from Islam, which they concealed and for which they devised tricks, he said "God is not unaware of what you do."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 100–101:

﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a party of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you, after your belief, to disbelievers﴾ It was revealed concerning a group of men from al-Aws and al-Khazraj who were sitting together conversing. Shas ibn Qays, a Jew, passed by them, and the harmony and gathering of their company angered him. He ordered a young Jew to sit with them and remind them of the Day of Bu'ath and recite to them some of what was said about it. The victory on that day had belonged to al-Aws. He did so, and the people quarrelled, boasted, became angry with one another, and cried, "The weapons! The weapons!" A great multitude gathered with the two tribes, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions went out to them, and he said, "Do you call to the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) while I am among you, after Allah has honoured you with Islam, cut off from you the matter of the Jahiliyyah, and joined your hearts together?" They knew that it was a prick from Satan and a plot from their enemy, so they threw down their weapons, sought forgiveness, embraced one another, and left with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Allah addressed them Himself after He had commanded the Messenger to address the People of the Book, to show the greatness of their station and to indicate that they are the worthy ones to be addressed and spoken to by Allah.

﴿And how can you disbelieve while the verses of Allah are recited to you and His Messenger is among you?﴾ This is a rebuke and an expression of wonder at their disbelief in a situation where the factors calling to faith and deterring from disbelief have all come together for them. ﴿And whoever holds fast to Allah﴾ whoever adheres to His religion or seeks refuge in Him in the all-encompassing matters of his affairs. ﴿has certainly been guided to a straight path﴾ he has, without doubt, been guided.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 102:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah as He should be feared﴾ — "as He should be feared" (ḥaqqa tuqātihi): its true fear and what is obligatory of it, which is exerting one's full capacity in performing the obligations and abstaining from what is forbidden, like His saying: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾. And on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: it is that He be obeyed and not disobeyed, thanked and not disbelieved, and remembered and not forgotten. It has also been said: it is that obedience be purified of looking toward it (i.e., of self-regard) and of expecting a reward for it. In this command there is an emphasis on the prohibition of obeying the People of the Book. The root of taqāh is wuqyah, so its vowelled waw was changed into a tā', as in tu'adah (deliberation) and tukhamah (indigestion), and the yā' became an alif.

﴿And do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ — that is, do not be in any state other than the state of Islam when death overtakes you. For the prohibition concerning something restricted by a state or other condition may apply to the act itself at one time and to the condition at another, and it may apply to the whole combined without either of them separately. The same applies to negation.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 103:

﴿And hold fast to the rope of Allah all together﴾, meaning the religion of Islam, or His Book, because of his saying, upon him be peace: "The Qur'an is the firm rope of Allah." He used the word "rope" as a metaphor (isti'ara) for it, since adhering to it is a means of salvation from perdition, just as adhering to a rope is a means of safety from falling. "Holding fast" (i'tisam) and "trusting in it and relying upon it" are used as a supporting image (tarshih) for the metaphor (majaz). "All together" means gathered upon it. ﴿And do not be divided﴾, that is, do not separate from the truth by falling into disagreement among yourselves as the People of the Book did, or do not divide as you divided in the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) when you fought one another, or do not mention what necessitates division and removes harmony. ﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾, which includes guidance and success in Islam, which leads to mutual affection and the removal of rancour. ﴿When you were enemies﴾ opposing one another in the Jahiliyyah. ﴿Then He brought your hearts together﴾ through Islam. ﴿So you became, by His favour, brothers﴾ loving one another, united in brotherhood for the sake of Allah. It was said that al-Aws and al-Khazraj were two brothers of the same parents, but enmity arose between their descendants, and the wars dragged on for one hundred and twenty years, until Allah extinguished them through Islam and brought them together through His Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire﴾, about to fall into the Fire of Hell because of your disbelief, for if death had overtaken you in that state, you would have fallen into the Fire. ﴿Then He saved you from it﴾ through Islam. The pronoun refers to the pit, or to the Fire, or to the brink. Its feminine form is due to the feminine gender of what it is attached to, or because it carries the sense of "edge," for the shafa (edge) of a well and its shafa-ah (lip) is its border, like "janib" and "janiba" (side). Its original form is shafw, and the waw was changed to alif in the masculine, and dropped in the feminine. ﴿Thus﴾, like this clarification, ﴿Allah makes clear to you His signs﴾, His proofs. ﴿That you may be guided﴾, meaning the desire that you remain firm upon guidance and increase in it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 104:

﴿And let there be among you a community (ummah) who invite to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong﴾. "Min" (مِن) here is partitive (lil-tab'id), because enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong are among the communal obligations (furud al-kifayah), and because not everyone is suited to undertake them, since the one who takes them up must meet conditions that are not required of the whole community, such as knowledge of the rulings (al-'ilm bil-ahkam), the grades of hisbah (al-ihtisab, the duty of public accountability), the manner of carrying it out (kayfiyyat iqamatiha), and the ability to perform it. He addressed everyone and demanded that some of them perform it, to show that it is obligatory upon all, so that if they all abandoned it entirely, they would all be sinful; but it is discharged by the action of some of them. The same applies to every communal obligation. Alternatively, "min" is explicative (lil-tabyin), with the meaning "and be a community who invite," like His saying, ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right﴾. Inviting to good encompasses inviting to whatever is of religious or worldly benefit. The conjunction of "enjoining what is right" and "forbidding what is wrong" after "inviting to good" is the conjunction of the specific upon the general, to indicate their excellence.

﴿And those are the successful (al-muflihun)﴾: those specially singled out for complete success.

It is narrated that he (ﷺ) was asked, "Who is the best of people?" and he said: "The one who most enjoins what is right, forbids what is wrong, is most God-fearing, and keeps the ties of kinship best."

Enjoining what is right may be obligatory or recommended, according to what it is enjoined to. Forbidding what is wrong is entirely obligatory, because everything the Law has disapproved of is forbidden. The more apparent view is that the sinner is obligated to forbid what he himself commits, because he is obligated to abandon it and to reject it; thus the obligation of one of the two does not lapse by neglecting the other.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 105:

﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed﴾ like the Jews and the Christians, who differed concerning the Oneness (tawhid) and the transcendence (tanzih) of God and the states of the Hereafter, as is known. ﴿after clear proofs had come to them﴾, i.e., the signs and the arguments that make the truth manifest and that necessitate agreement upon it. The more apparent view is that the prohibition here is specific to division in the fundamentals (usul) and not in the derivative rulings (furu'), because of his saying ﷺ: "The difference of my community is a mercy."

And because of his saying ﷺ: "Whoever exercises independent judgment (ijtihad) and is correct has two rewards, and whoever errs has one reward."

﴿And those, for them is a great punishment﴾: a threat for those who divided, and a warning against imitating them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 106–107:

﴿On the Day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾ It is in the accusative governed by what is in "lahum" (for them) of the sense of a verb, or by an implied "udhkur" (remember). The whiteness and blackness of the face are metaphors (kinayatan) for the manifestation of the radiance of joy and the gloom of fear in it. It has been said that the people of truth are marked by whiteness of the face, of the record (sahifah), by the brightness of the skin, and by light running before them and in their right hands, while the people of falsehood are marked by the opposites of these. ﴿As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?"﴾ This is with the implication of speech, meaning: it will be said to them, "Did you disbelieve?" The hamzah (interrogative particle) is for rebuke and for expressing wonder at their state. They are either apostates, or the People of the Book who disbelieved in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after believing in him before his mission, or all disbelievers who disbelieved after they had acknowledged [their Lord] when He took testimony from them against themselves, or who were able to attain faith through reflection on the proofs and signs. ﴿So taste the punishment﴾ is a command of humiliation. ﴿because you used to disbelieve﴾ because of your disbelief, or as recompense for your disbelief.

﴿As for those whose faces turn white, they will be in the mercy of Allah﴾ meaning the Garden and the everlasting reward. He expressed this by "mercy" to alert that the believer, even if he spends his entire life in obedience to Allah the Exalted, does not enter the Garden except by His mercy and grace. The proper order would have been to mention them first, but it was intended that the opening and closing of the discourse be the adornment and reward of the believers. ﴿They will abide therein forever﴾ is placed as a resumptive statement (isti'naf) for emphasis, as if it were said: "How will they be therein?" So He said: "They will abide therein forever."

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 108–109:**

﴿These are the verses of Allah﴾ revealed concerning His promise and His threat, ﴿which We recite to you with truth﴾, that is, accompanied by truth, with no doubt in them. ﴿And Allah does not intend any injustice to the worlds﴾, since injustice is impossible for Him, because nothing is due to Him so that He would wrong Him by withholding it, and He does not withhold anything so that He would wrong by His act, for He is the absolute owner, as He said.

﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾, so He recompenses each according to what He promised for him and threatened him with.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 3, verse 110:

﴿You were the best nation﴾ indicates their excellence in the past, and it does not indicate an excellence that has ended, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾. It has also been said that the meaning is: you were so in the knowledge of Allah, or in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or among the earlier nations. ﴿Brought forth for mankind﴾ means: made manifest to them. ﴿Enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) that explains why they are the best nation, or it is a second predicate (khabar thani) of *kuntum*. ﴿And believing in Allah﴾ includes belief in everything that must be believed in, because belief in Him is only valid and counted when belief in everything He commanded them to believe in has been realized. He delayed it, although its proper place is to come first, because by mentioning it He intended to show that they enjoined what is right and forbade what is wrong out of faith in Allah, affirmation of Him, and the manifestation of His religion. This verse has been cited as evidence that consensus (ijma') is a valid proof (hujjah), because it implies that they are enjoiners of every right and forbidders of every wrong, since the *al-* in *al-ma'ruf* and *al-munkar* is for comprehensiveness (li-l-istighraq). So if they were to agree upon falsehood, their command would be contrary to that. ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed as they should, it would have been better for them﴾: that is, faith would have been better for them than what they are upon. ﴿Among them are believers﴾ such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions. ﴿But most of them are defiant transgressors﴾: those who persist stubbornly in disbelief. This sentence and the one following it come as a digression (istitrad).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 111:

﴿They will not harm you, except with a little harm﴾, such as taunting and threatening. ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾, they will be routed, and they will not harm you by killing or taking captive. ﴿Then they will not be helped﴾: then there will be no one who helps them against you or repels your might from them. Their harm has been negated, apart from what occurs by way of speech. He confirmed this by saying that if they were to stand up to fighting, the defeat would be upon them. Then He informed that their outcome will be incapacity and abandonment. It has been read as «لا يُنْصَرُوا» (lā yunṣarū, "they will not be helped"), in coordination with yuwallū (they will turn), on the basis that thumma (then, "thumma") indicates delay in rank, so that the absence of help is restricted to their fighting. This verse is among the unseen matters (al-mughayyabāt, things hidden from the senses, i.e., future events) whose occurrence agreed with it, since that was the situation of Qurayza, al-Nadir, Banu Qaynuqa', and the Jews of Khaybar.

﴿Abasement has been decreed upon them﴾: it is the forfeiting of their lives, wealth and families, or the abasement of clinging to falsehood and paying the jizya (poll tax).

﴿Wherever they are found﴾ means wherever they are encountered. ﴿Except under a rope from Allah and a rope from the people﴾ is an exception (istithnāʾ) from the most general of general circumstances (aʿamm ʿāmm al-aḥwāl). That is, abasement is decreed upon them in all circumstances except when they are holding fast (muʿtaṣimīn) or are associated with (multabisīn) the protection (dhimma) of Allah, or His Book which was given to them, and the protection of the Muslims, or with the religion of Islam and following the way of the believers.

﴿And they returned with anger from Allah﴾ means they returned bearing it, deserving it. ﴿And humiliation was decreed upon them, poverty﴾: so it encompasses them like a house whose inhabitants are struck by it. The Jews, for the most part, are poor and needy.

﴿That﴾ refers to what has been mentioned: the decreeing of abasement and poverty and returning with anger.

﴿Because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right﴾: this is due to their disbelief in the signs and their killing of the prophets. The qualification "without right" (bi-ghayr ḥaqq), although it is so in reality, serves to indicate that it was not right even according to their own belief.

﴿That﴾, i.e., the disbelief and killing.

﴿Because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾: this is due to their disobedience and their transgressing the limits of Allah. Persistence in minor sins leads to major sins, and continuing in them leads to disbelief.

It has been said that its meaning is: the imposing of abasement in this world and the incurring of anger in the Hereafter, as it is caused by their disbelief and killing, is consequent upon their disobedience and transgression (p-34), in that they are also addressed with the subsidiary rulings (furūʿ).

Not all of them are alike (in the sense of being equal). The pronoun refers to the People of the Book.

Among the People of the Book (ahl al-Kitab) is a steadfast community (ummah qa'imah). This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), given to explain the negation of equality. Al-qa'imah means the upright and just, from aqamtu al-'ud fa-qama (I set up the stick and it stood straight). They are those among them who embraced Islam.

They recite the verses of God in the hours of the night, and they prostrate themselves. Yatlun means they recite the Qur'an during their tahajjud (night prayer). He expressed it by recitation during the hours of the night together with prostration, to make the praise clearer and more eloquent. It is also said that the intended meaning is the 'Isha' prayer, because the People of the Book do not perform it, based on what is related: "He (peace be upon him) delayed it, then went out, and behold, the people were waiting for the prayer, and he said: 'Indeed, among the followers of the religions there is no one who mentions God at this hour except you.'"

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 114–115:

﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds﴾ are further attributes of a community, described with characteristics that were not found among the Jews. For the Jews had deviated from the truth, did not worship devotedly in the night, associated partners with Allah, were heretical regarding His attributes, described the Last Day contrary to its true description, were lax in enjoining good (al-ihtisab) and slow to do good deeds.

﴿And they are among the righteous﴾, that is, those characterized by these attributes are among those whose conditions have become sound in the sight of Allah, and who deserve His pleasure and His praise.

"And whatever good you do, it will not be denied you" (fa-lan tukfarūhu): it will not be lost, and its reward will not be diminished in the least. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 114–115:

﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds﴾ are further attributes of a community, described with characteristics that were not found among the Jews. For the Jews had deviated from the truth, did not worship devotedly in the night, associated partners with Allah, were heretical regarding His attributes, described the Last Day contrary to its true description, were lax in enjoining good (al-ihtisab) and slow to do good deeds.

﴿And they are among the righteous﴾, that is, those characterized by these attributes are among those whose conditions have become sound in the sight of Allah, and who deserve His pleasure and His praise.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 116–117:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will avail them nothing against Allah at all﴾, meaning against the punishment, or against Allah's giving them relief (al-ghina'), in which case it is a verbal noun (masdar). ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire﴾, meaning those who are constant in it. ﴿They will abide therein forever﴾.

﴿The likeness of what they spend﴾: what the disbelievers spend as an act of devotion, or out of boasting and seeking to be heard of, or what the hypocrites spend out of showing off or out of fear. ﴿In this worldly life is like a wind containing frost﴾, that is, an intense cold. The common usage of the word for a cold wind is ṣarṣar, but it is originally a masdar that was used as an adjective, or an adjective describing cold, for emphasis, as in your saying "bard bārid" (intensely cold). ﴿It strikes the tilth of a people who have wronged themselves﴾ through disbelief and sins ﴿and destroys it﴾, as a punishment for them, because destruction that comes from anger is more severe. The intended meaning is to liken what they spent, lost to no benefit, to the tilth of disbelievers that was struck by a frosty wind, uprooted it, and left them no benefit from it in this world or the Hereafter. This is a compound simile (al-tashbih al-murakkab), and for this reason it does not matter that the particle of comparison is attached to the wind rather than to the tilth. It is also permissible to estimate the phrase as "like the destruction of a wind," which is the tilth. ﴿And Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾: that is, Allah did not wrong the spenders by losing their expenditures, but they wronged themselves by not spending in a way that would be counted for them; or Allah did not wrong the owners of the tilth by destroying it, but they wronged themselves by committing what made them deserving of punishment. It has been read as "wa-lākinna" (but indeed), meaning "but indeed they wrong themselves," and it is not permissible to estimate the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n) here, because it is not omitted except in cases of poetic necessity, as in his saying:

I was never one whom love would enter into his heart,
but whoever sees your eyelids falls in love.

(p-35)
