Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 118:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take as biṭānah (intimate confidants)﴾ a walījah (close associate), that is, one to whom a man reveals his secrets out of trust in him. It is likened to the lining of a garment (biṭānat al-thawb), just as it is likened to the shi'ār (undergarment, the one closest to the body).

He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "The Helpers (al-Anṣār) are the shi'ār, and the people are the diṯār (outer garment)."

﴿other than yourselves﴾, that is, other than the Muslims. It is connected either to "do not take," or to an omitted element that is an attribute of biṭānah, meaning: a biṭānah existing from among other than you. ﴿They do not spare you corruption﴾, that is, they do not fall short in causing you ruin. Al-alw (sparing, falling short) originally takes a particle, but here it is transitive to two objects, as in their saying: "I do not spare you counsel," by way of implying the meaning of withholding or diminishing. ﴿They wish what distresses you﴾, that is, they wish your suffering, which is severe harm and hardship; and mā is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah) particle. ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾, that is, in their speech, because they cannot control themselves due to the excess of their hatred. ﴿And what their breasts conceal is greater﴾ than what has appeared, because its appearing is not from deliberation and choice. ﴿We have already made the signs clear to you﴾, those indicating the obligation of sincerity and of loyalty to the believers and enmity toward the disbelievers. ﴿If you should understand﴾ what has been made clear to you. The four clauses come as independent sentences giving the reason; and it is permissible that the first three be attributes of biṭānah.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 119:

﴿Here you are, you are the ones who love them, but they do not love you﴾ That is: you are the ones who err in allying with the disbelievers, and you love them while they do not love you. This is an explanation of their error in allying with them. It is a second predicate, or a predicate of ﴿ulā᾽ (these)﴾, and the sentence is a predicate of ﴿antum (you)﴾, like your saying: "You are Zayd, you love him." Or it is a relative clause (ṣila), or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the governing element in it is the meaning of pointing (al-ishāra). It is also permissible for ﴿ulā᾽﴾ to be put in the accusative by a hidden verb that is explained by what follows, and the sentence is then a predicate. ﴿And you believe in the Book, all of it﴾ in the sense of the whole category of the Book. This is a circumstantial clause of ﴿they do not love you﴾, and the meaning is: they do not love you while you believe in their Book too; so why do you love them when they do not believe in your Book? In this there is a rebuke, that they are more steadfast in their falsehood than you are in your truth. ﴿And when they meet you, they say: "We believe"﴾ out of hypocrisy and deception. ﴿And when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾ because of it, in regret and grief, since they find no way to satisfy their vengeance. ﴿Say: "Die in your rage"﴾ This is a supplication against them, that the rage remain and increase, through the doubling of the strength of Islam and its people, until they perish from it. ﴿Indeed Allah is Knower of what is in the breasts﴾ So He knows what is in their breasts of hatred and rancor. It may be that this is part of what is said, meaning: "And say to them: Indeed Allah knows what is more hidden than what you conceal of biting the fingertips in rage." And it may be outside of it, in the sense of: "Say to them that, and do not be surprised at my being informed by Him of their secrets, for I know what is more hidden than their inner thoughts."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 120:

﴿If good touches you, it grieves them; but if evil befalls you, they rejoice at it.﴾ This explains that their enmity has reached such a degree that they envy whatever good and benefit you attain, and gloat over whatever harm and hardship befalls you. The word "touch" (al-massu) is used metaphorically for "reaching" or "befalling."

﴿And if you are patient﴾ in the face of their enmity, or in bearing the hardships of the obligations (al-taklif). ﴿and conscious of God﴾ of their friendship, or of what God, exalted is His majesty, has forbidden to you. ﴿Their scheming will not harm you at all﴾ by the grace of God, mighty and majestic, and His promised protection for those who are patient and God-conscious. Also, because one who is diligent in the matter and trained in God-consciousness and patience is little affected by emotion and bold against the adversary. The ḍamma on the rāʾ (in "lā yaḍurrukum") is for the purpose of following (al-ittibāʿ), like the ḍamma of a long vowel (ḍammat madd). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub recited "lā yaḍurrukum" from the verb "ḍarra, yaḍurru" (the form "ḍārra, yaḍīruhu"). ﴿Indeed God is encompassing﴾ of what they do, of patience and God-consciousness and other things. ﴿encompassing﴾ means His knowledge encompasses it, so He will recompense you for what you deserve. It was also read with the yāʾ (ya), meaning "what they do" (bi-mā yaʿmalūna), in their enmity against you; He is All-Knowing, so He will punish them for it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 3, verse 121:

﴿And [remember] when you set out from your family﴾: that is, remember when you set out. ﴿From your family﴾: that is, from the chamber of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her. ﴿You were settling the believers﴾: you were placing them. Or: you were arranging and preparing for them, and the recitation with the letter *lām* (*li-l-muʾminīna*, "for the believers") supports this. ﴿Positions for the battle﴾: stations and places for it. The words *maqʿad* (seat) and *maqām* (station) may be used in the sense of "place" by extension, as in His saying, ﴿in a seat of truth﴾, and His saying, ﴿before you rise from your place﴾. ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of your statements. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of your intentions.

It is narrated: "The polytheists camped at Uhud on Wednesday, the twelfth of Shawwal, in the third year after the Hijra (migration) [*al-hijra*, the Prophet's migration from Makka to Madina]. The Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, consulted his Companions, and he had summoned ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, whom he had not summoned before. He and most of the Ansar said: 'Remain in Madina, O Messenger of Allah, and do not go out to them. By Allah, we have never gone out from it to an enemy without being struck by them, nor has an enemy entered it against us without our striking them. So how much more so when you are among us? Leave them: if they remain, they will remain in the worst of confinements; if they enter, the men will fight them and the women and children will pelt them with stones; and if they return, they will return disappointed.' Some of them advised going out, and he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: 'I saw in my dream a slaughtered cow around me, so I interpreted it as good. I saw a notch in the edge of my sword, so I interpreted it as a defeat. And I saw that I had put my hand into a strong coat of mail, so I interpreted it as Madina. So if you see fit to remain in Madina and leave them, [then do so].' Men said: 'Badr escaped us, and Allah honored them with martyrdom on the day of Uhud. Lead us out to our enemies.' They insisted until he entered and put on his armor. When they saw that, they regretted their insistence and said: 'Do as you see fit, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'It is not fitting for a prophet to put on his armor and then take it off until he has fought.' He went out after the Friday prayer and in the morning was at the mountain pass of Uhud on Saturday. He descended at the edge of the valley, placed his back and camp toward Uhud, and arranged their ranks. He appointed ʿAbdullah ibn Jubayr over the archers and said: 'Shoot arrows at them to keep them away from us, so that they do not come at us from behind.'"

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 122:

﴿When two groups among you were about to lose heart﴾ is related to His saying: "All-Hearing, All-Knowing," or it is a substitute for "when you set out in the morning." ﴿Two groups among you﴾ were the Banu Salama of the Khazraj and the Banu Harithah of the Aws, and they were the two wings of the army. ﴿To lose heart﴾ means to become cowardly and weak.

It is narrated that "he (peace and blessings be upon him) went out with about a thousand men and promised them victory if they remained patient. When they reached al-Shawt, Ibn Ubayy withdrew with three hundred men and said: 'Why should we kill ourselves and our children?' Then 'Amr ibn Hazm al-Ansari followed them and said: 'I adjure you by Allah and by Islam, concerning your Prophet and yourselves.' Ibn Ubayy said: 'If we knew there would be fighting, we would have followed you.' The two groups were about to follow him, but Allah preserved them, and they went on with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

The apparent meaning is that it was not a firm resolve, based on His saying: ﴿And Allah is their Protector﴾, that is, the One who preserved them from following that passing impulse. It is also possible that the meaning is: Allah is their Helper, so why would they lose heart and not put their trust in Allah? ﴿And upon Allah let the believers put their trust﴾, that is, let them put their trust in Him alone and not in anyone else, so that He may help them as He helped them at Badr.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 123–124:

﴿And God had already given you victory at Badr﴾. This is a reminder of some of the benefits that trust in God (tawakkul) brought them. Badr is a water source between Mecca and Medina, which belonged to a man named Badr, and so it was named after him. ﴿While you were humiliated﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in "you." He said "humiliated" (adhillah) rather than "humiliations" (dhala'il) to draw attention to their small number together with their weakness, given the frailty of their condition and the scarcity of mounts and weapons. ﴿So fear God﴾ concerning the garments. ﴿That perhaps you may give thanks﴾ by your piety for what He bestowed upon you of His victory; or, "that perhaps you may give thanks" for God's blessings upon you, and so he placed "giving thanks" in the position of "bestowing blessings," because it is its cause.

﴿When you said to the believers﴾: this is an adverbial clause (zarf) governed by "your victory." It has also been said that it is a second substitute (badal) for "when you set out in the morning," with the understanding that his saying to them took place on the day of Uhud, and it was together with (p-37)

the condition of patience and piety against disobedience. So when they did not remain patient regarding the spoils and disobeyed the order of the Messenger ﷺ, the angels did not descend.

﴿Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?﴾ This is a rhetorical denial (inkar) of the claim that it would not suffice for them. The particle "lan" (never) was used to indicate that they were like those who had despaired of victory, due to their weakness and small number and the strength and multitude of the enemy. It has been said that God reinforced them on the day of Badr first with a thousand angels, then they became three thousand, then they became five thousand. Ibn 'Amir read "munazzalin" with the doubled letter, for intensification or for gradualness.

Then He promised them an increase beyond patience and god-consciousness (taqwa), urging them to these and strengthening their hearts, so He said: ﴿If you are patient and god-conscious, and they come upon you﴾, that is, the polytheists, ﴿from this very instant﴾, that is, from this very moment. Originally, "fawr" is a verbal noun from "faarat al-qidr" (the cooking pot boiled over) when it boiled, and it was borrowed for speed, then applied to the state in which there is no delay or postponement. The meaning is: if they come upon you immediately, ﴿your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels﴾ at the time of their coming, without delay or postponement. ﴿Marked﴾ (musawwimin), that is, distinguished, from "taswim," which is the showing of a thing's distinctive mark, based on his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, to his Companions: "Mark yourselves, for the angels have marked themselves." Or they were sent, from "taswim" in the sense of "usama" (grazing freely). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ya'qub read it with a kasra on the waw.

﴿And Allah did not make it﴾ means: He did not make the reinforcement of you with the angels ﴿except as good news for you﴾, meaning only as glad tidings for you of victory. ﴿And so that your hearts may be reassured thereby﴾ means: so that they may be at rest from fear through it. ﴿And victory is only from Allah﴾ means: not from equipment and numbers. This is a reminder that there is no need for them to be reinforced in order to achieve their victory. Rather, He sent the reinforcement and promised it to them as good news and as a steadying of their hearts, since the common people look more to the means (asbab). It also urges them not to be concerned about those who held back from them. ﴿The All-Mighty﴾ is He who cannot be overcome in His decrees. ﴿The All-Wise﴾ is He who grants victory and abandons, sometimes through intermediaries and sometimes without them, according to the requirements of wisdom and benefit.

The meaning is that He might diminish them by killing some and capturing others. This is what happened at the Battle of Badr, when seventy of their leaders were killed and seventy were captured. ﴿Or He may subdue them﴾, meaning humiliate them. So He will either destroy them, or humiliate them, or turn to them in forgiveness if they embrace Islam, or punish them if they persist, and you have no say in their affair at all. It is also possible that it is conjoined to "the matter" or to "a thing" with an implied "an" (idmār an, "that"), meaning: you have no say in their affair, nor in turning to them in forgiveness, nor in punishing them. "Or" may also be used in the sense of "unless" (bi-ma'nā illā an), meaning: you have no say in their affair, unless God turns to them in forgiveness, and you are glad of it, or He punishes them, and you take revenge upon them.

It is related: "That 'Utbah ibn Abi Waqqas wounded him on the Day of Uhud and broke his rubā'iyya (a front tooth), so he began wiping the blood from his face and saying, 'How can a people prosper who dyed the face of their Prophet with blood?' Then this was revealed." It is also said that he (ﷺ) intended to curse them, but God forbade him, because He knew that among them were those who would believe. ﴿For they are wrongdoers﴾ means they deserved punishment because of their wrongdoing.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 129–130:

﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ in creation and in ownership; so the command is entirely His, not yours. ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills﴾ is explicit in negating the obligation of punishment, and the restriction by repentance and its absence is, as it were, contrary to it. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ toward His servants, so do not hasten to invoke curses upon them.

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled﴾ — do not increase in repeated increments. The specification is perhaps in accordance with what actually occurred: a man among them would lend at interest until a term, then add to it another increase, until a trifling amount would swallow the debtor's property. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read "مُضَعَّفَةً" (muda''afah, "multiplied"). ﴿And fear Allah﴾ regarding what you have been forbidden. ﴿That you may be successful﴾ — hoping for success.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 131–132:

﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ by guarding oneself against following them and engaging in their deeds. In this there is an alert that the Fire is prepared for the disbelievers essentially (bi'l-dhat) and for the sinners incidentally (bi'l-'arad).

﴿And obey Allah and the Messenger, that you may be shown mercy﴾. He follows the threat with a promise, as a warning against opposition (tarhib) and an encouragement toward obedience (targhib). And "la'alla" (perhaps) and "'asa" (perhaps) in such contexts indicate the rarity (izzah) of attaining that which is made the predicate of them (khabar).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 133–134:

﴿And hasten﴾ (wa-sari'u): hurry and turn towards. ﴿to forgiveness from your Lord﴾: towards that which makes forgiveness deserved, such as Islam, repentance, and sincerity. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read sari'u without the waw (wa). ﴿and a Garden whose breadth is the heavens and the earth﴾: that is, its breadth is like their breadth. The mention of breadth (ʿarḍ) is for emphasis in describing its vastness, in the manner of figurative expression, since breadth is less than length. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "like seven heavens and seven earths if some of them were joined to others." ﴿prepared for the God-fearing﴾: made ready for them. In this is evidence that the Garden is created and that it is outside this world.

﴿Those who spend﴾ (alladhina yunfiquna): a descriptive epithet praising the God-fearing, or a praise (madh) in the accusative or nominative. ﴿in ease and in hardship﴾: in the two states of plenty and adversity, or in all conditions, since a person is never free of either pleasure or harm; that is, they never, in any state, cease to spend of what they are able to, whether little or much. ﴿and who restrain anger﴾ (al-kaziminal-ghayz): those who hold it back and refrain from carrying it out while able to do so; from kazamtu al-qirba, when you fill the waterskin and tie its mouth tight.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever restrains anger while he is able to act upon it, Allah will fill his heart with security and faith."

﴿and who pardon people﴾ (al-'afina 'ani'n-nas): those who leave off punishing those who deserve to be held accountable. And from the Prophet (peace be upon him): "Indeed, such people are few in my nation, except for those whom Allah protects." Yet they have been many in the nations that passed before. ﴿And Allah loves the doers of good﴾: this may be taken generically, so that these people enter under it; or by a specific reference (al-'ahd), so that the indication is to them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 135:

And those who, when they commit an abomination (fahishah), an act extremely ugly like fornication, or wrong themselves (zalamu anfusahum) by committing any sin whatsoever. It is said that the abomination is the grave sin and the wronging of oneself is the minor sin, and perhaps the abomination is that which extends to others, while the wronging of oneself is that which does not extend in this way. They remember (dhakarU) Allah, meaning they remember His threat (wa'id), or His command (hukm), or His great right (haqq).

So they seek forgiveness for their sins through regret (nadam) and repentance (tawbah). ﴿And who forgives sins but Allah?﴾ The interrogative here carries the sense of negation and is parenthetical (mu'tarid) between the two conjoined elements. Its purpose is to describe Him, exalted is He, with the vastness of mercy and the universality of forgiveness, to urge seeking forgiveness, and to promise the acceptance of repentance. ﴿And they do not persist in what they did, while they know﴾ (wa lam yusirru 'ala ma fa'alu wa lam yuqimu 'ala dhunubihim ghayra mustaghfirin), for the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "One who seeks forgiveness does not persist in sin, even if he returns to it seventy times a day."

And they know (wa hum ya'lamun) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "yusirru", meaning: they did not persist in their ugly deed while knowing it to be ugly.

﴿Those, their reward is forgiveness from their Lord, and gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of "those" (alladhina) if you begin with it, and it is a resumptive clause (jumlah mustaʾnafa) explaining what precedes it if you make it coordinated with "the God-fearing" or with "those who spend." It does not follow from the preparation of Paradise for the God-fearing and the repentant as their reward that the persistent (in sin) will not enter it, just as it does not follow from the preparation of Hell for the disbelievers as their reward that others than them will not enter it. The indefiniteness of "gardens" (jannat) in the first case indicates that what they receive is inferior to what is prepared for the God-fearing who possess the attributes mentioned in the preceding verse. And sufficient to distinguish between the two groups is that He concluded their verse by stating that they are good-doers (muhsinun) deserving of God's love, because they guarded the limits of the Law and went beyond them to be singled out with its noble qualities. He concluded the verse of these (the first group) with His words: ﴿and excellent is the reward of those who work﴾, because the one who makes up for his shortcoming is like the one who works to obtain some of what he had lost for himself. How great is the difference between the good-doer and the one who makes amends, and between the beloved and the hired worker. Perhaps the replacing of the word "recompense" (jaza') with "reward" (ajr) is for this subtle point. The object of praise (al-makhsus bi-l-madh) is omitted, and its estimated form is: "and excellent is the reward of those who work, that, meaning the forgiveness and the gardens."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 137–138:

﴿Indeed, there have passed before you precedents (sunan)﴾ — these are events which Allah established among the nations that denied (the truth), like His saying: ﴿and they were slain in battle﴾, ﴿the way of Allah with those who passed away before (you)﴾. It is also said that "sunan" means "nations." A poet said:

"No people has witnessed a grace like your grace, nor have they seen its like in the precedents of the past."

﴿So travel through the earth and see how was the end of those who denied﴾ — so that you may take a lesson from the traces of their destruction that you see.

﴿This is a clarification for mankind, and a guidance and an admonition for the God-fearing (muttaqin)﴾ — this refers to His saying "there have passed," or to the implication of His saying "so see." That is, although it is a clarification for the deniers, it is an increase in insight and an admonition for the God-fearing. Or it refers to what was summarized about the matter of the God-fearing and the penitent. His saying "there have passed" is a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'taridah) urging (people) toward faith and repentance. It is also said that it refers to the Qur'an.

ﷻ"And do not weaken, nor grieve" — this is consolation for them regarding what befell them on the Day of Uhud. The meaning is: do not weaken in jihad because of what afflicted you, and do not grieve over those among you who were killed. "And you will have the upper hand" — and your condition is that you are superior in rank, for you are upon the truth and your fighting is for Allah, and your slain are in Paradise, whereas they are upon falsehood and their fighting is for Shaytan (Satan), and their slain are in Hellfire. Or, because you inflicted upon them on the Day of Badr more than what they inflicted upon you today. Or, "and you will have the upper hand" refers to the final outcome, so it is a good tiding to them of victory and triumph. "If you are believers" — this is connected to the prohibition, i.e., do not weaken if your faith is sound, for it requires strength of heart through trust in Allah, or [it is connected] to "you will have the upper hand."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 140:

﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has already touched the people.﴾ Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, and Ibn ʿAyyāsh, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, read قَرْح with a ḍammah on the qāf (qurḥ), while the rest read it with a fatḥah (qarḥ). Both are two dialects, like الضَّعْف and الضَّعْف (ḍaʿf and ḍaʿf, meaning weakness). It is said that with the fatḥah it means the wounds themselves, and with the ḍammah it means the pain of them. The meaning is: if they inflicted wounds on you at the Day of Uhud, then you have inflicted a similar wound on them at the Day of Badr. Then, they did not become weak or cowardly, so you are more deserving of not becoming weak, for you hope from God for what they do not hope for. It is also said that both touches (al-massayn) occurred at the Day of Uhud, for the Muslims inflicted wounds on them before they disobeyed the command of the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿And those days We alternate among the people.﴾ We turn them among them: We give victory to these at one time and to those at another time, like His saying:

*"One day for us and one day against us, / and a day that grieves us and a day that gladdens us."*

The mudāwalah (alternation, lit. turning in turns) is like the muʿāwadah (repetition). One says: "I alternated the thing among them, so they alternated it." The word "days" (al-ayyām) may be a qualifier or a predicate, and "We alternate them" (nudāwiluhā) may be a predicate or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). What is meant by them is the times of victory and dominance.

﴿And that God may know those who believe﴾ is coordinated (ʿuṭifa) upon a deleted cause (ʿillah), meaning: We alternate them so that such-and-such may happen, and so that God may know. The mention of it indicates that the cause in it is not one only, and that what befalls the believer in it contains benefits that are not known. Or the verb governed by the causal particle is deleted, its estimated form being: "and so that those who remain steadfast in faith may be distinguished from those who are on the edge (ʿalā ḥarf), We did that." The intended sense in such statements and their opposites is not to affirm or negate His knowledge, the Exalted, but rather to affirm or negate the thing known, by way of proof (ʿalā ṭarīq al-burhān). It is also said that its meaning is: so that He may make them know with a knowledge upon which reward depends, which is knowledge of a thing as existent.

﴿and that He may take martyrs from among you﴾: and that He may honour some people among you with martyrdom, meaning the martyrs of Uhud. Or: that He may take from among you witnesses (shuhūd) declared upright (muʿaddalīn) by the steadfastness and patience they displayed in the face of hardships.

﴿And God does not love the wrongdoers﴾: those who conceal the opposite of what they show outwardly. Or it means the unbelievers, and this is a parenthetical clause (iʿtirāḍ). In it is an indication that God, the Exalted, does not truly grant victory to the unbelievers; rather He overcomes them at times as a gradual leading on (istidrāj) for them, and as a trial for the believers.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 141–142:

﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe﴾: that He may cleanse them and purify them of sins, if the turn of fortune was against them. ﴿And destroy the disbelievers﴾: and annihilate them, if the turn of fortune was against them. Al-mahq (destruction) is the diminishing of a thing little by little.

﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise﴾: rather, do you think so? Its meaning is denial. ﴿while Allah has not yet made evident those of you who strive [in His cause]﴾: while you have not yet striven. In this is evidence that jihad is a collective obligation (fard kifaya). The difference between lamma (لَمّا, "not yet") and lam (لَمْ, "did not") is that lamma implies the expectation of the act occurring in the future.

It was also read as ﴿yaʿlama﴾ with a fatḥa on the mim, its original form being yaʿlamna, with the nun dropped. ﴿And make evident the patient﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied an (أنْ), on the basis that the waw indicates conjunction (الجمع). It was also read in the nominative, on the basis that the waw indicates a circumstantial clause (الحال), as if he had said: "while you have not yet striven, and you are patient."

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 143:**

﴿And you certainly used to wish for death﴾, that is, the war, for it is among the causes of death, or death through martyrdom. The address is to those who had not witnessed Badr and who wished to witness a scene alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that they might attain the honour that the martyrs of Badr had attained. Thus they insistently pressed for going out on the Day of Uhud. ﴿Before you met it﴾, that is, before you witnessed it and knew its severity. ﴿Then indeed you have seen it while you were looking on﴾, that is, you have seen it with your own eyes when those of your brothers were slain before you. This is a rebuke to them for having wished for war and brought it about, and then turned coward and fled from it; or it is a rebuke for wishing for martyrdom, for in wishing for it lies a wish for the victory of the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 144:

﴿Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him.﴾ So they will pass away as they did, by death or by killing. ﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ This is a denunciation of their apostasy and their turning back on their heels from the religion, because he had passed away by death or killing, after they knew that the messengers before him had passed away while their religion remained, holding to it. It has been said that the fa' (fa) indicates causation and the hamza (interrogative) denies that they should make the passing away of the messengers before him a cause for turning back on their heels after his death.

It is narrated: "When Abdullah ibn Qumay'a al-Harithi struck the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a stone, breaking his front tooth and wounding his face, Mus'ab ibn Umayr, may Allah be pleased with him, who was the standard-bearer, defended him until Ibn Qumay'a killed him, thinking that he had killed the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. He said: 'I have killed Muhammad.' A crier cried out: 'Indeed Muhammad has been killed!' So the people scattered, and the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, began calling out: 'Come to me, servants of Allah!' Thirty of his companions gathered around him and defended him until they drove the polytheists away from him, and the rest dispersed. Some of them said: 'Would that Ibn Ubayy could obtain safe conduct for us from Abu Sufyan.' Some of the hypocrites said: 'If he were a prophet, he would not have been killed. Return to your brethren and your religion.' Anas ibn an-Nadr, the paternal uncle of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: 'O people, if Muhammad has been killed, the Lord of Muhammad is living and never dies. What good is life after him? Fight for what he fought for.' Then he said: 'O Allah, I apologize to You for what they say, and I disavow it before You.' He girded his sword, fought until he was killed, and then this verse was revealed." ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels will not harm Allah at all﴾ by his apostasy; rather he harms himself. ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾ for the blessing of Islam, by steadfastness upon it, like Anas and those like him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 145:

﴿And it is not for any soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾ — except by the will of Allah, the Exalted, or by His permission to the Angel of Death, upon him be peace, to seize its soul. The meaning is that for every soul there is a term appointed (ajal musamma) in His knowledge and decree, and they will not delay it by an hour nor hasten it, whether by shrinking back from fighting or by advancing into it. In this there is an exhortation and encouragement to fight, and a promise to the Messenger (ﷺ) of protection and of the postponement of his term. ﴿A decreed book﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar muakkid), since the meaning is "death was written as a book." ﴿Appointed﴾ is its attribute, meaning fixed in time, neither advancing nor delaying. ﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him of it﴾ is an allusion to those whom the spoils distracted on the day of Uhud. When the Muslims charged against the polytheists, routed them, and began to plunder, the archers, seeing this, turned to the plunder and abandoned their position. The polytheists seized the opportunity, attacked them from behind, and routed them. ﴿And whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him of it﴾ — that is, of its reward. ﴿And We will reward the grateful﴾ — those who gave thanks for the blessing of Allah, so that nothing distracted them from jihad.

**﴿وَكَأيِّنْ﴾** (*wa-ka-ayyin*, "and how many"): its original form is *ayyin*, to which the *kaf* (of comparison) was prefixed, and it came to have the meaning of *kam* ("how many"). The *nun* is *tanwin*, which was written in the script contrary to analogy. Ibn Kathir read **«وَكائِنٌ»** (*wa-ka'inun*), like *ka'in*. Its explanation is that he performed *qalb* (metathesis, the transposition of letters within a single word), as in the saying *ra'mali* for *la'amri* ("by my life"), so that it became *kay'an*. Then the second *ya'* was deleted for lightness, and the other *ya'* was changed to an *alif*, just as *ta'iyy* was changed from *nabiyy* (*Ta'i* from *Nabi*). This is an explanation of it.

**﴿قاتَلَ مَعَهُ رِبِّيُّونَ كَثِيرٌ﴾** (*Qatala ma'ahu ribbiyyuna kathir*, "many devoted ones fought alongside him"): *Rabbaniyyun* means scholars and pious people, or worshippers of their Lord. It was also said that they are groups, and *ribbi* is attributed to *ribba*, which means a group, for emphasis. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read **«قَتَلَ»** (*qatala*, "was killed"). Its subject is *ribbiyyun*, or the pronoun of the Prophet, and *ma'ahu ribbiyyun* is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from it. What supports the first is that it was also read with *tashdid* (*qatala*, emphatic form). *Ribbiyyun* was read with *fath* (**رَبِّيُّونَ**, *ribbiyyun*) according to the original, and with *damm* (*ribbuyyun*). The latter is one of the changes in the *nisba* (relative form), like *kasr* (*ribbiyyin*).

**﴿فَما وهَنُوا لِما أصابَهم في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾** (*Fa-ma wahanu limaa asabahum fi sabili-llah*, "so they did not weaken at what befell them in the way of Allah"): so they did not slacken, and their resolve was not broken by what befell them of the killing of the Prophet, or of some of them.

**﴿وَما ضَعُفُوا﴾** (*wa-ma da'ufu*, "nor did they become weak"): against the enemy, or in their religion.

**﴿وَما اسْتَكانُوا﴾** (*wa-ma istakanu*, "nor did they humble themselves"): nor did they submit to the enemy. Its root is *istakana*, from *al-sukun* (stillness), because the one who submits becomes still before his master so that he may do to him what he wishes. The *alif* is from the lengthening of the *fatha*. Alternatively, it is *istakwana*, from **الكَوْنِ** (*al-kawn*, existence/being), because he seeks from himself that he be for the one to whom he submits. This is an allusion to what befell them when the rumour of the Prophet's killing spread, upon him be peace and blessings.

**﴿واللَّهُ يُحِبُّ الصّابِرِينَ﴾** (*wa-llahu yuhibbu as-sabirin*, "and Allah loves the patient"): so He will help them and magnify their station.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 147–148:

﴿And their saying was only that they said: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affair, and make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾ That is: their saying, despite their steadfastness and strength in the religion and their being rabbaniyyun (devoted worshippers of the Lord), was nothing but this statement, namely attributing the sins and excesses to themselves in humility before them, and attributing what befell them to the evil of their deeds, and seeking forgiveness for them. Then they asked for firmness in the places of war and for victory over the enemy, so that this would proceed from humility and purity, and would thus be closer to being answered. He made their saying a predicate (khabar) because "an qalu" (that they said) is more definite, since it indicates the aspect of attribution and the time of the event.

﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter. And Allah loves the good-doers.﴾ Allah gave them, by means of seeking forgiveness and turning to Allah, victory, spoils, honour and good remembrance in this world, and Paradise and bliss in the Hereafter. He specified their reward with the adjective "good" (husn) to indicate its excellence and that it is the one that counts in the sight of Allah.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 149–150:

﴿O you who have believed, if you obey those who disbelieve, they will turn you back on your heels﴾, that is, to disbelief, ﴿and you will turn back as losers﴾. It was revealed concerning the saying of the hypocrites to the believers at the time of the defeat: "Return to your religion and your brethren; if Muhammad were a prophet, he would not have been killed."

It has also been said: "[It refers to] your submitting to Abu Sufyan and his followers, and seeking safe conduct from them, so that they turn you back to their religion." And it has been said that it is general, concerning yielding to the disbelievers and descending to their judgment, for that leads to being drawn into agreeing with them.

﴿Rather, Allah is your Protector (mawla)﴾, that is, your Helper. It has been read with the accusative (Allaha), on the assumption of a implied "rather, obey Allah, your Protector." ﴿And He is the best of helpers﴾, so be content with Him, rather than with the guardianship and help of anyone else.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 151:

﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve﴾ He means the fear that was cast into their hearts on the Day of Uhud, so that they abandoned fighting and turned back without any cause. Abu Sufyan called out, "O Muhammad, our appointment is the season of Badr next year, if you wish." So he (ﷺ) said, "If Allah wills."

It is said that when they turned back and were on part of the road, they regretted it and resolved to return to them in order to annihilate them, but Allah cast terror into their hearts. Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read (the word) with a damma, according to the original form throughout the Qur'an: ﴿for having associated with Allah﴾, meaning because of their associating partners with Him. ﴿for which He has sent down no authority﴾, i.e., gods for whose association there is no proof, and He has not sent down to them any authority concerning it. It is like his saying:

"And you will not see the lizard (dabb) entering its hole"

The root of sultan (authority) is strength, and from it comes al-saleet (oil), because of the strength of its burning, and al-salaata (eloquence/sharpness of tongue), because of the sharpness of the tongue. ﴿And their abode is the Fire, and wretched is the abode of the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., their abode, so the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun for emphasis and to give the reason.

﴿And Allah had already fulfilled His promise to you﴾, meaning His promise to give you victory on condition of piety and patience. This continued to be so until the archers disobeyed. When the polytheists advanced, the archers began shooting arrows at them, while the rest struck them with swords, until they were routed and the Muslims were pursuing them. ﴿While you were killing them by His permission﴾, meaning slaying them, from *hiss* (sensation), i.e., when their sensation is nullified. ﴿Until, when you lost heart﴾, meaning you became cowardly and your judgment weakened, or you inclined toward the spoils, for greed stems from weakness of intellect. ﴿And you disputed about the matter﴾, meaning the archers differed when the polytheists were routed. Some said, "What is our position here?" Others said, "We will not oppose the command of the Messenger." So their commander, with a group of fewer than ten, remained in his place, and the rest withdrew to plunder. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿and you disobeyed after He had shown you what you love﴾, namely victory, spoils, and the rout of the enemy. The answer to *idha* (when) is omitted, and it is "He tested you." ﴿Among you are those who desire this world﴾, and they are those who abandoned their post for the spoils. ﴿And among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾, and they are those who remained steadfast out of adherence to the command of the Messenger, peace be upon him. ﴿Then He turned you away from them﴾, meaning He restrained you from them, until the situation changed and they overcame you. ﴿That He might test you﴾ through calamities, and to examine your steadfastness in faith at that time. ﴿And certainly He has pardoned you﴾ out of grace, and because He knew of your remorse over the disobedience. ﴿And Allah is full of bounty to the believers﴾, bestowing on them pardon, or in all circumstances, whether they were given victory or defeated, since trial too is a mercy.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 153:

﴿When you were climbing up﴾ is related to ﴿He turned you away﴾, or to ﴿that He might test you﴾, or to an implied verb: ﴿remember﴾. The "iṣʿād" (climbing up, i.e. going off and moving away into the land) is used of going away: "We climbed up from Makkah to Madinah." ﴿And you did not look back at anyone﴾: no one would stop for anyone or wait for him. ﴿While the Messenger was calling you﴾: he was saying, "To me, servants of Allah! To me, servants of Allah! I am the Messenger of Allah; whoever turns back, for him is Paradise." ﴿From behind you﴾: in your rear, or your other group. ﴿So He repaid you with grief upon grief﴾: this is coordinated with ﴿He turned you away﴾, and the meaning is: Allah recompensed you for your cowardice and disobedience with grief following grief, from being distressed by the killing and the wounding, the victory of the polytheists, and the rumour of the killing of the Messenger ﷺ. Or: He recompensed you with grief because of a grief you caused the Messenger of Allah ﷺ through your disobedience to him. ﴿So that you would not grieve over what escaped you, nor over what befell you﴾: so that you would train yourselves in patience during hardships, so that afterwards you would not grieve over a benefit that had passed or a harm that had arrived. It has been said that "lā" is superfluous, and the meaning is: so that you would be sorry over what escaped you of victory and spoils, and over what befell you of wounding and defeat, as a punishment for you. It has also been said that the pronoun in ﴿so He repaid you﴾ refers to the Messenger ﷺ, meaning: he comforted you in distress, so he shared in the grief over what came down upon you, just as you grieved over what came down upon him, and he did not reproach you for your disobedience, as consolation for you, ﴿so that you would not grieve over what escaped you of victory, nor over what befell you of defeat﴾. ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾: Knowing of your deeds and of what you intended by them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 154:

﴿Then He sent down upon you, after distress, security in the form of drowsiness﴾ Allah sent down security upon you, to the extent that sleep overcame you. And on the authority of Abu Talha: "Drowsiness overcame us in the battle lines, to the point that the sword would fall from one of us, and he would take it, then it would fall and he would take it again." And amanah (security) means safety (al-amn).

It is in the accusative as an object (maf'ul), and nu'asan (drowsiness) is a substitute (badal) for it, or it is itself the object. And amanatan is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it, placed before it, or an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), or a circumstantial qualifier of those addressed, in the sense of "possessors of security," or it is the plural of amin, like barr and barara. It has also been read as amnatan with a sukun on the mim, as if it were the single instance of the verb amina. ﴿It envelops a group of you﴾, that is, the drowsiness. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the letter ta', referring back to amanah (security). The group (ta'ifah) refers to the truly believing.

﴿And another group﴾ are the hypocrites. ﴿Whose own selves had caused them concern﴾: their own selves put them into worries, or nothing concerned them except the concern for themselves and the pursuit of their own deliverance. ﴿They harbour thoughts about Allah that are not true, the thoughts of the Age of Ignorance (jahiliyyah)﴾: this is another attribute of the group, or a circumstantial clause, or a resumptive clause explaining what precedes it. "Ghayra al-haqq" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: they think about Allah other than the true thought that ought to be held about Him. "Zann al-jahiliyyah" is its substitute, and it is the thought specific to the ignorant creed and its adherents. ﴿They say﴾, that is, to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this is a substitute for "they harbour thoughts." ﴿Do we have any say in the matter at all?﴾: do we have any share at all in what Allah has commanded and promised of victory and triumph? It is said: Ibn Ubayy had received news of the killing of the Banu al-Khazraj and said this. The meaning is: we have been prevented from managing our own affairs and directing them by our choice, so nothing of the matter remains for us; or: will this compulsion be removed from us so that we would have some say in the matter? ﴿Say: Indeed the whole matter belongs to Allah﴾, that is, true dominance belongs to Allah the Exalted and to His allies, for the party of Allah are the victorious; or the decision belongs to Him, He does what He wills and judges what He desires. This is a parenthetical statement. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read "kulluhu" with a raised ending (damma) as the subject of a nominal sentence. ﴿They conceal within themselves what they do not reveal to you﴾: a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in "they say", meaning: they say, showing that they are seekers of guidance and seekers of victory, while concealing denial and rejection. ﴿They say﴾, that is, within themselves, and when some of them are alone with others; this is a substitute for "they conceal," or a resumptive clause explaining it. ﴿If we had any say in the matter at all﴾, as Muhammad promised, or claimed that the whole matter belongs to Allah and His allies; or: if we had choice and management and had not gone out, as Ibn Ubayy and others did.

﴿We would not have been killed here, had we had a say.﴾ Or: had we had a say, we would not have been defeated; or: had we had a say, those of us killed in this battle would not have been killed. ﴿Say: Even if you had been in your houses, those for whom killing had been decreed would have gone forth to their resting places﴾: that is, those for whom Allah had decreed killing and recorded it in the Preserved Tablet would have gone out to their places of death, and residing in Medina would not have benefited them, and none of them would have escaped; for He had determined and arranged affairs in His prior decree, and there is no one to repel His judgment. ﴿And that Allah might test what is in your breasts﴾: and that Allah might examine what is in your breasts and make manifest their secrets of sincerity and hypocrisy. This is the reason for an omitted verb, meaning: and He did that in order to test; or it is conjoined to an omitted element, meaning: it went forth because of the execution of the decree, or for many benefits and for the sake of trial; or it is conjoined to "so that you would not grieve." ﴿And that He might purify what is in your hearts﴾: that He might uncover and distinguish it, or cleanse it of whisperings.

﴿And Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾: of its hidden matters before they are made manifest. In this is a promise and a warning, and an admonition that He is free from need of trial; He did this only to train the believers and to display the state of the hypocrites.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 155:

﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met, it was only Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned.﴾ That is: indeed, those who fled on the day of Uhud, the cause of their flight was only that Satan sought from them a slip, so they obeyed him and committed sins by opposing the Prophet (ﷺ) through abandoning the post, and through greed for the spoils or for life. So they were denied support (ta'yid) and strength of heart. It has also been said that Satan's causing them to slip was their turning away, and that this was due to sins they had committed earlier, for sins drag one another along, just as obedience does. It has also been said that he made them slip by reminding them of sins that had passed from them, so they disliked fighting before sincerely repenting and leaving the injustice (mazhalah). ﴿And certainly Allah has pardoned them﴾ for their repentance and their apology. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ of sins ﴿Forbearing﴾, not hastening to punish the sin, so that they may repent.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 156:

﴿O you who have believed, do not be like those who disbelieved﴾, meaning the hypocrites. ﴿and said of their brothers﴾, i.e., concerning them and about them, (p-45)

The meaning of "their brothers" is their sharing in lineage or in creed. ﴿when they traveled through the land﴾, i.e., when they journeyed in it and went far away for trade or other purposes. Its (grammatical) original form, given the verb "said," should have been "those who said," but it came in the manner of relating a past state. ﴿or were raiders﴾, the plural of ghazin (raider), like ʿafin and ʿuffan (pardoning). ﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed﴾. This is the object of "said," and it indicates that their brothers were not the ones addressed by it.

﴿So that Allah may make that a regret in their hearts﴾. It is connected to "said," with the lam being the lam of consequence (lam al-ʿaqibah), like it in ﴿so that it would become for them an enemy and a grief﴾. Or (it is connected to) "do not be," i.e., do not be like them in uttering that statement and holding that belief, so that Allah may make it a regret in their hearts specifically. Thus "that" refers to what their statement indicated of belief. It has been said that it refers to what the prohibition indicated, i.e., do not be like them, so that Allah may make your not being like them a regret in their hearts, for opposing and contradicting them is something that distresses them. ﴿And Allah gives life and causes death﴾, as a refutation of their statement, i.e., He is the one who determines life and death, not residence and travel, for He, exalted is He, may give life to the traveler and the raider and cause death to the resident and the one who sits at home. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, a warning to the believers against becoming like them. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the letter ya' (yaʿmalūna, "they do"), on the basis that it is a threat to those who disbelieved.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 157–158:

﴿And if you are slain in the way of Allah, or you die﴾: i.e., you die in His way. Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read the mim with kasra, from māta yamūtu (to die).

﴿Surely forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they amass﴾: this is the response of the oath, and it takes the place of the conditional response. The meaning: travel and military campaign are not among the things that bring about death or hasten the appointed term; and even if that occurs in the way of Allah, then what you attain of forgiveness and mercy through death is better than what you amass of the world and its benefits had you not died. Hafs read it with the ya' (yajma'un, "they amass").

﴿And if you die or are slain﴾: i.e., in whatever manner your destruction occurs.

﴿Surely unto Allah you will be gathered﴾: surely unto your Deity toward whom you have turned, and for whose sake you have expended your lives, not unto anything else; without doubt you will be gathered, whereupon He will fully repay your recompense and magnify your reward. Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read mutimm with kasra.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 159:

﴿So it was by a mercy from Allah that you were gentle with them.﴾ That is, "so by mercy" (fa-bi-rahmatin). The particle "ma" is extra (zā'idah), for emphasis, alertness, and to indicate that his gentleness toward them was nothing but by a mercy from Allah, namely His steadying of his heart and His granting him success in being kind to them, to the point that he grieved for them after they had opposed him. ﴿And had you been harsh⁠—hard-hearted⁠—﴾ ill-tempered (sayyi' al-khuluq) and coarse (jafiyyan). ﴿Harsh of heart⁠﴾ hardened (qāsiyah). ﴿They would have dispersed from around you﴾ they would have scattered away from you and would not have settled near you. ﴿So pardon them﴾ in matters that concern you personally. ﴿And ask forgiveness for them﴾ in matters that concern Allah. ﴿And consult them in the affair﴾ that is, in the affair of war, since the discussion is about it; or in whatever it is correct to consult them about, seeking their opinion for support, soothing their hearts, and paving the way for the practice of consultation (mushawarah) within the community. ﴿And when you have resolved﴾ when you have determined yourself upon something after consultation. ﴿Then rely upon Allah﴾ in carrying out your affair in the way that is most right for you, for none knows it but Him. It was also read as "fa-idha 'azamtu" (in the first person), meaning: when I have resolved for you upon something and specified it for you, then rely upon Allah and do not consult anyone about it. ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him﴾ so He will give them victory and guide them to what is good.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 160:

﴿If Allah helps you﴾, like He helped you on the Day of Badr. ﴿then none can overcome you﴾, meaning none will be able to overcome you. ﴿And if He forsakes you﴾, like He forsook you on the Day of Uhud. ﴿then who is there that can help you after Him?﴾ After His forsaking you, or after Allah, meaning: if you go beyond Him, then there is no helper for you. This is a reminder of what necessitates reliance (tawakkul, trust in God) and an exhortation to what deserves help from Allah, and a warning against what draws down His forsaking. ﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾, so let them single Him out for reliance, because they know that there is no helper for them besides Him and they believe in Him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 161:

﴿It is not for a Prophet to deceive (yaghull)﴾ — meaning: it is not proper (ma sahha) for a Prophet to betray (yakhun) in the matter of the spoils (ghanaim), for prophethood is incompatible with betrayal. It is said: "ghalla shay'an min al-maghnam, yaghullu ghululan" and "aghalla, ighlalan," when one takes it secretly (fi khufyah). What is intended by this is either:

The exoneration of the Messenger, peace be upon him, from what he was accused of, for it is reported that a red woollen cloak (qatifah hamra') was lost on the day of Badr, and some of the hypocrites said: "Perhaps the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took it." Or, the archers (al-rumat) on the day of Uhud suspected him when they left their position for the spoils, saying: "We fear that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ will say: whoever takes anything, it is his, and he will not distribute the spoils."

Or, it is an emphasis in the prohibition addressed to the Messenger ﷺ, according to what is reported: he dispatched advance units (talai'), and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ acquired spoils and distributed them among those with him, and did not give a share to the advance units, so this verse was revealed.

Thus, calling the deprivation of some of those entitled (al-mustahiqqin) to their share "ghulul" is a second intensification and emphasis.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read ﴿an yughalla﴾ in the passive voice (al-bina' lil-maf'ul), and the meaning is: it is not proper for him to be found as one who betrays, or to be attributed with betrayal (al-ghulul).

﴿And whoever betrays will come on the Day of Resurrection bearing what he betrayed﴾ — he will bring that which he betrayed, carrying it upon his neck, as has come in the hadith. Or, with what he bore of its burden (wabal) and sin (ithm).

﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾ — meaning, it will be given the full recompense of what it earned. The fitting expression given what preceded would have been "then what it earned will be paid in full," but He generalized the ruling so that it would serve as a proof of the intended meaning and an emphasis upon it, for when every earner is recompensed for his deed, then the betrayer, with the enormity of his crime, is all the more deserving of this.

﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ — so the reward of the obedient among them will not be diminished, and the punishment of the disobedient among them will not be increased.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 162–163:

﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah﴾ by obedience. ﴿like one who returns﴾ goes back ﴿with wrath from Allah﴾ because of sins. ﴿And his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾. The difference between the destination (maṣīr) and the return (marji') is that the destination must differ from the former state, whereas the return need not.

﴿They are degrees with Allah﴾: they have been likened to degrees because of the differences among them in reward and punishment, or they are people of degrees. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾: He is Knowing of their deeds and their degrees, which proceed from them, so He will recompense them according to them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 164:

﴿Indeed, Allah has conferred a favour upon the believers﴾ He bestowed His blessing upon those among their people who believed together with the Messenger ﷺ. He singled them out, although the blessing of the sending of the Prophet is general, in order to increase the benefit they derive from it. It was also read as «liman manna Allahu» (for whoever Allah has favoured), being the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "such as His favour" or "such as His sending."

﴿when He raised among them a Messenger from themselves﴾ from their lineage, or from their own kind, an Arab like them, so that they might easily understand his speech and be aware of his state in truthfulness and trustworthiness, and take pride in him. It was also read as «min anfasihim» (from their most noble), meaning from their most noble, because he ﷺ (peace be upon him) was from the noblest of the Arab tribes and clans.

﴿reciting to them His verses﴾ that is, the Qur'an, after they had been ignorant and had not heard revelation.

﴿and purifying them﴾ cleansing them from the filth of dispositions and the corruption of belief and deeds.

﴿and teaching them the Book and the Wisdom﴾ that is, the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

﴿and indeed, they had been before in clear error﴾ "inna" here is the light form of the heavy "inna," and the "lam" is the lam that distinguishes it; the meaning is that indeed the matter was that they had been, before the sending of the Messenger ﷺ, in manifest error.

(p-47) ﴿Why is it that when a calamity struck you, although you had inflicted twice as much (on the enemy), you said, "How is this?"﴾ The hamza (alif of interrogation, ʾa) is for rebuke and affirmation (taqrir), and the waw is conjunctive, linking the sentence to what preceded of the story of Uhud, or to an omitted clause such as "Did you do such-and-such and say...?" The lamma (when) is an adverbial clause whose object is the phrase "what struck you," meaning: did you say this when a calamity struck you, namely the killing of seventy of you on the day of Uhud, while the situation was that you had inflicted twice that on the day of Badr, namely the killing of seventy and the capture of seventy? "From where is this to us, when Allah had promised us victory?" ﴿Say: It is from yourselves﴾, that is, from what your own souls had committed of disobeying the command by abandoning the position (markaz), for the promise was conditional upon steadfastness and obedience, or upon your choosing to go out of Madinah.

It is related from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, that it refers to your choosing ransom (fida') on the day of Badr. ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things Competent﴾, so He is able to grant victory and to withhold it, and to afflict you with (a calamity) and to afflict others through you.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 166–167:

﴿And whatever befell you on the day the two hosts met﴾ — the host of the Muslims and the host of the polytheists, meaning the Day of Uhud. ﴿Then it was by the permission of Allah﴾ — it occurred by His decree, or by His leaving the disbelievers free; He called it "permission" because it is among its necessary consequences. ﴿And that He might know the believers﴾

﴿And that He might know those who became hypocrites﴾ — and that the believers and the hypocrites might be distinguished, so that the faith of these and the disbelief of those would become manifest. ﴿And it was said to them﴾ — a conjunction with "became hypocrites," falling within the relative clause (ṣilah), or an independent statement. ﴿"Come, fight in the way of Allah, or repel [the enemy]"﴾ — a division of the command directed at them and a choice between fighting for the sake of the Hereafter or for the defence of selves and property. It is also said that its meaning is: fight the disbelievers, or repel them by increasing the number of the striving fighters, for the multitude of numbers is something that terrifies the enemy and breaks them. ﴿They said, "If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly follow you."﴾ — if we knew what could rightly be called fighting, we would have followed you in it; but what you are upon is not fighting, rather a casting of oneself into destruction. Or: if we were skilled in fighting, we would have followed you in it. They said this only as deceit and mockery. ﴿They were that day nearer to disbelief than to faith﴾ — because of their forsaking [the army] and this statement of theirs, for these were the first signs that appeared from them, indicating their disbelief. It is also said: they were nearer to the people of disbelief in support than to the people of faith, since their forsaking and their words strengthened the polytheists and discouraged the believers. ﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾ — they show the opposite of what they conceal; their hearts do not agree with their tongues in faith. The attribution of the saying to the mouths is an emphasis and a depiction. ﴿And Allah is most knowing of what they conceal﴾ — of hypocrisy. And whatever some of them confide to others, He knows it in detail with a knowledge that is obligatory; whereas you know it only in summary, through signs.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 166–167:

﴿And whatever befell you on the day the two hosts met﴾ — the host of the Muslims and the host of the polytheists, meaning the Day of Uhud. ﴿Then it was by the permission of Allah﴾ — it occurred by His decree, or by His leaving the disbelievers free; He called it "permission" because it is among its necessary consequences. ﴿And that He might know the believers﴾

﴿And that He might know those who became hypocrites﴾ — and that the believers and the hypocrites might be distinguished, so that the faith of these and the disbelief of those would become manifest. ﴿And it was said to them﴾ — a conjunction with "became hypocrites," falling within the relative clause (ṣilah), or an independent statement. ﴿"Come, fight in the way of Allah, or repel [the enemy]"﴾ — a division of the command directed at them and a choice between fighting for the sake of the Hereafter or for the defence of selves and property. It is also said that its meaning is: fight the disbelievers, or repel them by increasing the number of the striving fighters, for the multitude of numbers is something that terrifies the enemy and breaks them. ﴿They said, "If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly follow you."﴾ — if we knew what could rightly be called fighting, we would have followed you in it; but what you are upon is not fighting, rather a casting of oneself into destruction. Or: if we were skilled in fighting, we would have followed you in it. They said this only as deceit and mockery. ﴿They were that day nearer to disbelief than to faith﴾ — because of their forsaking [the army] and this statement of theirs, for these were the first signs that appeared from them, indicating their disbelief. It is also said: they were nearer to the people of disbelief in support than to the people of faith, since their forsaking and their words strengthened the polytheists and discouraged the believers. ﴿They say with their mouths what is not in their hearts﴾ — they show the opposite of what they conceal; their hearts do not agree with their tongues in faith. The attribution of the saying to the mouths is an emphasis and a depiction. ﴿And Allah is most knowing of what they conceal﴾ — of hypocrisy. And whatever some of them confide to others, He knows it in detail with a knowledge that is obligatory; whereas you know it only in summary, through signs.

﴿Those who said﴾ is in the nominative as a substitution (badal, apposition) for the waw of ﴿they conceal﴾. It may also be in the accusative (naṣb) as a vituperative (dhamm) or descriptive (waṣf) qualifier of ﴿those who were hypocrites﴾, or in the genitive (jarr) as an apposition for the pronoun in ﴿in their mouths﴾ or ﴿in their hearts﴾, as in the poet's saying:

"In a state where, even if Ḥātim were among the people, Ḥātim, despite his generosity, would withhold water."

﴿for their brothers﴾ means for their sake. It refers to those among their relatives or their kind who were killed on the day of Uhud. ﴿And sat back﴾ is a anticipated circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara), with qad implied, meaning: they said while having stayed back from fighting. ﴿If they had obeyed us﴾ refers to staying seated in Madina. ﴿They would not have been killed﴾ as we were not killed. Hisham read qutṭṭilū with the letter tā' doubled (intensive form).

﴿Say: "Then avert death from yourselves, if you are truthful."﴾ That is, if you are truthful in claiming that you are able to ward off killing from one whom it has been decreed for. So avert death from yourselves and its causes, for that is more fitting for you. The meaning is that sitting back does not protect against death, since the causes of death are many, just as fighting may be a cause of destruction and sitting back a cause of safety; the matter may in fact be the reverse.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 169:

﴿And do not think of those who have been killed in the way of God as dead.﴾ It was revealed concerning the martyrs of Uhud. It is also said that it concerns the martyrs of Badr. The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone. It is also read with the yaʾ (تَحْسَبَنَّ read as يَحْسَبَنَّ), by attributing it to the pronoun of the Messenger, or to whoever is doing the thinking, or to those who were killed. The first object is omitted, because in origin it is a subject (mubtada') whose deletion is permissible when there is an indicator (qarina). Ibn ʿAmir read qutThilu with the doubled letter (qattilu, tashdid), because of the large number of those killed. ﴿Rather, they are alive⦆ i.e., rather, they are alive. It is also read in the accusative (بَلْ أحْياءً, nasb), with the meaning: rather, I consider them to be alive. ﴿With their Lord﴾ they are those possessing nearness to Him. ﴿They are provided for﴾ from the Garden, and this is an emphasis on their being alive.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 170–171:

﴿Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾, namely the honour of martyrdom, the success of eternal life, nearness to Allah Most High, and enjoyment of the bliss of Paradise. ﴿And they rejoice﴾ means they are gladdened by good news. ﴿About those who have not yet joined them﴾, i.e., about their fellow believers who have not been killed and so have not joined them. ﴿Who are left behind them﴾, i.e., those who come after them in time or in rank. ﴿That no fear will befall them, nor will they grieve﴾ is a substitution for "those," and the meaning is: they rejoice in what has become clear to them of the matter of the Hereafter, and in the state of the believers they left behind, namely that when they die or are killed they are alive with a life that is not troubled by fear of something dreaded or grief over the loss of something loved. The verse indicates that the human being is other than the perceptible body, but rather is an essence that perceives by itself, which does not perish when the body is ruined, and whose perception, pain and pleasure do not depend on it. This is supported by the Most High's words concerning the people of Pharaoh, ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it﴾, and the verse, and by what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "The souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds that graze in the rivers of Paradise, eat of its fruits, and take shelter in lamps suspended in the shade of the Throne."

Whoever denies this and holds that the soul is nothing but wind and an accident says: they are alive on the Day of Resurrection, and they are described as living now only because its occurrence is certain and near, or they are alive through remembrance or through faith. The verse contains an exhortation to jihad, an encouragement toward martyrdom, an incitement to increase in obedience, praise for one who wishes his brothers the same blessing he has received, and good news to the believers of success.

﴿They rejoice﴾ is repeated for emphasis and so that what explains His saying ﴿That no fear will befall them﴾ may depend on it. It is possible that the first refers to the state of their brothers, and this to the state of themselves. ﴿With a blessing from Allah﴾, as a reward for their deeds. ﴿And a bounty﴾, an increase upon it, as in His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward and more﴾. The indefiniteness of both is for magnification. ﴿And that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾ is part of what they are gladdened by, and it is conjoined to "bounty." Al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra, as a parenthetical resumed statement indicating that this is a reward for them for their faith, and implying that whoever has no faith, his deeds are nullified and his rewards wasted.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 172:**

﴿Those who responded to God and the Messenger after the wound had afflicted them﴾ is a qualifier (ṣifah) of "the believers," or it is in the accusative of praise (naṣb ʿalā al-madḥ), or it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿For those among them who did good and were mindful of God, there is a great reward﴾ with its whole clause. The min in "minhum" is for explanation (li-l-bayān). The purpose of mentioning the two qualities is praise (madḥ) and causal justification (taʿlīl), not restriction (taqyīd), because all those who responded are good-doers and mindful of God.

It is narrated (ruwiya) that "Abu Sufyan and his companions, when they turned back and reached al-Rawha, regretted and resolved to return. This reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so he called his companions to go out in pursuit of them and said: 'None shall go out with us except those who were present with us yesterday.' So he (peace and blessings be upon him) went out with a group until they reached Hamra' al-Asad, which is eight miles from Medina. The companions had been wounded, so they forced themselves on, so that the reward would not escape them. God cast terror into the hearts of the polytheists, so they departed, and then this verse was revealed."

**Qur'an 3:173: "Those to whom the people said"**

﴿Those to whom the people said﴾: meaning the caravan (rakb) that met them from ʿAbd Qays, or Nuʿaym ibn Masʿud al-Ashjaʿi. The word "people" (al-nas) was applied to him because he was of their kind, as one says "So-and-so rides horses, though he has only one horse," because a group of people from Madinah joined him and spread his words. ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you, so fear them﴾: meaning Abu Sufyan and his companions.

It is narrated that when he [Abu Sufyan] was departing from Uhud, he called out: "O Muhammad, our appointment is the season of Badr next year, if you wish." So the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If Allah the Exalted wills." When the following year came, he set out with the people of Makkah until he halted at Marr al-Zahran. Then Allah cast terror into his heart, and it occurred to him to return. A caravan from ʿAbd Qays passed by him, heading to Madinah for provisions, and he stipulated for them a camel-load of raisins on condition that they discourage the Muslims.

It is also said: He met Nuʿaym ibn Masʿud, who had come as a pilgrim (muʿtamir), and asked him to do this, and promised him ten camels. Nuʿaym set out and found the Muslims preparing, and said to them: "They came to you in your homes, and not one of you escaped except as a fugitive. Do you think you will go out when they have gathered against you?" So they grew hesitant. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, I will go out even if no one goes out with me." So he went out with seventy riders, and they were saying: "Allah is sufficient for us."

﴿So it increased them in faith (īmān)﴾: the pronoun concealed in the verb (al-ḍamīr al-mustakinn) refers either to the saying (al-maqūl), or to the verbal noun of "said" (qāla), or to its subject (fāʿil), if by it is meant Nuʿaym alone. The overt pronoun (al-ḍamīr al-bāriz) refers to "to them" (lahum). The meaning is: they did not turn towards him, nor did they weaken; rather, their certainty in Allah was established by it, their faith increased, they displayed the zeal of Islam, and they made their intention sincere before Him. This is evidence that faith increases and decreases. Supporting this is the saying of Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both: "We said, O Messenger of Allah, faith increases and decreases. He said: Yes, it increases until it brings its possessor into Paradise, and it decreases until it brings its possessor into the Fire."

This is evident if obedience (ṭāʿa) is counted among faith, and likewise if it is not counted, since certainty increases through familiarity, frequent reflection, and the mutual support of proofs.

﴿And they said: Allah is sufficient for us﴾: muḥsibunā, meaning the one who suffices us and is enough for us, from aḥsabahu, when he sufficed him. That it has the sense of the one who suffices is shown by the fact that it does not gain definiteness through the genitive construction (iḍāfa), in your saying hādhā rajulun ḥasbuka (this is a man sufficient for you).

﴿And excellent is the Guardian (al-Wakīl)﴾: and excellent is the one to whom affairs are entrusted (al-mawkūl ilayhi), He.

﴿So they returned﴾ meaning they came back from Badr. ﴿with a blessing from Allah﴾ meaning well-being, steadfastness in faith, and an increase in it. ﴿and bounty﴾ meaning profit in trade, for when they reached Badr and set up a market there, they traded and made profit. ﴿No harm touched them﴾ meaning no wound and no plot by the enemy.

﴿And they followed the pleasure of Allah﴾, which is the means of attaining success in both abodes, by their courage and their going out. ﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾: He has graciously granted them firmness, an increase in faith, success in hastening to jihad, steadfastness in religion, displaying courage against the enemy, protection from everything that would harm them, and gaining benefit together with the assurance of reward, until they returned with a blessing from Allah and bounty. In this there is a rebuke of the one who stayed behind and a condemnation of his opinion, since he deprived himself of what they attained.

﴿It is only that Satan﴾: by this is meant the one who discouraged them, Nu'aym or Abu Sufyan. "Satan" is the predicate of "that" (dhalikum), and what follows is an explanation of his devilry or his description, and what follows is the predicate. It is also permissible that the reference is to the statement, with an omitted noun in the construction, meaning: "It is only the statement of Satan," that is, Iblis, upon him be the curse. ﴿He frightens his allies﴾: the ones who sat back from going out with the Messenger, or "he frightens you with his allies," who are Abu Sufyan and his companions. ﴿So do not fear them﴾: the pronoun refers to "people" on the first reading and to "allies" on the second. ﴿But fear Me﴾ in opposing My command, so fight alongside My Messenger. If ﴿you are believers﴾, for faith requires preferring the fear of Allah, exalted is He, over the fear of people.
