**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 176–177:**

﴿Let not those who hasten to disbelief grieve you.﴾ They fall into it quickly, eagerly. They are the hypocrites among those who stayed behind, or a people who apostatized from Islam. The meaning is: let not the fear that they will harm you and support one another against you grieve you, because of His saying: ﴿Indeed, they will not harm Allah at all.﴾ That is, they will not harm the friends of Allah at all by their hastening into disbelief; they harm only themselves by it. *Shay'an* (at all) may be an object (*maf'ul*) or a verbal noun (*masdar*). Nafi' read *yuhzinka* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *zay* wherever it occurs, except in His saying in al-Anbiya': ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾, where he read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *zay*. The others read it the same way throughout.

﴿Allah wills not to give them a share in the Hereafter﴾, that is, a portion of the reward in the Hereafter. This indicates the persistence of their transgression and their dying in disbelief. The mention of *will* (*iradah*) signals that their disbelief has reached its extreme, to the point that the Most Merciful of the merciful wills that they have no share of His mercy. Their hastening into disbelief is because He, exalted is He, did not will that they should have a share in the Hereafter. ﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾, in addition to being deprived of the reward.

﴿Indeed, those who have bought disbelief in exchange for faith will not harm Allah at all, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ This is a repetition for emphasis (*ta'kid*), or a generalization (*ta'mim*) to all disbelievers after the specification of those hypocrites among those who stayed behind, or those from among the Arabs who apostatized.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 178:

﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our giving them respite is good for them (lanfusihim)﴾ This is an address to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone who supposes. Alladhina (those who) is the object (maf'ul), and annama numli lahum (that Our giving them respite) is a substitute (badal) for it. He limited himself to one object because the reliance is on the substitute, which takes the place of the two objects, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do you suppose that most of them hear?﴾ Or the second object is with an elided noun (mudaf) in the sense of: "And let not those who disbelieve" (be taken as) companions of the belief that respite is good for them; or: "And let not the condition of those who disbelieve" (be supposed to be) that respite is good for them. Ma is verbal (masdariyyah), and its proper form was to be separated in writing, but it came joined in the Imam (the standard codex), so follow it.

And Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it with the ya' (yahsabanna), with alladhina as the subject (fa'il) and anna together with what follows it as the object. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and 'Asim read the sin (sinuhu) with a fatha throughout the Qur'an. Al-imla' (giving respite) means granting delay and prolonging life. It was said: leaving them and their affairs, from amla li-faraslihi (he loosened the rope for his horse), when he let out its tether so that it might graze as it wished.

﴿Indeed, We give them respite only that they may increase in sin﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) stating the cause of the ruling before it, with ma being restrictive (kaffah) and the lam being the lam of intention (lam al-iradah). According to the Mu'tazilah, it is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah). It was read "annama" with a fatha here and with a kasra on the first, and yahsabanna with the ya', in the sense: "And let not those who disbelieve suppose that Our respite to them is for the increase of sin, but rather for repentance and entry into faith." And "annama numli lahum khayrun" is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh). Its meaning: Our respite is good for them if they awaken and make up in it for what they neglected.

﴿And for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ On this reading it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw, meaning: that they may increase in sin, prepared for them is a humiliating punishment.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 179:

﴿It is not for Allah to leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good.﴾ The address is to the general body of the sincere believers and the hypocrites of his time. The meaning is: He will not leave you mixed together, such that your sincere ones cannot be known from your hypocrites, until He distinguishes the hypocrite from the sincere one, either by revelation to His Prophet concerning your states, or by arduous obligations which none endures or submits to except the pure, sincere ones among you, such as spending wealth and lives in the way of Allah, so that the Prophet may test your inner selves through it and infer from it your beliefs.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿yamiza﴾ here and in al-Anfal with a ḍammah on the yā' (ye), a fatḥah on the mīm and a kasrah on the yā' with shaddah (yumayyiza), while the rest read it with a fatḥah on the yā', a kasrah on the mīm and a sukūn on the yā' (yamiza). ﴿It is not for Allah to inform you of the unseen, but Allah chooses from His messengers whomever He wills.﴾ It is not for Allah to grant any one of you knowledge of the unseen so that he would know what is in the hearts of disbelief and faith; but Allah chooses for His message whomever He wills, so He reveals to him and informs him of some of the hidden matters, or sets up for him what indicates them. ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers.﴾ With the attribute of sincerity; or by knowing Him alone as the One who has knowledge of the unseen, and knowing them as chosen servants who know only what Allah has taught them and say only what has been revealed to them.

It is narrated (that the disbelievers said: "If Muhammad is truthful, let him inform us who among us will believe and who will disbelieve," so this was revealed).

From al-Suddi, that he (peace be upon him) said: "My community was displayed before me and I was informed of who believes in me and who disbelieves." The hypocrites then said: "If he claims that he knows who believes in him and who disbelieves, while we are with him and he does not know us," so this was revealed. ﴿And if you believe﴾ with true belief, ﴿and guard yourselves﴾ against hypocrisy, ﴿then for you is a great reward﴾ whose measure cannot be estimated.

**﴿Let not those who are stingy with what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them﴾.** The readings of this word are as already discussed. Whoever reads it with a *ta'* (the second person) supposes an omitted noun (*mudaf*) so that its two objects agree, meaning: "Do not let the stinginess of those who are stingy think it is good for them." The same applies to whoever reads it with a *ya'* (the third person) if he makes the subject the pronoun of the Messenger (ﷺ), or "one who thinks." If he makes the subject the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*), then the first object is omitted, indicated by "those who are stingy," meaning: "Let not the stingy think their stinginess is good for them."

**﴿Rather, it is bad for them﴾**, that is, stinginess is bad for them, **﴿because it brings punishment upon them﴾**.

**﴿They will have it hung around their necks on the Day of Resurrection, what they were stingy with﴾**: this explains the previous statement. The meaning is that they will be bound by the consequence of what they withheld, as a collar is fastened around the neck. It is narrated from him (ﷺ), upon whom be peace and blessings: "There is no man who does not pay the zakat of his wealth except that Allah will make it a serpent around his neck on the Day of Resurrection."

**﴿To Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾**: to Him belongs whatever is in them of what is inherited. So why do these people withhold their wealth from Him and not spend it in His way? Or, He will inherit from them what they hoard and do not spend in His way, by their destruction, and regret and punishment will remain upon them.

**﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾**, of withholding and giving, **﴿Acquainted﴾**, so He will recompense them. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a *ta'*, by way of *iltifat* (a shift from the third person to the second person), and this is more emphatic in warning.

The Lord has certainly heard the saying of those who said: "Surely Allah is poor, and we are rich." (3:181) It was said by the Jews when they heard: "Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan?"

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote, with Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), to the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa, inviting them to Islam, to establishing the prayer, to giving the zakat, and to lending Allah a goodly loan. Finhas ibn Azura said: "Surely Allah is poor, to the point that He asks for a loan." Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) struck him on his face and said: "Were it not for the covenant between us, I would strike your neck." He complained of him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but Finhas denied what he had said, and so this verse was revealed.

The meaning is that nothing is hidden from Him, and that He has prepared for them punishment (p-52) for it. "We shall record what they have said, and their killing of the prophets without right." (3:181) That is: We shall write it down in the scrolls of the scribes, or We shall preserve it in Our knowledge and not neglect it, because it is a grave utterance, being disbelief in Allah, mighty and majestic, and mockery of the Qur'an and the Messenger. For this reason it is placed alongside the killing of the prophets. In this there is an alert that it is not the first crime they have committed, and that whoever has dared to kill the prophets should not be considered unlikely to utter such a saying.

Hamza read "sa-yuktabu" with ya' and with a damma on it, a fatha on the ta', "qatlahum" in the nominative, and "yaqulu" with ya'. "And We shall say: Taste the punishment of the burning." (3:181) That is: We shall take vengeance upon them by saying to them: "Taste the burning punishment," and in this there are intensifications of the threat. Dhawq (tasting, i.e., perceiving by the palate) is the perception of flavours; in an extended sense it is used for the perception of all sensible things and states. It is mentioned here because the punishment is connected to their saying, which arose from stinginess and excessive attachment to wealth. Most of man's need for wealth is for obtaining food, and most of his stinginess with it is out of fear of losing it. For this reason the mention of eating is frequent alongside wealth.

"That" refers to the punishment. "For what your hands have sent forth" (3:182) refers to the killing of the prophets, this saying of theirs, and their other disobediences. "Hands" is used to mean the selves, because most of their deeds are done by them. "And that Allah is not a wrongdoer to the servants." (3:182) This is conjoined to "what your hands have sent forth," and its causal link to the punishment is that the negation of injustice necessarily implies justice, which requires rewarding the doer of good and punishing the doer of evil.

ﷺ

﴿Those who said﴾ were Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik, Huyayy, Finhas and Wahb ibn Yahudha. ﴿Indeed, Allah has taken a covenant from us﴾ — He commanded us and enjoined us in the Torah. ﴿That we should not believe in any messenger until he brings us an offering which fire devours﴾ — meaning: that we should not believe in any messenger until he brings us this particular miracle which was given to the prophets of the Children of Israel, namely that he offers a sacrifice, then a prophet stands and supplicates, and a heavenly fire descends and consumes it, i.e. transforms it into its own nature by burning. This is among their fabrications and falsehoods, for the consumption of the offering by fire only necessitated belief because it was a miracle, so it and all other miracles are equal in that regard. ﴿Say: Messengers before me have certainly come to you with clear proofs and with what you speak of; so why did you kill them, if you are truthful?﴾ This is a denial and a reproach: messengers came to them before him, such as Zechariah and John, with other miracles that necessitate assent, and with what they proposed, yet they killed them. So if the thing that necessitates assent were the coming of the offering, and their hesitation and refusal to believe were for its sake, then what is wrong with them that they did not believe in the one who came with other miracles, and dared to kill him?

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 184:

﴿If they deny you, then indeed messengers before you were denied, who came with clear proofs, and the Psalms, and the Book giving light.﴾ This is a consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding the denial of his people and of the Jews. "Zubur" is the plural of "zabur," which is the book restricted to rulings, from "zabartu al-shay'" meaning "I restrained it" (i.e., the root carries the sense of restraining and binding). "Kitab," in the usage of the Qur'an, refers to that which contains the laws (shara'i') and rulings (ahkam); for this reason "the Book and the Wisdom" appear joined together in most of the Qur'an. It has been said that "al-zubur" means admonitions and deterrents, from "zabartuhu" meaning "I rebuked him." Ibn 'Amir read ﴿wa-bil-zuburi﴾ and Hisham read ﴿wa-bil-kitabi﴾ with the preposition repeated, to indicate that these are distinct from the "clear proofs" in essence.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 3, verse 185:

﴿Every soul shall taste death.﴾ This is both a promise and a warning, for the one who affirms the truth and for the one who denies it. It was also recited (qira'a, a canonical variant reading) as *dha'iqatan al-mawt* with the accusative case, with and without tanwin (nunation), like His saying: ﴿nor those who remember God except a little﴾. ﴿You will only be paid your wages in full﴾, meaning you will be given the recompense of your deeds, good or bad, complete and full, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, the day of your rising from the graves. The wording "paid in full" suggests that some of the wages may come before it, and this is supported by the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: "The grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of the Fire."

﴿Whoever is distanced from the Fire﴾ is removed (*bu'ida*) from it. *Zahzahah* originally means repeated *zahh*, which is pulling with haste. ﴿And is admitted to Paradise, he has indeed triumphed﴾, through salvation and the attainment of what is desired. *Fawz* is the winning of the objective.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever loves to be distanced from the Fire and to enter Paradise, let his death come upon him while he believes in God and the Last Day, and let him treat people with what he loves to be treated with."

﴿And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion﴾, meaning its pleasures and adornments. He likened it to goods that are disguised to deceive the buyer and mislead him until he purchases them. This applies to the one who prefers it over the Hereafter. As for the one who seeks the Hereafter through it, it is for him a provision for reaching the goal. *Ghurur* (delusion) is either a verbal noun or the plural of *ghar* (one who deceives).

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 186:**

﴿You will surely be tested﴾, i.e., by Allah, you will surely be tested. ﴿in your possessions﴾ by the imposition of spending and by what befalls them of calamities. ﴿and in yourselves﴾ by jihad, killing, captivity and wounds, and what is inflicted upon them of fears, illnesses and hardships. ﴿And you will surely hear from those who were given the Book before you and from those who associate others with Allah much hurt﴾, from the satire of the Messenger (ﷺ), the disparagement of the religion, and the incitement of the disbelievers against the Muslims. He informed them of this before it occurred, so that they would prepare their souls for patience and endurance, and get ready to meet it, so that its descent would not overwhelm them. ﴿And if you are patient﴾ over that. ﴿and are mindful of Allah﴾, i.e., avoid opposing the command of Allah. ﴿Indeed, that﴾, meaning patience and god-consciousness (taqwa), ﴿is of the determined matters﴾, i.e., among the matters that must be resolved upon, or of what Allah has resolved upon, meaning He has commanded it and emphasized it.

Al-'azm (determination, resolve) in its basic sense is the firmness of one's judgment upon a thing so as to carry it out.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 187:

﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture﴾: i.e., remember the time when He took it. ﴿The covenant of those who were given the Scripture﴾: by this he means the scholars (ʿulamaʾ). ﴿You shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾: a report of the address made to them. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and ʿAsim, in the transmission of Ibn ʿAyyash, read it with the yaʾ (ya-tubayyinūnahu, "they shall make it clear"), since they are in the third person (ghuyyab). The lam is the answer to the oath (qasam), which is implied by his saying: "Allah took the covenant of those who..." and the pronoun refers to the Scripture (al-Kitab). ﴿But they cast it behind their backs﴾: i.e., the covenant; they did not heed it and paid it no attention. Casting something behind the back is a proverb for neglecting it, not giving it regard and not attending to it; its opposite is placing it before one's eyes and setting it between one's eyes. ﴿And sold it for a small price﴾: i.e., they took in exchange for it (badalahu) ﴿a small price﴾ of the debris (hutam) of this world and its goods (aʿrad).

﴿Wretched is what they bartered﴾: what they chose for themselves. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever conceals his knowledge from its people, he will be bridled with a bridle of fire."

And from ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him): "Allah did not take a covenant from the people of ignorance that they should learn, until He took a covenant from the people of knowledge that they should teach."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 188:

﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they have not done, do not think them safe from the punishment.﴾ The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ). Whoever reads the *bāʾ* (الباءَ) with a *ḍamma* makes the address to him and to the believers. The first object is *alladhīna yafrahūna* (الَّذِينَ يَفْرَحُونَ), and the second is *bi-mafāzatin* (بِمَفازَةٍ). His words *fa-lā tahsabannahum* (فَلا تَحْسَبَنَّهم) are an emphasis. The meaning is: Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done of deception (*tadlīs*) and concealing the truth, and love to be praised for what they have not done of fulfilling the covenant, manifesting the truth and telling the truth, are *bi-mafāzatin*, meaning *bi-manjātin* (by a deliverance) from the punishment; that is, they are triumphant (*fāʾizīna*) by being saved from it. Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read *yaḥsabanna* (يَحْسَبَنَّ) with the *yāʾ* (بِالياءِ) and a *fatḥa* on the *bāʾ* (وفَتْحِ الباءِ) in the first instance and a *ḍamma* on it in the second. On this reading, *alladhīna* is the subject, and the two objects of *yaḥsabanna* are omitted, indicated by the two objects of its emphatic form. It is as if it were said: "And let not those who rejoice in what they have done suppose, so let them not suppose themselves to be *bi-mafāzatin*." Alternatively, the first object is omitted, and his words *fa-lā tahsabannahum* are an emphasis on the verb together with its subject and its first object. ﴿And theirs is a painful punishment﴾, for their disbelief and their deception.

It is narrated that he (ﷺ) asked the Jews about something from what is in the Torah, and they informed him of something contrary to what was in it, and they showed him that they had told him the truth and rejoiced in what they had done, and so this was revealed. (p-54)

It was also said: It was revealed concerning a people who stayed behind from the expedition and then offered excuses, claiming that they saw the benefit in staying behind and sought praise for it. It was also said: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, for they rejoice in their hypocrisy and seek praise from the Muslims for a faith which they did not truly hold.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 189–190:

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, so He governs their affairs. ﴿And Allah is over all things Competent﴾, so He is able to punish them.

It was said that this is a rebuttal of their saying that Allah is poor. ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding﴾: clear proofs of the existence of the Creator, His oneness, and the perfection of His knowledge and power, for those with polished intellects, pure of the impurities of sense and imagination, as has passed in Surat al-Baqarah. Perhaps the restriction to these three in this verse is because the basis of inference is change, and these [three] are examples covering all its kinds: for it is either in the essence of a thing, like the change of night and day; or in its part, like the change of the elements through the alteration of their forms; or in something external to it, like the change of the celestial spheres through the alteration of their positions.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Woe to whoever recites it and does not reflect upon it."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 191:

﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ That is, they remember Him constantly in all conditions, standing, sitting, and lying down. It is also related from him, upon him be prayers and peace: "Whoever loves to frolic in the gardens of Paradise, let him increase remembrance of Allah."

It has also been said that its meaning is: they pray in the three postures according to their ability, based on his saying, upon him be prayers and peace, to Imran ibn Husayn: "Pray standing; if you cannot, then sitting; if you cannot, then on your side, signaling with a gesture."

This is evidence for al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, that the sick person prays lying on his right side, facing with the front of his body (the qibla). ﴿And they reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, deriving evidence and taking lessons. It is the best of acts of worship, as he, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "There is no worship like reflection," because it is specific to the heart and is the purpose of creation. It is also related from him, upon him be prayers and peace: "While a man was lying on his bed, he raised his head, looked at the sky and the stars, and said: 'I testify that You are a Lord and Creator. O Allah, forgive me.' So Allah looked at him and forgave him."

This is a clear indication of the nobility of the science of usul (the principles of jurisprudence) and the virtue of its people. ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾, with the verb of saying understood: that is, they reflect saying this. "This" refers to the object of reflection, namely the creation; it is taken to mean the created things of the heavens and the earth, or it refers to the two, since they carry the sense of the created. The meaning is: "I did not create it in vain, aimlessly, without wisdom, but I created it for great wisdoms, among which is that it is a source for the existence of man, a means for his sustenance, and a sign guiding him to Your knowledge, urging him to obey You, so that he may attain eternal life and everlasting happiness in Your neighborhood." ﴿Glory be to You﴾, declaring You far above futility and the creation of vanity; this is a parenthetical phrase. ﴿So protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, because of neglecting to reflect on it and to act according to what it requires. The function of the fa' (so) is to indicate that their knowledge of the purpose for which the heavens and the earth were created led them to seek refuge.

﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit into the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾, to the utmost degree of disgrace. This is like their saying: "Whoever reaches the pasture of security has indeed reached [it]." The purpose is to magnify the thing from which refuge is sought, drawing attention to the intensity of their fear and their seeking protection from it. It also implies that spiritual punishment is more dreadful. ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾. By "the wrongdoers" he means those who are admitted [into the Fire], and the explicit noun (al-muẓhar) was placed in the position of the pronoun (al-muḍmar) to indicate (p-55)

that their wrongdoing is the cause of their being admitted into the Fire and of the cutting off of help for them in being delivered from it. Negating help does not necessitate negating intercession, because help is repelling by force.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 193:

﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith﴾ He made the verb govern the hearing (al-masma') and omitted the thing heard (al-masmu') because its description indicates it. In this there is an intensification (mubalaghah) not present in making the verb govern the thing heard itself. Also, in indefinitely expressing the caller (tankir al-munadi), leaving him unrestricted (itlaq), and then restricting him (taqyid), there is a glorification of his status. What is meant by him is the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, though it has been said it is the Qur'an. Calling (al-nida'), supplicating (al-du'a') and similar verbs are followed by ila (to) and al-lam (for), because they include the meaning of reaching a destination (al-intiha') and specification (al-ikhtisas).

﴿That believe in your Lord, so we believed﴾ That is, "to the effect that: believe," so we complied (fa-amtathalna).

﴿Our Lord, so forgive us our sins﴾ meaning our major sins (kaba'ir), for they carry consequence (dhat tab'ah).

﴿And remove from us our evil deeds﴾ meaning our minor sins (saghair), for they are disliked (mustaqbahah), but they are expiated (mukaffirah) for one who avoids major sins.

﴿And take us in death with the righteous﴾ specially in their companionship (makhsusina bi-suhbatihim), counted among their group (ma'dudina fi zumratihim). In this there is an indication that they love to meet Allah, and whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him. Al-abrar is the plural of barr or barr, like arbab and ashab.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 194:

﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾, that is, what You promised us of reward for affirming Your messengers. Since he [the believer] has shown his compliance with what he was commanded, he asks for what was promised for it, not out of fear that the promise would be broken, but out of fear that he might not be among those promised [the reward] because of a bad end, or a shortfall in compliance, or [he asks it] as an act of worship and humble submission. It is permissible to attach ʿalā (upon/through) to a deleted element, its estimate being: "what You promised us, sent down upon Your messengers," or "carried upon them." It was also said that its meaning is "upon the tongues of Your messengers." ﴿And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection﴾, by Your protecting us from what would call for it. ﴿Indeed, You do not break the promise﴾, by rewarding the believer and answering the supplicant. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "al-mīʿād" is the resurrection after death.

The repetition of "Our Lord" is for emphasis in supplication and to indicate the independence of the requests and the elevated status of their subject matter.

And in the reports: "Whoever is struck by a matter [of distress] and says five times, 'Our Lord,' Allah will deliver him from what he fears."

﴿So their Lord answered them﴾ by granting their request. The verb *istajāba* is more specific than *ajāba* (to respond), and it takes its object directly or with the preposition *lām*. ﴿That I do not waste the work of any worker among you﴾ means "that I do not waste." It is also read with a *kasra* (*innī*), on the understanding that a verb of saying is implied. ﴿Whether male or female﴾ explains "worker." ﴿You are of one another﴾ is because the male comes from the female and the female from the male, or because they both come from one origin, or because of their close connection and unity, or because of their gathering together and agreement in religion. This is a parenthetical clause (*jumla mu'tarida*), through which he showed that women share with men in what was promised to the workers.

It is narrated that Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "O Messenger of Allah, I hear Allah mention the men in regard to emigration, and I do not hear Him mention the women." So this was revealed. ﴿Those who emigrated﴾ and so on is a detailing of the deeds of the workers and of what has been prepared for them of reward, in the manner of praise and glorification. The meaning is: those who emigrated from polytheism, or from homelands and tribes, for the sake of religion. ﴿And were expelled from their homes and were harmed in My cause﴾ because of their faith in Allah and for His sake. ﴿And fought﴾ the disbelievers. ﴿And were killed﴾ in jihad. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the reverse order, because the *wa* (and) does not necessitate sequence, and the latter is more excellent. Or, because what is meant is that some of them were killed while the rest fought and did not weaken. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read *quttilu* with emphasis, for the sake of multiplicity. ﴿Surely I will remove from them their misdeeds﴾, meaning I will erase them. ﴿And surely I will admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from Allah﴾, meaning I will reward them with that as a reward from Allah, by His bounty. Therefore it is an emphatic infinitive (*ta'kid*). ﴿And with Allah is the best reward﴾ for the acts of obedience, ﴿He is able to do so﴾. (p-56)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verses 196–197:

﴿Let not the moving about of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you.﴾ The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is his community; or it is a strengthening of him in what he was upon, like His saying ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾; or it is addressed to everyone. The prohibition is, in meaning, directed at the one addressed. The "moving about" is attributed to the cause (the disbelievers' activity) as if it were the effect, for emphasis. The meaning is: do not look at the abundance and fortune that the disbelievers enjoy, and do not be deceived by the outward appearance of their expansion in their gains, their trade, and their farms.

It has been narrated: "Some of the believers used to see the polytheists in ease and comfortable living, and they would say: 'The enemies of Allah are, in what we see, in good, while we have perished from hunger and hardship.' So this was revealed."

﴿A little enjoyment﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., that moving about is a little enjoyment, because its duration is short compared with what Allah has prepared for the believers.

He (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The world, in comparison with the Hereafter, is only like one of you dipping his finger into the sea; let him see with what it returns." ﴿Then their refuge is Hell, and what an evil resting-place﴾, i.e., what they have prepared for their own souls.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 198:

﴿But for those who fear their Lord, there are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever; a welcome provision from Allah.﴾ The nuzl (النُّزُلُ) and nazal (النَّزَلُ) are what is prepared for the guest of food, drink and gifts. Abu al-Shi'r al-Dabbi said:

؎ وكُنّا إذا الجَبّارُ بِالجَيْشِ ضافَنا ∗∗∗ جَعَلْنا القَنا والمُرْهِفاتِ لَهُ نَزَلا

"Whenever a tyrant came upon us with his army as a guest, we made the spears and the sharp swords his nuzl."

Its accusative position is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "gardens" (jannāt), and the governing element in it is the adverbial phrase (ẓarf). It is said that it is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid), and the implied sense is: "They are made to alight in them as a nuzl." What is with Allah is better for the righteous than what the wicked enjoy and turn about in, because of its abundance and permanence, while the latter is scant and quickly passes away.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 199:

﴿And among the People of the Book are those who believe in God﴾ It was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam (ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam) and his companions. It is also said that it was revealed concerning forty men from Najran, thirty-two from Abyssinia, and eight from Rome, who had been Christians and then embraced Islam. It is also said that it was revealed concerning Ashama al-Najashi (al-Najashi), when Gabriel informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of his death; so he went out and performed the funeral prayer over him. The hypocrites said, "Look at this man, praying over a Christian foreigner (ʿilj) whom he has never seen!" The lam (lam of emphasis) was attached to the noun (ism) only to separate it from inna (inna) by means of the adverbial phrase.

﴿and what has been revealed to you﴾ — that is, of the Qur'an. ﴿and what has been revealed to them﴾ — that is, of the two Scriptures. ﴿humbling themselves before God﴾ — a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the subject of "believe"; it is in the plural form in consideration of the meaning, not the wording. ﴿They do not sell the signs of God for a small price﴾ — as their rabbis who distort (the Scripture) do.

﴿Those will have their reward with their Lord﴾ — that is, the reward specifically assigned to them and His promise in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾. ﴿Indeed, God is swift in reckoning﴾ — because of His knowledge of the deeds and of the recompense they merit, and His independence from deliberation and precaution. The meaning is that the promised reward arrives swiftly, for swiftness of reckoning entails swiftness of recompense.

**[Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 3, verse 200]**

﴿O you who have believed, be patient﴾ in the difficulties of acts of obedience and in whatever afflictions and hardships befall you. ﴿And endure﴾ and outdo the enemies of God through patience in the hardships of war. The greatest of your enemies is the one you must be patient against: opposing your desires. The specific mention of endurance after the general command to be patient is because of its severity. ﴿And maintain your positions﴾ with your bodies and your horses on the frontiers, watching for the raid, and with your souls in obedience. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Part of maintaining the frontier is waiting for the prayer after the prayer." And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever maintains a frontier post for one day and one night in the way of God, it is equal to the fast of the month of Ramadan and its night prayers. He does not break his fast, and he does not turn away from his prayer except for a need." ﴿And fear God that you may succeed﴾: fear Him by disassociating yourselves from anything other than Him, so that you may attain the utmost success. Or: fear the ugly deeds so that you may succeed by attaining the three ranks, which are arranged in order: patience through the bitterness of acts of obedience, the soul's endurance in abandoning habits, and the secret self's maintaining its post at the threshold of the Truth, to watch for the divine inspirations. These are expressed as the sharia (the outward religious law), the tariqa (the spiritual path), and the haqiqa (the inner reality).

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the chapter of Al Imran will be given security for every verse of it on the bridge of Hell."

And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever recites the chapter in which Al Imran is mentioned on Friday, God and His angels will send blessings upon him until the sun is veiled."

And God knows best.
